A wild horse gallops and yet does not move;
the sun and moon traverse the heavens and yet do not complete their circuits.
All of these are due to the extreme rapidity of birth and extinction.
It cannot be moved. A question is asked:
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
Abandoning impermanent form,
one attains permanent form; feeling,
perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
It is further said:
"That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma.
Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal."
These are the three bodies (trikāya), which are quiescent, non-transmigrating, and immutable.
Why, then, is it now said that they are subject to arising and ceasing and do not abide?
What is the meaning of this?
The commentary states:
This dispute is not merely of today.
Generally, those great virtuous ones who are scholars of the *Nirvāṇa* say:
The three bodies are all eternal, neither arising nor ceasing.
Extensive citations from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Bodhisattva-mūla-karman-avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
and other texts serve as proof that the three bodies are all eternal.
This is largely based on scriptural authority.
There are certain venerable masters who, relying on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts,
explain that the Buddha possesses three bodies and is eternally endowed with these three types.
First is eternal quiescence,
which refers to the Dharmakāya Buddha;
second is unceasing eternity.
This refers to the Sambhogakāya Buddha,
which is eternal in its threefold continuity;
and the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha.
Although each is designated as "permanent," their meanings differ;
for the latter two bodies arise from generative causes,
as stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Because the two bodies— the retribution body and the transformation body—
are produced by causes, all that is created is impermanent;
if they were immutable, [they would not be so].
It should be identical to the Dharmakāya as realized through the cause of illumination (*vidyā-hetu*);
furthermore, it should neither be the aggregates (*skandha*) nor possess the functions of cognition, speech, or movement.
One should infer this by means of these numerous principles.
It is not a state of static permanence;
this is established in detail in works such as the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Furthermore, this is discussed in terms of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature).
Sentient beings erroneously conceptualize that the Buddha comes and goes.
In order to shatter their false attachment that there is a Buddha existing outside the mind who comes and goes,
and to destroy their deluded sentiments, [the Buddha] says this.
This is because it is said that there is neither coming nor going.
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "Welcome, Mañjuśrī."
To come without the characteristic of coming;
to see without the characteristic of seeing— and so forth.
The fact that this *Contemplation Sūtra* speaks of coming and going does not contradict the various Mahāyāna sūtras;
each is based on a particular perspective.
All of this has been excellently explained. It is asked:
The *Dharmapada* states:
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnaprabhāsa, saying:
"Good son, you should now observe these names of the Buddhas: are they existent, or are they non-existent?"
"Is it real? Or is it unreal?
Son of good family, if names exist..."
It is said that when food is given to people, they ought to be fully satiated;
if they were already fully satiated,
then all food and drink would be of no use.
For what reason is it said that one eats?
Because one is immediately satiated and has no further need for food.
According to the meaning of this sutra:
To clarify that the nature of names and words is empty and cannot fully express all phenomena,
[the Buddha] now teaches people to single-mindedly recite the name of the Buddha,
which can eliminate the sins of heavy obstructions.
"To be reborn in the Western Land—
how is this different from saying that eating food satisfies hunger or talking of drink quenches thirst?
The commentary states:
Based on the various subtle and profound Mahāyāna sūtras, it is universally stated that names are provisional and false, lacking any fixed reality;
therefore, a sūtra says: "The nature of letters is detached from letters; there are no letters."
Furthermore, it is said:
"Name and meaning are mutually adventitious;
the bodhisattva should investigate them."
Yet he remained silent and speechless,
sitting serenely in meditation;
thus, Kauṇḍinya had no hope of attaining the Way.
At the time Subhadra realized the fruit, there was only a difference between what was spoken and what was understood;
it is not possible to speak of being satiated by food.
In the end, names possess the power of expression;
yet it is through words that one accords with principle. Because one accords with principle through words, [the ultimate is realized].
The analogy of the finger pointing at the moon arises because the nature of names and words is empty; thus,
the metaphor of abandoning the boat is employed.
The Buddha [taught that] because foolish people are attached to names,
they give rise to delusions— either craving or anger— based upon those names.
They commit various transgressions;
they revile me and praise me;
they give rise to birth and bring about death.
Because those who possess the ten evil karmas fall into the three miserable realms,
he shatters their deluded attachments.
Words and letters are false and illusory;
even if one praises or reviles you, how could they bring honor or disgrace to your body?
If you say that because of praise your body becomes glorious and flourishing, [it is not so].
To slander is to damage your own physical form;
one should likewise say that eating brings satiety while fire consumes the body.
Though one may speak of the flavors of delicacies all day long with the mouth, [the body remains unfulfilled].
Unable to escape the distress of hunger and emptiness,
he spent the entire night speaking by the light of a torch,
yet never saw the calamity of his body being consumed by fire.
Thus, one knows that the substance of names and words is empty;
they are fundamentally without reality.
Yet ordinary beings fail to awaken to this.
Waves of love and hatred arise;
they contend for fame at court and sink into the evil realms.
If one were to say that names are useless because they cannot express the essence of phenomena,
then one should likewise summon water and fire, or command men and women to come;
yet they would each respond to their respective calls.
There is no discrepancy whatsoever.
Thus we know that the trap and the snare are not in vain;
the fish and the rabbit are thereby obtained.
Therefore, the Brahma King was moved to entreat him to turn the wheel of the True Dharma;
the Great Sage, responding to the capacities of beings, widely proclaimed its sublime purport.
Thus, the profound essence of the Tripiṭaka shone brilliantly within the Dragon Palace.
The twelve divisions of the sutras illuminate and manifest upon Vulture Peak;
humans and devas, ordinary beings and sages, all receive these ultimate words;
those in the five realms and the four modes of birth alike follow these bequeathed instructions.
The benefits of hearing, reading, and reciting [the scriptures] are vast and profound.
Even when invoking the Buddha's name to attain rebirth in the Pure Land,
one must not claim that names are merely false and devoid of referential meaning.
Question: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that it is only Bodhisattvas of the third stage who are born in the Pure Land.
What is the intention behind now exhorting ordinary beings, Śrāvakas, and others who have not yet reached the stages (*bhūmi*) to be born [there]?
The commentary states:
The various sūtras and śāstras speak of being born in the Pure Land;
each is based on a particular meaning,
and thus their points of emphasis and omissions differ.
Alternatively, there is the discourse on the meaning of superior and inferior persons.
Since the Pure Land possesses various distinctions such as coarseness and subtlety, excellence and inferiority,
those who attain birth therein likewise possess various grades of superiority and inferiority.
As also stated in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*:
"Only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land;
the three levels of worthies and the ten stages of sages dwell in the land of retributive fruition."
This means that those from the tenth bhūmi downward cannot all be born in the Pure Land.
Because the pure land manifested by the Buddha’s Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is untainted (anāsrava),
it is termed "pure."
The various pure and wondrous lands manifested by the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) from the tenth stage downward are impure;
therefore, they are not called "pure."
Because the eighth consciousness is the consciousness of retribution (*vipāka-vijñāna*),
the land transformed by it is called the land of retribution (*vipāka-kṣetra*).
If one distinguishes [the types of lands] based on the practice of giving, morality, meditation, and the separation from the obstacles to the outflow-free concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*):
One who is able to take birth at will in various pure lands through the power of meditative concentration is a Bodhisattva of the third stage who has attained mastery over concentration. Thus,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Bodhisattvas on the third stage and above are born in the Pure Land.
This occurs when they attain non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*),
thereby severing the afflictions of the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) consisting of the dualistic grasping at persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*).
One realizes the pervasive dharma-realm,
awakens to the gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas,
and attains birth in the pure lands of all Buddhas.
Thus, those from the first bhūmi upward attain birth in the Pure Land;

yet, by means of their original vows and great compassion, they draw in all ordinary and ignorant sentient beings, even those of the lowest grade who have committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds.
However, simply by generating the bodhicitta, one attains rebirth there in its entirety,
as fully explained in the sutras.
One must not rely solely on the statement in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* that rebirth is attained at the third stage (*bhūmi*).
This would imply that even Bodhisattvas of the first and second stages could not be born in the Pure Land;
yet, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna received a prophecy from the Buddha that upon reaching the first stage, he would be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
How could it be that one who has not yet reached the third stage is said to be unable to be born in the Pure Land?
To claim so would contradict this very sutra.
Furthermore, according to the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra*,
a bodhisattva on the first stage attains the "gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas" and beholds the pure lands of a hundred buddhas;
how then can it be said that they cannot be born in a pure land?
Furthermore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states that an ordinary bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind on enlightenment and vows to be born in a pure land will immediately attain rebirth there.
Therefore, one should know that the Yogācāra treatises speak from the perspective of attaining mastery over meditative concentration based on a single characteristic,
thereby transcending hindrances.
Question: Regarding the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, and other such treatises,
there were the great masters Asaṅga and Vasubandhu.
In explaining the various textual meanings of the sūtras and śāstras,
there are four intentions and four types of secret speech.
Regarding those who attain rebirth in the Western Land solely through the power of making vows:
This refers to the intention of another time.
Today, when one is exhorted to cultivate the practices for the Western Paradise,
one attains rebirth therein immediately.
How could this possibly constitute sound reasoning?
From the time of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* until now, more than a hundred years have passed;
all the masters of the Dharma have witnessed this passage in the treatise.
If one does not cultivate the pure karma of the Western Land yet now claims to have attained rebirth there,
would this not contradict the treatises?
The commentary states:
Regarding the statement in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* that one attains rebirth there solely by means of making a vow:
This refers to the intention of a different time (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*). Nevertheless,
the virtuous masters of antiquity all used this passage as scriptural evidence.
This refers to the meaning of "at another time," indicating that birth is not attained immediately;
now, let us examine this passage in detail.
This demonstrates that one attains rebirth [in the Pure Land] precisely upon such realization;
this clarifies the intention of the author of the treatise. Why is this so?
The treatise states that "only by means of making a vow" has the sense of exclusion and retention;
it excludes the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.
One merely grasps at the aspiration for emptiness alone;
there is no further practice.
Thus, one stands isolated with this aspiration.
Therefore it is said: "It is solely by means of making a vow.
If one is born [in that realm] merely by making a vow, this refers to the intention regarding a different time (*kāla-antara-abhiprāya*).
It is not that one is reborn in the Pure Land immediately at the time of making the vow; rather, it occurs after death.
Therefore, it is called "another time" (*kāla-antara*).
At present, recollecting the Buddha with a sincere heart is itself a virtuous action of mental karma;
it is the invocation of the Buddha’s name.
This refers to wholesome conduct of speech.
Joining the palms and prostrating refers to wholesome conduct of body.
By means of these three types of virtuous action,
one can extinguish the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eight billion kalpas; thus,
practice and vows support one another.
One immediately attains rebirth there.
How could this be due to mere aspiration alone?
The Master of the Treatise stated that this occurs solely through the act of making a vow.
This clearly indicates that the two practices are performed concurrently and not at separate times.
Those who are deluded do not carefully examine the meaning of the text;
they vaguely and generally assume they are performed at different times.
If the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is also [an example of] a different time,
for what reason does the treatise not state that "the attainment of rebirth in the Western Land through mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha" is likewise a matter of a different time?

Since it does not state that the text concerning the practice of the sixteen contemplations and the three types of meritorious deeds through mindfulness of the Buddha is a teaching for a different time,
we know that through mindfulness of the Buddha and other practices, one is born in the Western Land.
This is not intended to mean that it is a different time.
Some commentators say that one should practice mindfulness of the Buddha by cultivating the sixteen contemplations and so forth.
This refers precisely to the generation of the vow.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation which states:
although the Master of the Treatise mentions the word "vow," [it implies more].
The "intention" (abhiprāya) also refers to the recollection of the Buddha;
this too is an intention regarding another time.
These are the two interpretations presented here.
It is for the purpose of manifesting benefit,
and for the purpose of manifesting the understanding of the meaning. If it manifests benefit...
By interpreting the text in this way,
you cause immeasurable sentient beings to continue transmigrating through impure lands and to wander through the three miserable realms.
One will not attain rebirth in the Pure Land to escape the cycle of birth and death.
If one seeks to understand the meaning,
one should carefully extract the meaning based upon the words and phrases of the text.
Still fearing that it might not accord with the path of the school,
he interpreted the treatises in a hazy and obscure manner; yet,
through this very approach, he was able to grasp their essential meaning.
How can this be erroneous?
It is like the various points of contention among the schools found in the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* and other such works.
Citing their sacred teachings to establish the definitive purpose,
they have picked out single words and pairs of words.
Since the gains and losses of the various schools have already been established,
how much more so regarding the teachings of the *Sūtra on Contemplation* and other scriptures,
which fully set forth all manner of diverse practices?
Some describe three types of dispersed goodness as the direct cause for the Pure Land;
others speak of the sixteen sublime contemplations.
This constitutes the correct practice for the Western [Pure Land].
How could it be taken as a whole to be a text for making vows?
Furthermore, the reason we know that the Master of Treatises did not intend for the recitation of the Buddha's name to refer to a different time is as follows:
This involves eight points.
First, when a master of the treatises explains a sutra,
it is because the intended meaning of the sutra is inherently difficult to understand.
It is a teaching of profound depth;
when ordinary people read it,
none are able to comprehend or awaken to its meaning.
I have composed this treatise to explain Buddhism so that both the ignorant and the wise may understand it.
This is as taught in such works as the *Amitābha-sūtra*, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, and the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha-upadeśa*.
To recollect Amitābha Buddha and thereby attain birth in the Western Land:
the meaning of these words is clear and evident.
Both the foolish and the wise understand this;
why then would one need a formal treatise to explain what is not understood?
Second, the Bhikṣu Dharmagupta made forty-eight great vows.
To guide and lead sentient beings,
desiring to cause them to be born in the Buddha’s Pure Land—
how could this be interpreted as referring to a different time?
And how do they give rise to great vows to lead and receive sentient beings?
Within those vows:
He then said: "I shall not attain perfect enlightenment if those who recite the Buddha's name do not attain rebirth [in the Pure Land];
I do not say that I shall not attain perfect enlightenment if only those who have made vows do not attain rebirth."
Therefore, one should know that practices such as mindfulness of the Buddha will certainly result in rebirth,
as they are included within the Forty-eight Vows.
It is not a matter of another time;
it is simply that due to the making of vows, one does not attain rebirth immediately.
This is not included among the Forty-eight Vows.
Therefore, this is intended as a statement for another time.
Third, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states that the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, extend their broad and long tongues.
To realize rebirth— how could this mean that realization occurs at another time?
Thus do all Buddhas extend their tongues.
This was originally intended for sentient beings who find it difficult to believe;
lest they think that the merit of reciting the Buddha's name is not sufficient to cause them to be born in the Pure Land upon the exhaustion of this present life.
They all gave rise to doubt and slander,
and did not believe in this sutra;
therefore, [the Buddha] manifested the mark of a tongue that is not false or deceptive.
He uttered the mantra of ultimate truth,
causing sentient beings to behold his form and hear his words so that their doubts might be dispelled and faith born.
He then declared this to be a teaching for a future time, meaning that one would not attain rebirth in the Western Land immediately.
Since one attains birth [in the Pure Land] upon reaching the first bhūmi,
why would sentient beings harbor any doubt?
Would they need the Buddha to extend his tongue as a sign to certify their rebirth in the Western Land?
The *Sūtra of the Fourfold Immeasurability* first exhorts that one should make a vow to be born in that land,
and subsequently teaches the recitation of the Buddha’s name for a period of one to seven days.
It is said that when the Noble Assembly approaches at the time of death, they will come to welcome the practitioner so that they may attain rebirth.
If one says that mindfulness of the Buddha is itself the vow,
it has already been explained previously.
Since it is said that one is made to form a vow,
what further need is there to instruct them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha?
Therefore, we know that the preceding passage refers to a vow.
The subsequent passage concerns practice.
When practice and vows support one another,
one attains birth in the Pure Land.
How could it be permissible to claim that the practice of reciting the Buddha's name is this very vow?
Both the *Wujingtu lun* (Treatise on the Five Pure Lands) and the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) were composed by the same master, Vasubandhu Bodhisattva.

How could it be permissible for Vasubandhu, in composing the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-śāstra*, to state that through mindfulness of the Buddha one attains rebirth in the Western Land without intending it to mean "at another time"?

Yet, when commenting on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, he says that mindfulness of the Buddha and so forth are of the nature of "another time" and do not result in rebirth immediately. How can these two statements be reconciled?
Regarding these two individuals who composed the treatises,
it is permissible that the intentions of the two masters differ;
why must the *She lun* necessarily capture the essential purport of the sūtra?
The *Pure Land Treatise* has become confused regarding the sacred words [of the Buddha].
Moreover, since both treatises were composed by Vasubandhu,
their textual expressions and meanings cannot be contradictory.
Since one seeks the intentions of others through discourse,
it is known that "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) refers to a different time.
The *Six Treatises on the Pure Land* state that there are five gates.
First, the gate of physical action through prostration;
second, the gate of verbal action through mindfulness of the Buddha;
third, the gate of mental action through contemplation.
The fourth is the gate of generating vows;
the fifth is the gate of dedication.
If one practices, that itself constitutes the generation of vows.
What is the difference between the first three types of karmic action and the fourth, the gate of making vows?
If they are one and the same, why this distinction?
There would then be no five gates;
since they are distinct from one another,
we know that the former refers to the gate of practice (saṃskāra-mukha).
The *Awakening of Faith* was composed by Aśvaghoṣa;
its statement that one attains rebirth in the Western Paradise through mindfulness of the Buddha is precisely the gateway of practice.
This is not intended as a "different-time" [teaching].
Therefore, one should know that the intent of the treatises composed by Vasubandhu is likewise the same;
he does not regard such approaches as the gateway of mindfulness of the Buddha and so forth as being of a "different-time" nature.
As stated by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa in the *Awakening of Faith*,
he composed this treatise for the sake of beginner bodhisattvas based on eight causes and conditions.
The seventh contemplation is presented to demonstrate the skillful means of single-minded mindfulness,
so that one may be born before the Buddha and certainly never retreat from the faith.
Furthermore, when sentient beings first study this Dharma and seek to attain right faith,
their minds become timid and inferior.
Because they dwell in this Sahā world,
they fear that they may not always encounter the Buddhas to personally receive their teachings and make offerings;
they dread that their faith might be difficult to bring to fulfillment.
For those whose resolve wavers,
one should know that the Tathāgata possesses supreme skillful means to gather and protect their faith.
That is to say, by means of the causal condition of single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha,
one will, in accordance with one's vows, attain birth in a buddha-land of another direction and constantly behold the Buddha.
They will forever be free from the evil realms. As stated in the sūtras:
"If a person single-mindedly recollects Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss..."
Dedicating the roots of goodness cultivated,
one vows to seek birth in that world and immediately attains rebirth there.
Because one constantly beholds the Buddha, there shall ultimately be no regression;
if one contemplates that Buddha’s *tathatā*-dharmakāya,
one should always diligently practice it.
One will ultimately attain birth [in the Pure Land],
because one abides in right concentration.
Eighth, if one were to say that mindfulness of the Buddha is not for the practitioner, [it would be so].
Are the threefold merit, the sixteen contemplations, and so forth, practice?
Or are they not practice?
If they are practice, [then...]
As stated in the "Contemplation of the Earth," one who performs this contemplation eliminates the offenses of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
Upon casting off this body for the next world, one will certainly be born in a pure Buddha-land;
let the mind be free from doubt and recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
Furthermore, in every moment of thought,
one extinguishes the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas and attains rebirth in the Western Land.
For what reason is it that while the eradication of offenses is the same for both,
that is considered practice while this is not?
If that [state] arises,
does this not arise? If both are non-practitioners, [how can this be so]?
Regarding Queen Vaidehī and her five hundred attendants,
does the Buddha’s teaching that they will be reborn there result from performing these visualizations and so forth,
or do they attain rebirth through other practices?
If these contemplations and so forth were to arise by means of this [unconditioned state],
since this is not a conditioned formation (*saṃskāra*),
how could they possibly arise?
If one cannot give rise to contemplation through such practice,
why did the noble lady request that the Dharma of non-arising be taught?
Did the Tathāgata then preach the Dharma of non-arising for her sake?
Furthermore, if these were all merely gates of aspiration, they should be only one;
why then is it necessary to distinguish them as sixteen contemplations?
Furthermore, this interpretation not only fails to understand the scriptural text,
but also subverts correct view.
To harm oneself and harm others is of no benefit whatsoever, whether toward persons or toward the Dharma.
Question: If it is only the mere making of a vow that constitutes the "intention for another time," how so?
What is meant by "intention for another time"?
Answer: The Buddha [observed] that because the afflictions of sentient beings were blazing intensely,
they transmigrated through birth and death, sinking and wallowing in the sea of suffering.
There is no time of emergence [from suffering].
For this reason, he extols the fourfold adornments of both the primary and secondary rewards in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss,
exhorting all sentient beings to be born in that Pure Land.
Although various classes of sentient beings hear the Buddha-dharma,
their obstructions may be either light or heavy.
Enlightenment has degrees of depth,
which consequently results in distinctions of superiority and inferiority according to the teachings.
There is a class of sentient beings...
Although they have heard the pure teachings,
they slander and revile them; not only will they fail to be born in the Western Land, [but they will also fall into the evil realms].
They themselves will likewise sink into the evil realms;
this is entirely far removed from the Western [Pure Land].
There is a class of sentient beings...
Although they hear the pure teachings and believe them deeply without slandering them,
their minds are entangled by the five desires,
and they take pleasure in dwelling in a defiled land.
Neither making vows nor practicing cultivation—
this person cultivates goodness.
Some are reborn among humans or devas;
others, having committed evil,
sink and wallow in the miserable realms.
For such a person to hope to be reborn in the Western Land would also be far-fetched,
as they lack any intentional aspiration to seek it.
Furthermore, because of slandering and disparaging [it],
the *Qingjing pingdengjue jing* states:
"If there are sentient beings..."
Upon hearing the teachings on the Pure Land,
they hear as if they have not heard,
and instead give rise to slander.
I say that this person has not yet attained liberation;
they have only just emerged from the three evil realms and lack faith and aspiration.
You likewise lack both practice and vows;
therefore, you have not yet attained liberation.
There is a class of sentient beings...
As their karmic conditions from past vows with Amitābha Buddha ripened,
they heard the teachings of the Pure Land school;
with pure hearts, they believed and revered them, and gave rise to great vows of universal salvation.
I aspire to be reborn in the Western Pure Land;
I no longer wish to seek the fruits of reward within the realms of humans or devas.
Although I hold this vow, [it remains as such].
However, this person,
due to the causes and conditions of afflictions,
becomes addicted to and attached to the five desires.
Or again, they may be indolent and negligent,
unable to cultivate the Path because they have encountered evil associates.
They have extensively committed the ten non-virtuous actions;
or perhaps at the time of death they do not encounter virtuous friends;
or their bodies are afflicted by grave illness.
They become deranged and lose their minds;
or for many days they remain disoriented,
unable to understand human speech.
Consequently, my vows have remained empty words;
I have never cultivated pure conduct, and thus,
though I have not been reborn in the Pure Land, [I am here].
This vow is the remote cause of birth; or,
through the superior power of having made the vow,
one will certainly be able to practice later on.
Alternatively, even those who have merely given rise to the aspiration for practice must necessarily possess the intent to cultivate it;
although they may not yet be able to initiate actual practice.
When there is the merit of initiating practice,
for the two aforementioned types of persons,
there is the meaning of being born at a distant time.
Therefore, the sutras record that this person is praised for attaining rebirth in the Western Land.
Fools will then assume that one obtains this result immediately, without needing to cultivate other pure causes.
The Master of Treatises explains this scriptural passage as having the meaning of "another time.
It does not mean that one attains rebirth in the Western Land solely by virtue of making a vow.
Later readers, failing to understand the Treatise,
immediately claim that one cannot attain rebirth there;
this is a profound error.
Furthermore, there is a class of sentient beings whose roots of goodness are profound and whose afflictions are slight;
they encounter superior conditions.
Having heard the pure teachings,
they give rise to profound, pure faith;
they make vows to practice so as to be reborn in the Pure Land at the time of death.
As fully explained in the sutras,
by being complete in these practices and vows,
one will immediately attain rebirth there.
Because this differs from those who harbor empty aspirations,
it is not a teaching for a future time;
for the Buddha addressed these two preceding types of people regarding the day when they have not yet attained rebirth.
The commentator records that those who have made the vow attain rebirth;
fearing that those who possess both practice and the vow would immediately attain rebirth,
he separates them from those who possess the vow alone.
This is the meaning of "another time.
Therefore, the vow is likened to the first coin;
the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha and so forth are likewise so.
These nine hundred and ninety-eight gold coins in the interim are the first thousand gold coins for rebirth in the Pure Land; thus,
the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says:
It is like trading a single gold coin and obtaining a thousand gold coins;
it is also like recollecting the Buddha Prabhūtaratna—
yet one has not yet reached the stage of non-retrogression.
The stage of non-retrogression begins at the initial mind of the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*).
When such a person contemplates the Buddha Prabhūtaratna,
it may be the mind prior to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
Alternatively, those at the initial stage of the ten faiths and so forth are not yet able to contemplate the Buddha Prabhūtaratna;
they immediately transcend ten thousand kalpas of the ten faiths and arrive at the initial stage of the ten abidings.
Because one must further cultivate eighty-four thousand *pāramitā* practices during the intermediate stage before reaching the initial resolve (*prathamacitta*),
the recollection of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna serves as a remote condition for non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
Therefore, it is called the "intention regarding another time.
Thus far, many meanings have been used to clarify the intention regarding another time.
As for myself, I am one who merely makes vows, not one who undertakes actual practice.

This refers to the intention of "another time" (*kāntarābhiprāya*) expressed by the masters of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*. Furthermore, regarding the "intention of another time" in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, it means that while one is to seek rebirth in the Pure Land,
one should exclusively practice the recitation of the Buddha's name.
In principle, one is not yet reborn;
however, if one transforms the pure land through the sole practice of mindfulness of the Buddha,
one will certainly attain rebirth immediately.
As stated in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra,
there is no need for doubt. Question:
Among those sentient beings who attain rebirth there,
only those in the human realm are able to cultivate pure karma and thereby achieve rebirth.
Is it possible for those who have not yet passed away to attain rebirth,
as well as for those who have already died to attain rebirth while within the realm of the dark path?
The commentary states:
Within the five destinies,
one is fully able to cultivate the pure karma of the Western [Pure Land].
One shall attain birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
According to the text of the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*, since the various devas are able to come and listen to it,
the following passage in the sūtra states:
Immeasurable devas, nāgas, and yakṣas,
having heard what the Buddha had spoken,
were all greatly filled with joy.
In the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, among those listed in the assembly,
it is stated that immeasurable devas, asuras, and others have all come to listen to the Dharma for the sake of hearing the teaching. Thus,
we know that they all desire to be reborn in the Pure Land.
All are able to cultivate pure karma and attain rebirth in the Western Land.
Furthermore, according to the fourth fascicle of the *Bodhisattva-tsa-t'ai ching* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb):
A nāga born by transformation observed the eightfold precepts of the upavāsa;
the garuḍas desired to eat him but could not,
so they inquired about the method for doing so.
The dragon expounded the Dharma of the Eight Precepts of the Fast for him.
The garuḍa followed the dragon to the palace of the Dragon King in the ocean.
At that time, the dragon’s son spoke a verse to the garuḍa:
At that time, the hearts of the dragon prince and dragon princess were opened and their minds were liberated;
after the end of their lives, they shall all be reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
Furthermore, according to the *Suiyuan wangsheng jing* (Sutra on Rebirth According to One’s Vows):
If one uses the articles for adorning the deceased’s body, as well as their halls, houses, gardens, and bathing pools,
to make offerings to the Triple Gem,
this merit will be greatest and its power of virtue most potent.
One may thereby uproot the calamities of that hell.
By these causes and conditions, one shall attain liberation from the affliction of sorrow and suffering,
and achieve lasting liberation.
They will be reborn in the pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
By this one may infer the same for sentient beings of the five destinies.
All shall attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
It is asked:
"How can one receive birth within this impure land of the three realms?"
All those who possess form and shape undergo the intermediate state (antarābhava) when dying here and being born there.
The transmigrating consciousness possesses four modes of existence, namely:
intermediate existence (antarābhava), birth existence (upapattibhava), fundamental existence (mūlabhava), and death existence (maraṇabhava).
It is not yet known whether those born from this [state] into a pure land also possess an intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The commentary states:
There are two explanations for this.
One says that there is no intermediate state (antarābhava);
it is by means of this [state] that one passes away and sits within a lotus flower.
Therefore, it is known that this refers to being subsumed within the womb.
Because entering into the lotus is similar to being in the womb,
it is now explained.
This principle is not necessarily so. For instance,
regarding the method of taking birth in a defiled land,
one must reach that place of birth before receiving the aggregates of birth.
For example, when one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the form realm,
one must first undergo death in the desire realm and receive the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm;
only upon reaching that form realm does one receive the aggregates of birth (*upapattibhava*).
There is no case of one who has experienced existence in the desire realm receiving a birth-existence body (*upapatti-bhava-kāya*) in the form realm;
the principle here for being born in a pure land is likewise.
It is not possible that one who dies in an impure land would receive a birth-existence body in a pure land within that same impure land.
One must necessarily reach that Pure Land, specifically within the precious ponds there, for the existence of a physical body to be fully realized.
Furthermore, in the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu), where there is no form,
it would be impossible for consciousness to be transmitted through an intermediate state (antarābhava) to undergo rebirth.
The Pure Land possesses form;
since its location is distinct [from this world],
why do you not grant that it exists?
Is there a transmission of consciousness within the intermediate state (antarābhava) that reaches the birth-state aggregate (upapattibhava-skandha) there?
Question: [Is this so?]
If there were an intermediate state (antarābhava),
then one should first be born there and arrive at the pool of jewels;
only then would one enter the flower to sit, after which the flower would bloom.
How is it that one enters into these flowers?
In what way does this differ from being born with the aggregates (*skandha*)? Answer:
How could it be that by entering those flowers during the intermediate state (antarābhava),
one is immediately subsumed under the birth-state (upapattibhava) of that [lotus],
such that one is born in that Pure Land?
The power of merit is superior;
although one in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) rides upon a flower to attain rebirth,
this differs from the intermediate state in the defiled lands, where there are no flowers.
Although the intermediate and subsequent aggregates are both within the flower,
they differ in terms of superiority and inferiority,
and there is a distinction between clarity and obscurity.
Because there is a distinction between the two aggregates within the *bhava-aṅga* (the link of becoming),
and because there is a distinction in meaning between the *gati-jāti* (birth according to destiny) and the *upapatti-jāti* (birth as arising),
the aggregates within the *bhava-aṅga* are different.
It is not that there is a distinction between existence and non-existence based on whether flowers are present or absent.
If one were to claim that because they are equally situated within the flowers, they are difficult to differentiate,
then it would follow that there is no intermediate state (antarābhava) at all.
That is also acceptable.
In the defiled lands, the two aggregates arise together,
and likewise there are no flowers.
One should say that the two aggregates (skandhas) in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) are not distinct.
If it is argued that although the intermediate state and the state of birth both lack flowers, there are nevertheless distinctions such as conception (*garbhāvakrānti*),
then there could likewise be distinctions among the three modes of birth, such as the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*).
How could there be any distinction between those born through transformation and those born from the womb?
For this reason, we know that there is an intermediate state (antarābhava).
Furthermore, the intermediate state (antarābhava) of those in hell has already been scorched by fire;
how could it not be indistinguishable from the state of existence at birth?
This serves to clarify that the categories of wholesome karma for rebirth in a Pure Land are similar to those for rebirth within the [five] destinies.
However, regarding this aforementioned intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
I have not yet seen any sutra or śāstra stating that for one who goes to a Pure Land, the departing body is an intermediate state or is not an intermediate state.
It cannot be definitively determined as either existent or non-existent.
Although there is no explicit scriptural passage,
the sense of its existence is accepted.
It is not so for the sake of superiority.
What is it that is said to depart from the body? He asked:
If there are beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava),
it is not yet known whether those in the intermediate state of this Pure Land wear robes.
He does not wear robes.
Answer: There is no scriptural or commentarial authority for this.
Nevertheless, one should certainly wear robes according to the established rule,
for the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that among the intermediate state beings (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm, all except for the pure white bhikṣuṇīs [wear them].
All other intermediate states (*antarābhava*) are entirely without clothing,
because those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) lack a sense of shame (*ahrīkya*) and dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*).
All intermediate states belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), however, possess clothing.
Because they possess a sense of shame and dread of blame.
By this standard, one should know that the Pure Land surpasses the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
How is it that there are no garments in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
Therefore, in the Pure Land, those in the intermediate state all possess clothing. Question:
What are the characteristics of the intermediate state (antarābhava) in the Pure Land?
The answer is:
they are also to be understood by inference based on this same principle.

The intermediate state (antarābhava) for those born in the heavens from this defiled land has their feet downward and their heads upward; the intermediate state for those bound for hell has their heads downward and their feet upward.
With heads below and feet above—
humans, ghosts, and animals—
like birds in flight.
To keep the body level is the practice of walking; thus,
one will now be born in the Pure Land,
with the feet below and the head above.
This very scriptural passage—
sitting within a lotus flower—
is precisely its characteristic mark.
Another explanation states that there is a distinction: the intermediate state (antarābhava) for those being born in the heavens.
Standing upon the crown of your head,
you shall immediately proceed to take birth within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the Pure Land.
"Sitting" refers to the process of proceeding toward rebirth.
Question: What is the intermediate state (antarābhava) within the Pure Land?
Since they have not yet reached that world of Ultimate Bliss,
what do they eat during the interval while passing through those hundred trillion buddha-fields?
The commentary states:
In the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
the conditions for rebirth have not yet converged.
One may dwell for a long time in that intermediate state body;
in order to proceed toward the existence of rebirth, one must consume fragrances.
This applies even to the intermediate state of a pure land.
In the time it takes to snap one's fingers,
one immediately attains rebirth there;
thus, the duration is not long.
There was no need for food.
Furthermore, having traversed through the midst of ten trillion buddha-fields,
he remained suspended in mid-air.
They consume the fragrant vapors of the various Buddha-fields to sustain their physical aggregates as they proceed toward their place of rebirth.
The meanings contained therein are immeasurable and manifold;
they cannot be fully explained.
It is asked:
For what reason does the Tathāgata preach the sūtras?
It is entirely to accommodate the capacities of beings and transform them;
it is preached solely for those who have faith and incline toward the Dharma.
It is not proclaimed for those who harbor doubts;
thus, the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra* says:
"The Buddha bestows [this teaching] upon those who have faith."
It is not for those who harbor doubts that he speaks;
yet, within the midst of his preaching,
he displays the mark of the extended tongue to exhort sentient beings to give rise to faith.
There are those who do not extend their tongues [in idle chatter] but proclaim only the sublime principles;
they also expound the most profound Dharma,
which ordinary people find difficult to understand.
Doubt gives rise to slander; for instance,
when the Lotus Sūtra teaches the merging of the two vehicles into one,
those of the two vehicles do not give rise to faith.
The World-Honored One Prabhūtaratna emerges from his jeweled stupa;
together with the Buddha of Verified Realization,
he extends his tongue to manifest non-deception as a sign of truth.
Having three times set forth words that ought to be believed, he now proclaims these words of ultimate truth:
the present *Amitābha Sūtra* speaks exclusively of the pure and majestic characteristics of the two types of retribution— the environment and the inhabitants— in the Western Quarter.
If it is sufficient to exhort sentient beings toward rebirth and facilitate the arising of right faith,
why is it necessary for the Buddhas of the six directions or the ten directions to simultaneously extend their tongues to exhort beings to develop faith?
The commentary states:
According to the subsequent passage of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*,
the Buddha himself recounted this.
The Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
each seeing Śākyamuni Buddha preaching the *Sūtra on the Praise of the Pure Land*,
were clearly present in their own respective lands.
With one voice and in unison, they all simultaneously uttered this praise:
"Śākyamuni Buddha is able,
within the five turbidities of this evil world, the Sahā world..."
Having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
he preaches for the sake of all sentient beings this Dharma which is extremely difficult to believe in throughout all worlds.
When Śākyamuni Buddha had received the simultaneous praise of all the Buddhas with one voice,
he addressed Śāriputra:
In this world of the five turbidities,
I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of all sentient beings.
To say that this is a teaching difficult for all the world to believe is indeed most difficult;
for although the Tathāgata has preached hundreds of thousands of such sūtras, [this remains the most difficult].
He did not speak of difficult-to-explain matters,
but only praised the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* in nine sheets of paper.
The Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as the World-Honored One Śākyamuni,
all declare that this sutra is difficult to believe and difficult to expound;
for it is because the Buddha has preached the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
All non-Buddhists will give rise to slander,
whereas all disciples of the Buddha will develop faith.
Now, I shall speak the Amitābha Sūtra.

It is said that even sentient beings who have committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil acts, provided they are able to mindfully recite the Buddha's name, will all be reborn in the Pure Land;
yet, even among the Buddha’s disciples who place their faith and inclination in this teaching,
there are those who harbor doubts and suspicions.
Do not disbelieve these words;
it is evident that even now, all four assemblies possess right faith.
One may still doubt that through the practice of nianfo one will not immediately attain birth [in the Pure Land].
Thus, we know that this sutra is extremely difficult to believe.
The One of All-Knowledge (sarvākārajñatā) foreknows this.
In the future, there will be sentient beings who harbor doubts; therefore,
they all extend their tongues in this manner.
It manifests the ultimate truth of the Dharma,
exhorts sentient beings to practice and study it,
and furthermore leads them to rebirth in the Pure Land.
Bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness above the stage of practice and understanding, or figures such as Nāgārjuna,
attain rebirth in the Western Land;
even ordinary beings of extreme evil can likewise give rise to correct faith and be born there.
Those superior persons have abundant merit and little transgression;
that they are born in the Pure Land is not at all surprising.
Even an ordinary person burdened with the evils of the five heinous crimes and the ten non-virtues,
if they recite [the name] ten times with single-minded sincerity that penetrates to the core, [shall attain liberation].
Riding upon the fundamental vows of the Buddha,
they are born in the Western Land,
together with the assembly of Bodhisattvas of the ten stages and the three levels of worthiness.
They also believe in this matter and do not give rise to doubt;
they speak only of the lower grade of the lowest birth resulting from the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds.
Such foolish people commit every kind of evil;
yet when they encounter a virtuous friend who teaches them to recite the name of the Buddha, [they are transformed].
One who possesses ten recitations is immediately reborn in the Pure Land.
Yet these very people— beings of the ten evil deeds—
do not believe that through the recitation of the Buddha's name one may attain birth in the Pure Realm.
Since we are sinful ordinary beings who have committed every transgression since beginningless time,
what merit is there in reciting the Buddha’s name ten times?
"May my grave offenses be extinguished and may I be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
This is merely the Buddha’s words of guidance,
or it is a case of describing something distant as if it were near.
This is the method for the second stage.
Alternatively, it may be said that because of the intention regarding a different time,
various divergent interpretations arise, leading to a lack of faith.
Deception and slander are extremely prevalent,
while faith and compliance are exceedingly rare;
therefore, these teachings are seldom encountered by those who possess faith.
All Buddhas together extend their tongues,
completely covering the trichiliocosm,
certifying that the Dharma is not erroneous and that one will certainly attain rebirth therein.
He protects and keeps in mind those who practice,
causing them to be born in the Pure Land.
It is asked:
As stated in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra:
"All Buddhas are equal,
for they all possess the fulfillment of all practices."
Only when his original vows are fulfilled does he attain perfect enlightenment and receive the title "Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings.
This is the current *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra*.
Only the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha-buddha-pūrvacaryā-sūtra* speaks of the twelve great vows he made when practicing the bodhisattva path;
[these are not found] in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and other such texts.

The account of Amitābha Buddha’s initial generation of the bodhicitta and his cultivation of the bodhisattva practices leading to the formulation of the forty-eight vows differs from the text of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra;
what is the significance of this?
The commentary states:
The intent of these two sūtras each relies on a single meaning;
they are likewise not mutually contradictory.
To speak according to reality,
all Buddhas are fully endowed with all supreme and wondrous vows;
there is neither increase nor decrease.
If there were even a single vow that was not fulfilled or a single practice that was not perfected,
one would not attain the Way or achieve the title of Perfectly Enlightened One (Samyaksaṃbuddha) nor be called an Omniscient One (Sarvajña);
it would follow that the merits of the Buddhas possess the fault of inequality.
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states that the merits of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are entirely equal; yet,
the Bhaisajyaguru Sūtra speaks of twelve vows.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* speaks of forty-eight vows;
these were taught in accordance with the capacities of those to be converted.
Thus do all Buddhas teach and transform sentient beings.
All are based on having the karmic affinity for being guided and received;
sentient beings share this affinity with the Buddha,
and thus necessarily rely upon the original vows of the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata transforms and guides all classes of beings,
causing them all to be born through transformation by riding upon his great vows.
It was from this that all Buddhas originally resolved to attain Bodhicitta.
One then abides in a vast mind, thinking:
"I shall cause all realms of sentient beings to enter nirvana without remainder and bring them to liberation."
However, the realm of sentient beings is infinite in number.
From the Bodhisattva’s initial generation of the mind until his attainment of Buddhahood,
an incalculable eon (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa) has both a beginning and an end.
While practicing the bodhisattva path therein and attaining equal and perfect enlightenment,
it is impossible for all sentient beings to universally see the bodhisattva’s cultivation and offerings.
A bodhisattva cannot finish teaching and benefiting all beings within the realm of sentient beings before that realm is exhausted; yet,
the bodhisattva has already attained buddhahood.
Although the mind is vast, great matters are difficult to encompass entirely;
nevertheless, at the stage of the causal ground,
sentient beings made twelve great vows before the Buddha Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabha.
With utmost sincerity and profound earnestness,
their vows have now reached maturity.
This concerns the forty-eight great vows originally made by Amitābha Buddha.
With utmost sincerity and profound earnestness,
his vows have also matured;
although both Buddhas possess vows as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, [his are now fulfilled].
For the sake of those to be converted, the specific vows are explained exclusively;
for while sentient beings' faculties have matured regarding the twelve great vows of Bhaisajyaguru Buddha,
their faculties have not yet matured regarding the forty-eight extensive vows of that same Buddha.
Therefore, the Buddha specifically cited the twelve vows.
As for the forty-eight vows of Amitābha Buddha, the capacities of those to be converted were particularly mature;
although he possessed the twelve vows and others as well, the Buddha did not speak of them.
It is like a great physician’s pharmacy, which,
although it contains every kind of medicinal herb,
administers different treatments for those suffering from various ailments, such as cold-natured disorders, heat-natured disorders, vomiting, or diarrhea.
The prescriptions for compounding medicines differ;
from among all medicinal herbs, one specifically selects three, five, or more ingredients that are appropriate for the specific ailment,
then pounds, sifts, and blends them together.
Alternatively, one may give the pills to the patient to consume.
It is not that the number of medicines is insufficient; rather, it is because one does not trust that the Medicine King’s pharmacy contains every medicine.
It is not that all various medicines are provided for a single disease.
How much more so when it comes to compounding medicinal decoctions that employ all manner of cold and hot medicines?
The Buddha is also like this,
as described in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Truly possessing all vows,
they are entirely equal,
like the medicine in the medical storehouse of that King of Physicians.
Some speak of that Buddha’s twelve vows;
others speak of this Buddha’s forty-eight vows.
It is like prescribing medicine and decoctions for a patient according to their specific ailment.
Therefore, these two sutras do not contradict one another.
Question: Regarding those sentient beings who are reborn there by practicing the karma of purity—
What are the signs by which one knows that one will immediately attain certain rebirth in the Western [Pure Land]?
Is there any scriptural authority or evidence for these signs?
The commentary states:
There are three scriptural authorities that prove rebirth has already been attained.
To verify a person through the teachings is itself the proof;
this is exactly as stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*: [“If one hears this teaching... and so forth.
In this world-system of defilement during the evil age of the five turbidities,
if there are sons or daughters of good family who possess pure faith and hear such teachings as these, which are difficult for all the world to believe.
They are able to give rise to faith and understanding,
receive and uphold [the teachings], expound them,
and practice according to the instructions.
One should know that such a person is truly rare and extraordinary;
having planted roots of goodness under immeasurable Buddhas,
this person will, upon the end of their life, certainly be reborn in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
Second, as stated in the *Sutra on the Pure and Equal Enlightenment*:
"If a person hears the teaching of the Pure Land,
the hairs on their body stand on end."
I say that such a person, like one who has pulled [a thorn] out, will certainly attain liberation.
As stated in the first fascicle of the Bhadrapāla-sūtra:
sentient beings who have attained the samādhi of the presence of all Buddhas hear the name of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitābha.
Being able to bind the mind in continuous contemplation,
proceeding in sequence without confusion,
one clearly beholds that Amitābha Buddha.
This is the Bodhisattva’s contemplation for the full accomplishment of the Samādhi of the Manifest Presence of All Buddhas.
Because he was able to see the Buddha by means of this samādhi,
he then questioned that Amitābha Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, by accomplishing what dharmas do these bodhisattvas obtain birth within this buddha-field?
At that time, Amitābha Buddha spoke to those bodhisattvas, saying:
If a person resolves their mind to seek birth in this land,
they should always bind their thoughts with right mindfulness in continuous succession;
then they shall attain birth in the land of Amitābha Buddha.
Practitioners and others should personally examine these three sutras;
whichever one they find corresponds with their own practice,
they will know that they shall be reborn in the Pure Land.
Question: In this defiled land,
even the various devas of the form realm (rūpadhātu) are likewise free from sorrow and suffering.
Since there is only joy and bliss,
how does this differ in terms of superiority or inferiority from that Pure Land?
I vow to be born in the Pure Land.
"Do you not delight in being born in the heavens of the form realm and so forth?
The commentary states:
"Although those gods of the form realm lack sorrow and suffering and possess only joy and bliss..."
However, it is not ultimate bliss; ultimately, there is still the experience of suffering.
Therefore, practitioners do not aspire to be reborn there.
Briefly stated, eight points demonstrate that it is not the Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī):
first, there is no quiescent bliss above;
second, one falls into the wheel of suffering below.
Third, there is no noble refuge;
fourth, not hearing the true Dharma;
fifth, possessing various savorful concentrations.
Sixth, the increase of the delusions of false views;
seventh, the destruction of the environment by the three calamities;
eighth, the formation of bodies through the eight difficult conditions.
Regarding "the supreme, unsurpassed bliss of tranquility":
this refers to the bliss of the tranquil extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*) of Great Nirvana,
which ordinary beings cannot realize upon being born.
Regarding the second [category], those who fall into the cycle of suffering:
after they have exhausted their retribution in the realms of form and formlessness,
their karma in the desire realm ripens, and they are reborn in the lower regions.
Third, regarding those who lack a noble refuge:
although there are five Pure Abodes in the realm of form,
how can they compare to the Western Land, which abounds with Bodhisattvas in their final birth?
Regarding the fourth point, those who do not hear the True Dharma:

how could the devas of the form realm compare to the pure lands, where the assembly of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, along with the water birds and forest trees, constantly proclaim the wondrous Dharma throughout the six periods of day and night?
Regarding the fifth point, those who possess various flavors of meditative concentration (rasa-samādhi):
although there is pure concentration within that aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), it is largely characterized by various flavors of concentration.
Because these characteristics are intermingled, afflictions increase;
this is not the case in the Pure Land.
Sixth, as for the increase of the delusion of wrong views:
Those born in the realm of form include various non-Buddhists;
some harbor wrong views,
and others receive the retribution of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi*).
To claim that what is about to arise is already extinguished,
or to slander the Noble Ones and Nirvana, leads to falling into hell.
Seventh, the destruction of the environment by the three calamities.
Below the third dhyāna,
[worlds] are destroyed first by fire, then by water, and finally by wind;
these do not exist in the Pure Lands.
Eighth, regarding the body formed through the eight difficulties:
although there is no sorrow or suffering in the form and formless realms,
