how could one rely upon them to establish a definitive compass for guidance?
However, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life* itself contains a sincere teaching, stating:
"If one cuts across the five evil destinies,
the evil destinies will naturally close."
The ascent to the Way is boundless;
it is easy to travel, yet no one does so.
This is precisely Buddhism.
It is evident that these constitute eight differences.
The preceding section contains fifteen identical passages.
It is already difficult to describe it as being hard to reach;
how much more so when there are eight distinct gates,
yet you say it is difficult to go there.
I request that all students seek out both principle and teaching,
and by examining these two gates of difficulty and ease,
they may forever eliminate their delusions.
Exhausting the principles of the sacred teachings,
one may either praise or disparage a single dharma-gate.
All of these are skillful means for encouraging entry into the Way;
they serve the present purpose of abandoning stubborn attachment and deluded confusion.
Please examine this carefully.
It is asked:
According to the Abhidharma-śāstra, there are nine modes of death and rebirth.
That is to say: dying in the desire realm and being reborn in the desire realm;
dying in the desire realm and being reborn in the form realm;
and dying in the desire realm and being reborn in the formless realm.
When one reaches such a state near the point of death and is about to undergo rebirth there,
the afflictions of that realm arise to moisten the process of birth.
"What afflictions arise in this life to moisten rebirth in the Western [Pure Land]?
The commentary states:
There are two explanations for this.
If one who has not yet abandoned the desires of the desire realm is born in the Western [Pure Land],
they give rise to craving for the desire realm.
They are born in a moist pure land.
If one who has already abandoned desire for the desire realm attains a meditative absorption of the form realm,
they give rise to craving for the form realm.
They are born in the moist pure lands.
If one who has already abandoned desire for the form realm attains a formless attainment,
one of a nature subject to regression will regress and give rise to afflictions of the desire and form realms.
One will be born in the Western Land;
if one does not regress,
one will certainly be born in the Pure Land.
He says that the Pure Land is comprised within both the desire realm and the form realm. Others say:
Although it is not subsumed within the two realms of desire and form,
because it is a land characterized by form,
one cannot be free from the afflictions of the realm of form.
One attains the meditative absorption of the formless realm and is born into a pure land characterized by form.
Some commentators state that at the time of death when one is born into a pure land, the Great Sage comes to welcome them.
Blessed by the grace of compassion,
his mind remained undeluded as he passed away.
If afflictions arise,
they are termed "perversions";
yet, the process of taking birth necessarily requires afflictions.
This employs the seeds of affliction to moisten the factors of existence (bhavāṅga),
causing the continuity [of rebirth] to arise.
Nor is there any fault in this.
Question:
Can a noble one in training (śaikṣa) produce rebirth through the moistening of seeds?
Since they are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*),
they employ only active afflictions (*samudācāra-kleśa*);
how can it be said that seeds moisten rebirth?
Answer: This treatise is based on taking birth in a defiled land;
ordinary beings therein employ only active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).
Because ordinary beings die with their afflictions raging and their minds entirely inverted,
they are reborn in the Pure Land,
where they receive the Buddha’s protective grace.
The mind is not inverted and afflictions do not arise;
this cannot be equated with the phenomena produced in a defiled land.
Although there is no explicit scriptural teaching on this, its meaning can be inferred by analogy:
just as it is necessarily the case when one dies in an unconscious state, so too must it be here.
Alternatively, it may arise as active manifestation;
this interpretation also incurs no fault.
[The opponent] asks:
Regarding those born in the Pure Land:
while the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are subsumed within the three realms (*traidhātuka*),
it is not yet known under which category the dependent origination of the stages (*avasthā*) of the Pure Land is subsumed.
The commentary states:
There are two interpretations of this. The first interpretation is as follows:
The Pure Land is subsumed within the triple world;
those who have not yet abandoned the afflictions of desire are reborn in the Pure Land.
The members of ignorance and formations are the desire realm itself;
the five resultant seeds— consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling—
are likewise the desire realm.
Since the links of craving, grasping,
and existence belong to the desire realm,
how could their fruits— birth, aging, and death— not also belong to the desire realm?
If one has already become free from desire for the realm of desire and attains a mind belonging to the realm of form,
the twelve links of existence are then subsumed within the realm of form;
this is the definitive meaning according to the principles of dharmic characteristics.
Some say that the Pure Land is not part of the three realms (*tridhātu*);
this has already been established at length above.
These twelve links of existence are explained with reference to the three realms;
therefore, they are not differentiated within the Pure Land.
Furthermore, these twelve links of existence pertain to the defiled land.
Furthermore, this does not encompass all phenomena exhaustively.
For instance, when a distinct determinate karma (*niyata-karma*) receives a distinct retributive fruit,
how could it be said that such is subsumed within the twelve links?
Therefore, one should know that dependent origination in terms of states does not encompass all phenomena exhaustively. Question:
If one who is born in the Pure Land does not give rise to various evils,
does it also mean they do not give rise to various afflictions (*kleśa*)?
For instance, consider a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
There still remains the subtle stain of impaired precepts;
Bodhisattvas on the third stage still give rise to the grasping of a self;
and from the seventh stage onwards, there still exists the obstacle of attachment to the Buddha and attachment to Bodhi.
How is it that one who is born in that land,
though appearing as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
does not give rise to any evil afflictions (*kleśa*)?
The commentary states:
Although ordinary beings born there possess afflictions,
they lack adverse objects.
What harm is there in not arising?
It is like the sentient beings in the hells,
who [suffer] through the ten unwholesome paths of action.
Only five courses of action arise:
covetousness, malice, wrong view, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.
Although hell is an evil destiny, [these five alone are present there].
Since even here there still lack five evil karmas,
how much more so in the Pure Land, where there is no deficiency and no evil arises?
A question is asked:
Is it that in those pure lands no other afflictions whatsoever arise suddenly,
or can there also arise afflictions that are obscured and indeterminate (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*)?
The commentary states:
As for those afflictions deluded regarding principles that arise simultaneously with birth, they too can arise;
for such ordinary persons have not yet realized the profound true nature of suchness.
It is not precluded that they arise.
As for those that arise through discrimination, they do not manifest.
The treatise states that the discrimination of the view of self arises from false teachings;
however, since those [beings] lack false teachings, it does not manifest.
I perceive these to be the root of all afflictions;
once the root does not arise,
the derivative afflictions will not be produced.
Spontaneous afflictions do not arise based on teachings;
since these are the afflictions of ordinary beings,
their arising cannot be prevented.
However, according to the Abhidharma treatises,
these afflictions are also unwholesome if they arise spontaneously and are capable of inciting evil conduct.
The afflictions arising therein do not incite unwholesome conduct;
therefore, they are subsumed under the category of obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) nature.
The sūtra excludes them from being unwholesome (akuśala).
It is not said that they are "obscured," but merely that they lack the designation "unwholesome";
this does not preclude the arising of afflictions.
Attachment to the Buddha and attachment to the Dharma of Bodhi are afflictions of clinging.
A question is asked:
The Sūtra says:
Those born in that Western Land are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive);
some say they belong exclusively to the group of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*).
There are no such things as those of wrong determination or the indeterminate group;
however, the stage of *avaivartika* is not that of an ordinary person,
for it belongs to the group of right determination, having ascended the path to the fruit of sainthood.
Since one is currently an ordinary person (pṛthagjana),
even if one is reborn in the Pure Land,
how could one immediately become a sage (ārya)?
One might indeed suddenly transcend incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya*) to attain the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*);
however, when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has regressed is born there,
they cannot immediately reach the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
Those in the groups of the wrongly fixed and the unfixed will immediately ascend to the group of the rightly fixed.
As for "not obtaining":
This would immediately contradict the text of the *Sūtra on Contemplation* and other such works; furthermore,
as for those who hold this view,
it also runs counter to the doctrinal meanings of numerous sūtras and śāstras.
Regarding the two texts concerning the spear and shield, I request an explanation.
The commentary states:
These two scriptural passages are indeed contradictory;
however, since the realms of the Pure Land and the defiled land differ,
the capacities of those born here and those born there are likewise distinct.
Therefore, the categories of the group of those fixed in rightness (*samyaktvaniyāma*) and so forth are distinguished by their varying degrees of loftiness or inferiority;
likewise, there are distinctions between the shallow and the deep levels of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
However, in this defiled land of Sahā, the holy are few and the commoners many;
those who believe are rare, while the masses are prone to slander, and those with shallow faculties and conduct are numerous.
They frequently encounter conditions for regression;
fanned by perverse winds,
they all turn back from their progress.
According to various sūtras and śāstras, there are four types of regression:
first, regression of faith;
second, regression of stage.
Third is the falling away from realization;
fourth is the falling away from practice.
Regarding the falling away from faith:
Within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), during the first five mental states (*citta-kṣaṇa*),
there is still the possibility of regression, such as the arising of false views or the severing of the roots of goodness;
this is not the case in the subsequent stages.
Regarding "retrogression from the stages":
within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), during the first six mental states,
one may still undergo retrogression and fall back into the level of the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*) and so forth.
The subsequent stage is not so. Regarding those who have regressed from realization:
this refers to the stages of ordinary beings prior to the ten bhūmis.
Regarding that which was previously realized, there may still be regression;
however, this is not the case for the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Those who regress in their practice are those from the seventh stage and below.
Regarding the practices they have heard, they still give rise to timidity and inferiority;
they are unable to practice and study them,
nor can they constantly cultivate superior conduct in every moment of thought.
When, in the interim, various defiled afflictions, such as the two types of grasping at self and phenomena, arise within the mind,
it is called a lapse in mindfulness.
At this point, the Bodhisattva of the eighth stage enters the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
There are no four kinds of regression.
Among all conditioned phenomena, one fully cultivates every practice,
at all times, with continuous succession from moment to moment.
They constantly give rise to the untainted contemplation of the emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*).
Not for a single thought-moment do they give rise to tainted minds—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above possess the four types of non-retrogression.
Therefore, they are called *avaivartika* bodhisattvas.
In the other seven stages and so forth, there are no four kinds of non-retrogression;
thus, they do not at all receive the name *avaivartika*.
If one follows this single interpretation,
a bodhisattva in the first stage enters the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa by virtue of having entered the stream of the noble ones.
Having severed the two obstacles of conceptualization on the path of seeing,
one realizes the all-pervading *tathatā* and attains the gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas.
Abiding on the Stage of Joy,
one possesses both the non-retrogression of realization and the non-retrogression of practice; this is also termed *avaivartika*.
Up until the seventh stage,
there still exists the manifestation of obstacles consisting of attachment to the Buddha and attachment to bodhi,
which occasionally give rise to outflowing (sāsrava) states of mind and the like.
They have not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression,
and thus they are also called "non-avaivartika.
Nevertheless, in a limited sense, they may also be called avaivartika bodhisattvas.
According to the *Bodhisattva-mūla-karman-avataṃsaka-sūtra* and other scriptures,
the sixth stage is called the Stage of the Right Mind (*samyak-citta-vihāra*).
At this level, a bodhisattva may still regress from the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) and revert to becoming a follower of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* or *pratyekabuddha*).
Śāriputra and others were such as these. From the seventh stage upward, there is no such regression;
therefore, among the four types of non-regression, [this refers to that category].
Only those who have attained the three types of non-retrogression through the stages of realization and practice possess the first type of non-retrogression;
those who attain it according to their respective degrees are also called *avaivartika*.
According to the *Awakening of Faith* and other such texts,
from the initial stage of the "Abiding in the Mind" (*cittotpāda-vihāra*) onward, one is generally said to have entered the stage of non-retrogression.
Those Bodhisattvas in the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) prior to the ten abidings are termed "external ordinary beings" (*bāhya-prthagjana*).
They are also called "ordinary persons with light hair.
Just as light hair is carried east and west by the wind,
they likewise undergo regression.
A Bodhisattva of the Ten Abodes is not like light down;
because their roots of goodness are firm, they are not moved by the winds of evil.
Having entered the stage of the ordinary person within, they do not regress from that position.
Such a person is called an *avaivartika* bodhisattva. However,
in this defiled land, a bodhisattva at the stage of the ten faiths may be scattered and moved by the winds of heterodoxy,
thereby regressing from the bodhicitta.
They retreat from the bodhisattva practice,
transmigrate through the three evil realms,
and are not *avaivartika*.
Regarding the purification of the buddha-land: for those who have entered the first five stages of the ten faiths,
as well as all sentient beings who have not yet entered the ten faiths,
although their stage of faith is not yet firm, it is nonetheless present.
They are like light feathers,
yet they are not stirred by the winds of evil,
such that their resolve for bodhicitta might be made to regress.
Having committed various grave offenses, they would otherwise wander through the evil realms of saṃsāra;
yet, because they lack the conditions for regression and possess no means of falling back,
they have only the exceptional conditions for advancing upon the path.
Although they have not yet entered the stage of *avaivartika*, they may nevertheless be called *avaivartika*.

These include those of the nature of falling back (*parihāṇadharman*), those of the nature of reflecting (*cetana-dharman*), those of the nature of protecting (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), those of the nature of abiding (*sthitākampya-dharman*), and those of the nature of being capable of penetration (*prativedhanādharman*).
Although both those who are still training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa) among the noble ones may possess dull faculties, they are collectively termed "subject to regression.
If such a person is born among humans and encounters the five conditions for regression—
namely, chronic illness, long-distance travel, disputes, monastic affairs, and the practice of recitation— these are the five conditions that lead to regression.
Although one has attained the noble path and severed the afflictions,
upon encountering such conditions for regression,
one may nevertheless fall back and give rise to various afflictions once again.
If one is born in the heavens, there are no five conditions for retrogression;
although one has not yet refined the faculties to reach the immovable lineage (*akopyadharman*),
because the conditions for retrogression are absent, one does not retrogress or give rise to afflictions.
Although their lineage is nominally distinct from that of the immovable (akopyadharman),
they are no different from those of the sixth immovable lineage (akopyagotra) in their non-retrogression regarding the afflictions of cultivation.
It is the same for them: in order to be born in the Pure Land, they shall be free from any conditions that lead to regression.
Even those such as the bodhisattvas of the provisional name of the ten stages of faith are all entitled to be called *avaivartika*.
This is so within a defiled land.
In the Small Vehicle, the stages of *ūṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, and in the Great Vehicle, the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and so forth,
involve faculties that are not yet fixed;
thus, one may encounter adverse conditions.
Falling back, they commit the five heinous crimes and enter the group of those fixed in error;
"error" refers to the fruits of the three evil realms.
The "fixed" refers to the karmic causes of the five heinous crimes (ānantarya).
If a person creates the causes for the five heinous crimes,
they will certainly fall into the three evil realms without interval.
This is called the group of those with false resolve;
however, if they encounter superior conditions and cultivate the path,
they may attain entry into the stage of non-retrogression.

This is called the "group of those fixed in rightness" (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*). "Right" (*samyak*) refers to the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, which is disjunction and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
"Fixed" (*niyata*) refers to the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*) consisting of the two kinds of emptiness: that of persons and that of phenomena.
Having cultivated and attained the Noble Path,
one is certain to realize the ultimate fruit of Nirvana— the disjunction that is analytical cessation— and is thus termed one of the "Noble Assembly" (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi).
The remainder are called the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi),
because they may either create the group of the fixed in error (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi) or may cultivate the group of the fixed in correctness (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi).
Those who abide in the two indeterminate states are called the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*).
These three classes of sentient beings are not merely one in number.
Therefore, it is called a "group" (*rāśi*).
Now, having been born in the Western Land,
there are no adverse conditions, nor have you committed the crimes of immediate retribution that would cause one to enter the group of those fixed in error (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*).
Although their stage and practice are shallow, because they encounter only superior conditions,
they advance in the cultivation of the Mahāyāna holy path moment by moment,
remaining resolutely free from regression.
Therefore, they are designated as the "group of those fixed in rightness" (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi).

One must not, however, equate each instance with the stages of regression found in this Sahā world-system when determining the relative heights of the levels of non-retrogression (avaivartika) and the stage of being fixed in rightness.
This would mean that the Pure Land, being a place where there is no falling back, is identical to this world;
for there is a distinction between the two lands—the pure and the defiled—based on the presence or absence of the conditions for falling back or not.
Therefore, in this [Pure Land], one is not yet at the stage of *avaivartika* (non-retrogression).
Those who are not yet in the stage of the fixed group (niyata-rāśi) but are born in that Western Land are all designated as non-retrogressive (avaivartika) and members of the fixed group.
Because those born in that land have no conditions for regression,
and because they are certain never to create the category of beings fixed in error (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*). Question:
As stated in the Lotus Sūtra:
"Blinded by delusion and attached to pleasure.
It further says:
They are attached to worldly pleasures and lack the mind of wisdom.
Furthermore, the holy teaching says:
"If one does not feel weary of suffering..."
Do not seek nirvana out of attachment to pleasure;
if you do not seek nirvana out of attachment to pleasure,
you will instead become attached to and delight in saṃsāra.
If that were the case,
being born in that Pure Land would contradict the aforementioned principle and would consequently become a hindrance to the Path.
First, they are addicted to worldly pleasures and lack the aspiration for transcendence;
second, they lack the mind of wearying disenchantment with suffering.
To sever the quest for the fruit of nirvana is a great loss;
why would one wish to be born [in such a state]?
The commentary states:
This meaning is distinct.
This objection is not valid.
In this defiled land, the five desires increase greed,
leading one to commit the ten non-virtuous actions and transmigrate through the evil realms.
Therefore, the Sūtra says that those attached to pleasure are blinded by delusion.
Although the purification of Buddha-fields possesses manifold pleasures,
they accord with the supramundane, untainted mind.
The bliss of the Mahāyāna Dharma and the bliss of samādhi-concentration are not the bliss of defiled attachment; therefore,
they are able to guide ordinary sentiments.
In order to cause the noble path to increase,
the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"Within the pure buddha-field of the world of Ultimate Bliss..."
Six times throughout the day and night, various kinds of exquisite celestial flowers—
glossy, fragrant, pure, fine, soft, and multicolored— constantly rain down,
causing those who see them to experience physical and mental delight.
Yet they do not become greedily attached to them.
They cause sentient beings to increase their immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable, supreme merits.
Furthermore, it says:
May they never regress from the joy of the Mahāyāna Dharma;
may their immeasurable practices and vows increase with every thought-moment,
and may they swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, those who aspire to be born [there] all loathe these defiled sufferings and joyfully seek nirvana.
Only then can one joyfully proceed to the West to practice the bodhisattva path;
this already involves a sense of aspiration and aversion,
yet it further gives rise to a method for non-retrogression.
Is it necessary for suffering to entangle the body before one gives rise to the contemplation of quiescence?
Furthermore, the earnest seeking of nirvana is not merely a matter of wearying of suffering.
Some hear of the inconceivable merits of the Buddhas;
some hear of the six pāramitās and the various factors of the path;
and some behold the great bodhisattvas sporting with supernatural powers.
Whether smelling exquisite fragrances or tasting fine delicacies,
they are all able to advance on the Path.
Seeking nirvana, they turn their backs on saṃsāra and head toward the return to quiescence.
This is not the only path. One must not simply say that there is no suffering to be weary of,
and thereby fail to allow for the joyful seeking of nirvana.
Question: As it is said in the treatise,
regarding the grave offenses committed during past lives.
Even if one cultivates superior wholesome deeds and attains the state of an Arya,
one still undergoes the karmic retribution of past determinate actions,
as was the case with the Arhat Revata and others.
Now that you have already committed grave offenses,
even if you are reborn in the Western Land,
once born in that Pure Land, there will be no Noble Path.
Having been born in that land, do they undergo suffering,
or do they not undergo suffering?
If they undergo suffering, [then...]
One should not say that there is no suffering and that one experiences only pleasure.
If one does not experience [suffering],
then an ordinary person born there has not yet given rise to even a single thought of the untainted noble path.
How is it that one who has committed such grave offenses never experiences suffering?
The commentary states:
This meaning is not fixed;
it cannot be generalized.
Those who undergo suffering do so in order to be born in a defiled land.
Even if one attains sainthood,
the body remains a body of suffering;
one must ride upon this body of suffering.
Undergoing these bitter fruits of suffering,
they are born in that Pure Land;
such are ordinary beings possessed of delusions.
Although they lack the noble path and thus do not yet equal the noble ones,
they possess the exceptionally sublime and pure bodies of the Land of Ultimate Bliss,
where they behold the Buddha and hear the Dharma.
Practicing the Mahāyāna,
by virtue of the Buddha’s original vow, one can transcend these sages and not undergo the retribution of suffering.
For instance, those of the lineage of the "regressive" (parihāṇadharman) do not equal those of the lineage of the "contemplative" (cetana-dharman);
yet, those of the superior lineage of the contemplative are born among human beings.
There are five conditions for retrogression;
even those who are superior may fall back.
One of the lineage subject to retrogression (parihāṇadharman) may be born among the gods.
Lacking the five conditions for regression,
one does not regress despite being inferior;
nor does one regress while remaining superior due to an inferior nature.
It is not that one who excels by nature would fall back when situated below;
this case is likewise.
Although one has attained the Noble Path, one may be born in a defiled land.
Yet they undergo the fruits of suffering.
To be born in the Pure Land,
although one is still an ordinary person, there is no retribution for evil.
Through the augmenting power of virtuous conditions, there shall certainly be no retribution of suffering;
this is as with King Ajātaśatru, who was certain not to undergo suffering.
*Explanatory Treatise on Doubts Regarding the Pure Land*, Scroll Four.
*Discourse on Resolving the Multitude of Doubts Concerning the Pure Land*, Scroll Five, composed by the Venerable Huai’gan of Qianfu Monastery in the Western Capital. Question:
The *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "What is called an evil spiritual friend (*pāpa-mitra*)? What is called a virtuous spiritual friend (*kalyāṇa-mitra*)?"
[Regarding] consciousness. The Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"If there is a bhikṣu..."
He instructed the other bhikṣus:
"You should practice mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṅgha, mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of generosity, and mindfulness of the devas.
In this way, you should contemplate only nirvāṇa—its security and its tranquility."
To teach that craving alone is ultimately pure is called false teaching.
Such a person is called a bad friend.
This person is one who slanders me and assists non-Buddhists;
I do not permit such an evil person to receive even a single drink of water for their own sustenance.
A person who practices the teachings of Māra further says:
"It would be better to accomplish the five heinous crimes."

One does not achieve [the realization that transcends] the view of a self, the view of sentient beings, the view of a life-span, the view of a soul, or the views regarding the aggregates, bases, and elements.
These are all instances of practicing mindfulness of the Buddha and so forth with a mind that grasps at something to be attained.
After the World-Honored One had issued these various reprimands,
this very sūtra further states:
"Hearing the dharma of emptiness and non-apprehension..."
He immediately realized for himself that all he had previously accepted were false views;
regarding the dharma of emptiness where nothing is apprehended, he was without doubt or regret,
penetrating it deeply and thoroughly.
Not relying on any view of self or view of a person—
I say that such a person is called one whose holy life is pure, and so forth.
Now that you have already encouraged others to practice mindfulness of the Buddha with a mind of grasping and through the perception of signs,
will this not surely incur the reproach of all the Buddhas?
The commentary states:
The Buddhas’ preaching of the Dharma is always intended to accommodate the capacities [of sentient beings].
These capacities vary, being either deep or shallow, great or small.
Because there are delusions regarding the distinctions between the views of persons and phenomena, as well as those of cultivation,
he set forth the essentials of the Dharma to transform the capacities of sentient beings.
Some disparage existence and praise emptiness;
some revile emptiness and extol existence;
some cause others to abandon the minor [teachings] and embrace the major.
Or, they may first study the Hīnayāna and subsequently study the Mahāyāna; thus,
while sentient capacities follow ten thousand paths,
the Dharma is established as eighty-four thousand.
To transform sentient beings in accordance with conditions is inconceivable;
it is just as described in this very sutra.
He censured the attainment of a mind that grasps at anything;

you are free from internal suffering and affliction.
Externally possessing favorable conditions,
they are unwilling to practice; they wait until their end to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Although one may still attain rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha at the time of death,
such people will not succeed in doing so even once in ten thousand instances;
furthermore, it is uncertain whether they will encounter a virtuous friend by chance.
Some are so entangled by manifold sufferings that they have no leisure to mind the Buddha;
some are struck by apoplexy and rendered mute, unable to recite His name;
others are deranged and lose their minds.
How could one possibly focus one's thoughts?
Or if one should suddenly encounter water or fire,
there would be no leisure for sincere devotion.
Or you may suddenly encounter jackals and wolves,
thereby meeting an untimely death;
or you may meet evil companions who destroy your faith.
Some die from excessive drinking leading to stupor and sleep;
some perish suddenly in the midst of military battles;
and some fall headlong from high cliffs.
The practice of the correct path is difficult to cultivate;
because the multitude of obstacles and hindrances is vast, it is impossible to describe them exhaustively.
One must not fail to practice single-mindedly, becoming instead addicted to these five desires.
It is said that a single thought arises throughout the entire day;
one should therefore arouse a mind of diligent effort, eliminate thoughts of indolence,
exert oneself in these three karmas, and rouse oneself during the six periods of the day.
Diligently studying day and night, one competes with time;
having purified the Land of Bliss in this single lifetime, one shall forever be free from the hindrances and entanglements,
never regressing until the attainment of Bodhi.
The benefit is vast and extensive; one ought to apply the mind [to this practice].
It is asked:
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
If one is born there, one quickly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; yet,
since a hundred years on that path correspond to a single day here,
how can one possibly realize unsurpassed, great bodhi so swiftly?
The commentary states:
It is reckoned that within this suffering, practicing the path for a single day can surpass [the merit of] those hundred years;
yet, one may encounter adverse conditions.
It takes many kalpas for one who has regressed to advance again;
though a hundred years for them may be but a single day for us,
they must only progress and never regress.
This is called attaining supreme enlightenment swiftly.
Just as a person who travels in haste may reach their destination sooner than one who rests frequently for long periods,
practicing this path for a single day is superior to doing so for a hundred years.
The Buddha does not say that one realizes enlightenment quickly in this manner.
It is like a person walking slowly who reaches their destination swiftly because there is no stopping along the way;
therefore, it is called the "quick realization of enlightenment."
Question: Regarding the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti), it is said that it is not difficult for those who have practiced and studied it for a short time.
At the time of death, the moment is extremely fleeting; moreover,
one is afflicted by suffering and distress,
such that one cannot extensively cultivate the profound Buddha-dharma, such as the precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
For those who have not yet reached the end [of suffering], there shall be no further affliction to oppress their minds for a long time.
For what reason do they not contemplate emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)?
Why do they not cultivate the various factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) and extensively study all the profound dharma-gates?
What is the significance of frequently exhorting sentient beings to practice only the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*)?
The commentary states:
A practitioner who throughout their life cultivates the practices for the Pure Land is not merely encouraged to focus exclusively on the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha; however,
among those who engage in such cultivation, there are differences in the sharpness or dullness of their faculties.
Since there are varying depths of learning, the Sūtra divides the practice into two gates: the concentrated and the distracted;
and among persons, there are nine grades of distinction.
For those of sharp faculties whose minds are tranquil,
one teaches the profound and equal Dharma-gate of the contemplations on both the signless and the with-sign;
whereas for those of dull faculties who are distracted—
They practice exclusively the karma of the three grades of the three meritorious deeds;
they do not merely encourage exclusive recitation of the Buddha's name,
but also cultivate various dharma-gates.
If one is unable to practice extensively,
even recollecting the Buddha will lead to birth in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, the Dharma-gates for recollecting the Buddha may be either profound or shallow.
It encompasses both the concentrated and the dispersed states;
those with great roots and little practice can all engage in its cultivation.
As for concentration, it begins with ordinary beings and culminates in the tenth stage.
The practice of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi is profoundly deep and subtle;
the *Avataṃsaka*, *Nirvāṇa*, *Mañjuśrī*, *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, *Bhadrapāla*, and *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* sūtras all collectively praise it as inconceivable.
For example, when the youth Sudhana requested instruction on the practice of the bodhisattva path from the bhikṣu Guṇamegha,
the bhikṣu Guṇamegha taught him only the method of the buddhānusmṛti-samādhi.
This is indeed the profound Dharma.
Even when distracted, all sentient beings— whether walking or sitting—
can at all times and in all places practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
It does not hinder one's various affairs;
even until the end of life, one will perfect these practices.
Furthermore, by cultivating these various deeds, one will be reborn in the Western Pure Land.
Although the scriptural passages of the holy word stating that one attains rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha are few,
the teachings [on this subject] are extremely numerous.
I shall briefly set forth three or five points to enlighten those who are deluded.
First, as stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Amitābha Sūtra),
it teaches exclusively that by recollecting Amitābha Buddha, one attains rebirth in the Western Land.
The Buddhas of the six directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, extend their tongues to collectively testify that practitioners of mindfulness of the Buddha shall all attain rebirth.
This is evidenced by the scriptural passages concerning the three grades of rebirth—lower grade, upper birth; lower grade, middle birth; and lower grade, lower birth—in the *Contemplation Sūtra*.
They all declared that they would only recite the name of Amitābha Buddha to attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
They further said:
"The Buddha embraces and does not abandon those sentient beings who practice mindfulness of him."
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* further states: "Regarding the superior,
middling, and inferior grades of practitioners, although their practices vary in depth,
they all consist solely in single-mindedly and exclusively recollecting Amitābha Buddha."
One shall attain birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Furthermore, among the forty-eight great vows,
one specifically makes a single vow regarding the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha, saying:
"Even if [the thought of rebirth] does not arise after ten recitations, I shall not attain perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, in such sūtras as the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, and the *Bhadrapāla*,
it is taught that all sentient beings who single-mindedly and exclusively recollect Amitābha Buddha for seven days and seven nights shall obtain a vision of the Buddha.
Having thus questioned the Buddha, he asked:
"By practicing what dharma do sentient beings attain birth in the Pure Land?
Amitābha Buddha replied:
If one desires to be born in my land, one should constantly recollect my name without ceasing;
then one will be born in my land.
Furthermore, according to the *Drum-Sound Dhāraṇī Sūtra*:
He also teaches sentient beings to recollect Amitābha Buddha for ten days and ten nights so that they may attain birth in the Buddha-land.
Furthermore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
Through the samādhi of buddha-remembrance, one will certainly see the Buddha;
after the end of life, one will be born before the Buddha.
Seeing others at the point of death, one should exhort them to practice buddha-remembrance.
Furthermore, he displays sacred images for them to behold and revere.
Moreover, the *Sūtra on Divination and Observation* states:
"If one wishes to be reborn in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions..."
One shall attain rebirth there simply by recollecting the name of that land’s Buddha.
Such are the passages from immeasurable Mahāyāna sūtras.
It is frequently taught that through mindfulness of the Buddha one attains rebirth in the Pure Land;
my current exhortation to practice mindfulness of the Buddha is not intended to exclude other sublime practices one may cultivate.
It is simply that those who practice the recitation of the Buddha's name have frequently been encouraged and praised [to do so] whether walking or sitting.
Since one can practice this mindfulness of the Buddha until the end of one's life,
it is considered stable and convenient;
therefore, I exhort you to practice it.
Question: Those born in that Pure Land have not yet entered the stream of the noble ones; since they are still ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), [how can they be so]?
Being possessed of all various afflictions,
how could one not give rise to unwholesome karmas?
If they were to arise, it would contradict one's original vow.
It is said that in my land, among sentient beings, there is not even the name of anything unwholesome.
How is this to be interpreted?
The explanation states:
Although those ordinary persons born there have not yet attained the fruits of sainthood,
all their unwholesome states no longer manifest;
thus, the unwholesome do not proceed.
There are several meanings here:
either one eliminates those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) by taking the Noble Path as an object once it has arisen,
or one suppresses their active manifestation through the cultivation of skillful means for the Noble Path.
Alternatively, these evil objects may not arise because their conditions are lacking; or,
by constantly encountering favorable conditions, one has no occasion to commit transgressions.
Alternatively, by relying on various superior provisions, one prevents transgressions from arising; or,
by relying on the fundamental vows of the Buddha, evil cannot be provoked,
so that although the seeds of affliction exist, they cannot manifest.
Thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states:
"Although various exquisite incenses and flowers bring physical and mental delight to those who see them,
they do not increase the greed and attachment of sentient beings."
It is further stated that the water of eight virtues can cause those who drink it to increase various kinds of extraordinary and excellent roots of goodness,
just as the food of the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa performs the work of a Buddha through its offering.
Because of these various conditions, all evils do not arise.
Question: The Sūtra says:
There are four kinds of karma:
first, karma to be experienced in the present life;
second, karma to be experienced in the next life.
Third, karma with retribution in a subsequent life;
fourth, indeterminate karma.
The first three are determinate karma.
Because it necessarily brings about its retribution;
whereas the latter one is an indefinite karma,
because it may or may not bring about its retribution.
Furthermore, there are eight types of karma:
first, karma with fixed retribution but indefinite timing;
second, karma with fixed timing but indefinite retribution.

1. Determinate karma with fixed results in all three periods of time; 2. Indeterminate karma with fixed results in all four periods of time; 3. Determinate karma with fixed results in all four periods of time; 4. Indeterminate karma with fixed results in all four periods of time.
Of these, the first and third are determinate karma.
The second and fourth are indeterminate karmas.
The Sūtra states that the five heinous crimes are karmas with retribution in the next life.
If this is so, then both the retribution is fixed and the karma is fixed;
how then can one interpret the sutra’s statement that the five heinous crimes are extinguished and one attains birth in the Western Land?
The explanation says:

These four kinds and eight kinds of karma were taught by the Buddha within the ninefold scriptures of the provisional teachings for the sake of ordinary persons who do not believe in the results of karma.
It was spoken with intentional meaning that there are determinate retributions;
however, within the definitive teachings of the Mahāyāna,
it is taught that all karma is entirely indeterminate.
As stated in the nineteenth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
Jīvaka expounded the method of repentance for King Ajātaśatru,
whereby his transgressions were extinguished.
Furthermore, Your Servant has heard that the Buddha taught that cultivating a single virtuous mind can destroy a hundred kinds of evil,
just as a small amount of poison can harm sentient beings.
The same applies to even a small amount of goodness,
which can destroy great evil.
Furthermore, the thirty-first [chapter] states:
Good son, there are sentient beings who,
regarding the causal conditions of karma, harbor a light mind and lack faith;
for the sake of delivering them, I have made such a statement.
Good son, all karmic actions are either light or heavy.
Each of these two types—light and heavy—further has two varieties: first, the determinate; [the second being the indeterminate].
Second, it is not fixed.
Furthermore, it is said that there may be heavy karma that can be made light.
There may be light karma that can become heavy;
however, a person of wisdom, by the power of their insight,
is able to cause even the most grave karma of the hells to be experienced lightly in the present life.
For a foolish person, light karma in the present life results in heavy retribution in hell;
yet King Ajātaśatru, having repented for his transgressions, did not enter hell.
When Aṅgulimāla attained arhatship,
the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that what has not yet attained liberation is called "determined karma" (*niyata-karman*).
That which has already attained liberation is called "indeterminate karma.
Thus do various Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras all speak of the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) and so forth.
All these are called indeterminate karma;
they shall all be extinguished. Now, observing that this sutra is a Mahāyāna scripture, [it is clear that such benefits will be obtained].
It is clear that by mindful recollection of Amitābha Buddha, the five heinous offenses are extinguished;
what doubt could there be?
A question is asked:
As in various treatises, scriptural sūtras are cited together,
stating that there is black-black karma, white-white karma, mixed karma, and non-black-and-white karma that is without ripening.
Black-black karma refers to unwholesome karma of the desire realm.
White-white karma refers to... [wholesome karma].
Wholesome karma of the form and formless realms;
mixed karma is wholesome karma of the desire realm.
Karma that is neither black nor white and has no ripening is untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*).
It is not yet known what kind of karma one is currently creating in the Western [Pure Land].
Among the four types of karma, to which category does it belong?
The commentary states: Some say...
Among the four types of karma, this is subsumed under both pure-white karma and mixed karma;
for black-black karma is unwholesome and is capable of inducing rebirth in the three miserable realms.
How could it possibly summon the retribution of a pure land?
An outflow-free (anāsrava) karma cannot induce such retribution;
although its essence is pure, it is not a cause of maturation (vipāka-hetu).
Only the remaining two types of karma bring about the retribution of the Pure Land.
If one has not yet attained the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) of the higher realms,
but cultivates the practice for the Western Land with a mind belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu), [the result is as follows].
This refers to those who are reborn in the Western Land through mixed karma.
If, however, one has already subdued the afflictions of desire and gives rise to a pure mind belonging to the higher realms to be reborn in the Western Land, [the situation is different].
This refers to being born in a pure land through purely white karma.
Some say this is not so.
These three types of karma are categorized according to the two realms of desire and form within the defiled lands,

and are distinguished by their nature as either wholesome or unwholesome; they do not pertain to the discussion of "white-white" and other such wholesome karmas in relation to rebirth in the Western Land.
Furthermore, mixed karma refers to the karma of humans and devas within the desire realm;
it is capable of producing mixed retribution.
Although one experiences the fruit of pleasure, it also brings about the retribution of suffering.
Therefore, within the desire realm one experiences the fruits of suffering and pleasure;
whereas being reborn in the Pure Land is free from all suffering and is consistently peaceful and blissful.
How could it be permissible for mixed karma to serve as the cause for a pure land?
If only pure white karma were the cause for a pure land,
then it would be like one who has not yet attained the four dhyāna concentrations.
Since one is born in the Western Land due to what karma as its cause,
we know that the primary cause for the Pure Land is not subsumed under the aforementioned karma.
The preceding four types of karma subsume the [other] dharmas.
What harm is there in not exhausting the underlying principle?
Furthermore, there are scriptural passages stating that karma of the formless realm is not subsumed under the four types of karma;
by this one may infer [the same].
The four types of karma do not exhaustively encompass all karma.
Question: Furthermore, both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna treatises cite sūtras.
It is taught that there are three kinds of karma: meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable.
Among these three kinds of karma, one wonders which kind is used to attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The commentary states:
Some say that among the three types of karma, one is born in the Western Quarter by means of meritorious karma (*puṇya-karma*) and immovable karma (*āniñjya-karma*).
The three blessings are themselves meritorious karma;
if one attains the concentrated mind of the sixteen contemplations,
they constitute immovable karma.
Some say that it is not subsumed under the three types of karma,
because the three types of karma are all explained with reference to the karma of the defiled lands and do not pertain to the discussion of the pure lands.
Therefore, the karma for the Pure Land is not [limited to] the three types of karma.
Question: It is not yet known how one may attain birth in the Western [Pure Land].
How many kinds of supreme benefits are there for exhorting sentient beings to be reborn [there]?
The commentary states:
According to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*, and the forty-eight great vows of the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha-sūtra*,
thirty benefits are briefly enumerated. What are these thirty?
First, the benefit of enjoying the purity of Buddha-fields adorned with various merits;
second, the benefit of the Dharma-joy of the Mahāyāna;
third, the benefit of drawing near to and making offerings to Amitāyus Buddha.
Fourth is the benefit of traveling through the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas;
fifth is the benefit of hearing the Dharma and receiving predictions of enlightenment from all Buddhas;
sixth is the benefit of swiftly fulfilling the provisions of merit and wisdom.
Seventh, the benefit of swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
eighth, the benefit of being gathered together in the same assembly as all the great beings;
ninth, the benefit of never falling back.
Eleventh, the benefit of the ten immeasurable practices and vows increasing and progressing in every thought-moment;
twelfth, the benefit of the parrot-sarīs proclaiming the sound of the Dharma;
thirteenth, the benefit of the pure wind moving the trees like the music of celestial hosts.
Thirteenth, the flowing water of mani-jewels proclaims the benefits of suffering and emptiness;
fourteenth, various musical sounds perform the benefits of the sounds of all dharmas;
fifteenth, among the forty-eight great vows, there is the benefit of forever severing the three miserable realms.
Sixteenth, the benefit of a body of true golden color;
seventeenth, the benefit of having no beauty or ugliness of form;
eighteenth, the benefit of being fully endowed with the five supernormal powers.
Nineteenth, the benefit of abiding in the stage of right determination;
twentieth, the benefit of being free from all unwholesome states;
twenty-first, the benefit of a long life span.
Twenty-two: the benefit of clothing and food being provided spontaneously;
twenty-three: the benefit of experiencing only manifold pleasures;
twenty-four: the benefit of the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Twenty-fifth, the benefit of not being born as a woman lacking jewels;
twenty-sixth, the benefit of not falling into the Lesser Vehicle;
twenty-seventh, the benefit of being free from the eight difficulties.
28. Attainment of the benefit of the three dharmas of patience.
29. The body possesses radiance, with a constant light throughout the entire night.
30. Attainment of the benefit of the strength of Nārāyaṇa.
I have briefly enumerated thirty benefits;
were they expanded, they would be immeasurable and boundless.
For this reason, I exhort you to be reborn in the Western Land.
If one remains in this Sahā world,
one will long circulate through birth and death, suffering only the loss of thirty years;
how could there ever have been any benefit from it?
Question: The *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states that one must cultivate ten kinds of mindfulness in order to attain rebirth [in the Pure Land].
First, one should constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
Second, one must not disparage the conduct of any sentient being;
if one does so, one will ultimately never attain rebirth there.
Third, one must give rise to deep compassion for all sentient beings and harbor no intent to harm them.
Fourth, they resolve to protect the Dharma, not begrudging even their own bodies or lives.
Fifth, they do not give rise to denial or slander regarding any phenomenon.
Sixth, they develop a resolute mind and a profound mind within the practice of patience.
Pure and free from craving for gain and offerings,
they give rise to the mind of omniscience in seven ways,
constantly and daily mindful of it without rest or cessation.
Eighth, one gives rise to a mind of respect toward all sentient beings;
setting aside pride, one speaks with humility.
Ninth, one does not develop a mind of attachment toward worldly talk.
Drawing near to the mind of enlightenment, they deeply give rise to various causes and conditions for roots of goodness;
tenth, they do not give rise to a mind of clamor or distraction,
but with right mindfulness contemplate the Buddha and eliminate all discursive thoughts.

According to this scriptural passage, the "ten recitations" (śuddha-smṛti) are distinct [from the ten recitations of the name]. How then can one attain rebirth by merely uttering the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times?
Is this not an error?
The commentary states:
The practice gates for rebirth in the Western Land are not limited to one;
there may be, for instance, three types of merit.
Whether by means of the sixteen contemplations or through rebirth in the nine grades,
each of their respective practices leads them all to attain birth in the Pure Land.
One will be reborn in the Pure Land.
According to the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra*,
one may also attain birth there by practicing ten methods for rebirth therein, as personally recounted [by Maitreya].
The *Contemplation Sūtra* itself states that those of the lowest of the low grades attain rebirth by reciting the Buddha’s name ten times at the moment of death;
each of these is a sacred teaching.
Thus, they mutually explain the dharma-gates for rebirth in the Pure Land.
All constitute pure karma.
For what reason do you take that to be correct while rejecting this as false?
It is merely that you yourself do not understand the sutras,
and thus you have misled other scholars;
it is like the nine grades of those who have entered the stream.
The Commandant of the County served in the inner palace;
he was able to master one of the Confucian classics and pursued the studies of a jinshi candidate.
Some were ranked among the meritorious grades outside the official registers;
some were born into the seven-colored hereditary lineages;
and some became sons of the ten-year-old rank.
They all attained entry into the stream [of the Dharma] and were appointed as assistant magistrates;
how could they be restricted to a single occupation, such as that of a Scholar of the Literary Forest?
Rebirth is likewise so;
it is not that one is born in that Western Land through practice alone.
Therefore, both the gates of meditative concentration and non-concentration are fully contained within the teachings of the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*.
The practice of cultivating merit through the three grades of rebirth originates from the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Merely reciting the name of the Buddha is,
indeed, the teaching of Amitābha.
Whether upholding the sublime scriptures of the Mahāyāna or filially supporting one's two parents,
these constitute the roots of goodness pertaining to both the mundane and the supramundane.
Regarding the two types of karma— concentrated and non-concentrated—
they both serve to sustain the body and speech; since both wholesome states arise together in the Pure Land,
how could they be restricted to a single gate?
You must read widely across the various scriptures to open up right faith in living beings.
How can you observe only a single sutra and immediately compose a treatise that serves as a compass for all?
To claim that the remaining teachings of the Noble Ones are not causes for rebirth—
how deluded this is! Furthermore,
there are ten thousand ways of cultivating the causes.
The attainment of the fruits has many stages;
it cannot be restricted to a single cause, for causes do not lack distinct categories. Question:
Now, the Bodhisattva’s practice takes the benefiting of sentient beings as his primary concern;
with great compassion arising in every thought-moment,
it is logically necessary that he personally traverse the evil realms.
Having traversed the three miserable realms, I take pity on those submerged in suffering and vow to cause them all to be free from it.
Now, I shall abandon this defiled world and aspire to be born in the Pure Land.
Seeking only their own happiness and wishing no benefit for others,
they have been bound by the ties of beginningless causal conditions— parents, brothers, six types of relatives, and friends—
and have all been confined within the prison of the triple world.
To abandon them and fail to rescue them,
utterly devoid of compassion—
how could this constitute the mind of a Great Being?
To act thus is the practice of a bodhisattva.
To now wish to be born in a pure land is not a virtuous mind.
I do not know its origin;
I pray that you will explain this matter.
The commentary says:
Now, to resolve upon bodhicitta and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva,
one must necessarily give rise to great compassion.
Out of compassion for sentient beings,
he extensively brings about their deliverance, uprooting suffering and bestowing peace;
yet, there are varying degrees of depth in his practice.
The faculties have higher and lower levels.
If a bodhisattva’s deep learning is dominated by great compassion,
they will have attained non-retrogression and will not fear harm to themselves.
Desiring solely to benefit others,
they mostly act extensively for the welfare of beings in defiled realms;
few are born in the Pure Lands to personally attend upon the Honored Sages.
Alternatively, there may be bodhisattvas of shallow practice whose superior great wisdom still undergoes regression;
though they possess compassion for suffering sentient beings,
they regress from the bodhisattva conduct whenever they encounter adverse conditions.
By committing various evil karmas, one loses the bodhicitta.
This is explained at length in the *Bodhisattva-mūla-karman-avataṃsaka-sūtra* regarding the Prince Dharmatāla and others.
This constitutes the loss of both self-benefit and benefit for others.
Since this results in harm to both oneself and others,
I vow to be reborn in a Pure Land to distance myself from such adverse conditions,
to draw near to the Noble Honored Ones, and to constantly hear the True Dharma.
Together with various bodhisattvas, they gathered in one place;
traveling to other directions, they made offerings by scattering flowers and further heard the sublime, pure, and wondrous Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
From moment to moment they progress further without ever regressing;
furthermore, there is no longer any destruction of the supreme resolve for the Path by those of the Two Vehicles, icchantikas, or non-Buddhists.
Although their hearts that uproot suffering do not abandon this resolve for even a single thought-moment.
The practice of self-benefit is the foundation for the practice of benefiting others.
If the foundation is not firm, the branches will likewise not be stable.
Therefore, one must first aspire to be born in a pure land to nurture the roots and sprouts of a bodhisattva’s bodhi, ensuring they become steadfast.
Even if you encounter adverse conditions, you shall not regress;
only then may you leave this Pure Land to be reborn in Saṃsāra,

in order to rescue and gather those with whom you share a karmic affinity— your parents, six types of relatives, friends, teachers, and all sentient beings throughout the Dharma realm who have been submerged in suffering since beginningless time.
This meaning has already been extensively cited by Master Chao in the *Anleji* (Anthology on Peace and Bliss):
"Suppose one's parents were drowning and about to be swept away by a swift current."
The only son followed him into the water and immediately attempted to rescue him,
but he could not save him;
consequently, he was drowned.
A single son returns home, prepares a boat,
and goes directly to the deep current to rescue his parent from distress;
this principle is likewise so.
Those who possess wisdom attain understanding through analogies.
It is asked:
The *Treatise on the Pure Land* says:
In the realm of the Mahāyāna roots of goodness and so forth, even the name "reproach" does not exist.
Women, those with impaired faculties, and those of the two vehicles do not arise there.
How, then, could there be śrāvakas in that realm?
But does the Sūtra not state that there are immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples, all of whom are arhats and so forth?
The commentary says:
There are four explanations for this.
One interpretation states:
regarding those of the two vehicles whose seeds do not arise,
this is according to what is taught in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
There are five vehicles of sentient beings.
Since beginningless time, they have naturally and inherently possessed the distinct lineages of these five vehicles.
The first is the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
Second, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas;
third, the vehicle of the śrāvakas;
fourth, the vehicle of humans and devas.
Regarding the five indeterminate vehicles,
it is said that those of the two-vehicle lineage do not arise;
these refer to the pratyekabuddha vehicle and the human-and-deva vehicle.
Those who follow the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas are certain to receive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, yet they are mostly born in worlds where no Buddha resides;
they cannot be born in a pure land,
because a Buddha is present in a pure land.
Furthermore, they do not believe that there are pure lands in the ten directions;
they hold that those in the vehicles of humans and devas are merely ordinary beings who transmigrate through birth and death,
and thus cannot be reborn in a pure land.
This is because the sentient beings of the Pure Land are all destined to attain unsurpassed bodhi;
thus there are two interpretations. The former meaning is not correct.
If those of the two vehicles do not produce [the aspiration for enlightenment],
yet take up the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas or the vehicle of humans and devas,
then those of the śrāvaka vehicle will attain birth [in the higher realms].
For what reason is it said that there is a "boundary of Mahāyāna roots of goodness"?
Furthermore, why is it said that not only do these three kinds of entities not exist, but even the names for these three kinds do not exist?
Now, the seeds of the two vehicles do not arise.
Regardless of whether one belongs to the vehicle of humans or devas,
among the three vehicles, excluding the two vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is what is meant by "the seeds of the two vehicles not arising."
Question: If the seeds of the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not arise,
for what reason are there śrāvakas in that land?
Answer: To say that there are no two vehicles (dviyāna) means that there are no [beings] of fixed lineage belonging to the two vehicles.
In that land, those of the two vehicles are all śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage,
all of whom are capable of turning their minds toward and entering the Mahāyāna.
The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, relying on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, composed various treatises.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states:
"One should consult the *Viniscaya-saṃgrahaṇī* to explain the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
The *Viniscaya-saṃgrahaṇī* is precisely the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* section within the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

Now, in composing the *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on the Rebirth in the Pure Land), I again rely upon that treatise’s fundamental tenet regarding the meaning of the five vehicles and their respective dispositions; therefore,
it is said that those of the two-vehicle lineage are not born [in the Pure Land].
Third, following the explanations of the former virtuous masters, this passage states:
"There are two kinds of śrāvakas: first, those who follow the Dharma of the ignorant (dhammānusārī)."
The first refers to those śrāvakas who, in this life, have not yet been able to turn away from the Lesser Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle.
The second refers to those who are not deluded regarding the Dharma,
meaning they have already been able to turn away from the Lesser Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle.
The former are called those of the two vehicles' lineage;
because they do not turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle and do not believe in the existence of the Pure Land,
they have no aspiration to be born there.
The latter refers to those who do not belong to the lineage of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha);
although they practice minor deeds, they aspire to be born in the Pure Land through faith in the Mahāyāna.
The fourth explanation states:
When those who have turned their minds toward the Great Vehicle cultivate the noble path to sever delusions,
it is all for the sake of proceeding toward unsurpassed bodhi;
they are not called followers of the two vehicles.
To achieve the fruit of Buddhahood, one must necessarily sever the two attachments to persons and phenomena;
both the active afflictions and their latent tendencies must be extinguished, and the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena must be realized.
Only upon reaching ultimate fulfillment can one be called a Buddha.
For those [followers] of the former stage, it was the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna),
which involves weariness toward the grasping at a self and the afflictions.
For this reason, they first sever [the afflictions];
by attaining those four fruits, they receive the name Arhat and are also called Śrāvakas.
However, they are not of the Hīnayāna.
The name "Arhat" does not refer exclusively to those of the lesser fruit,
for even a Buddha may be designated as an Arhat.
As stated in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*:
After the Buddha had delivered Ājñātakauṇḍinya, he said:
"In this trichiliocosm there are two arhats:
one is the Buddha."
The second was Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
Therefore, the title of Arhat is not merely a designation for those of the Lesser Vehicle;
the name Śrāvaka also applies to those of the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra says:
"We are now truly śrāvakas; by means of the sound of the Buddha-way, we cause all to hear."
These are indeed bodhisattvas and śrāvakas;
we, however, are now true arhats among all the world’s devas, humans, māras, and brahmās.
They should universally receive offerings therein;
these are indeed Mahāyāna bodhisattvas.
Although their names are identical to those of the [followers of] the small fruits, they differ nonetheless.
The meaning is distinct.
Those śrāvakas, arhats, and others in the Pure Land are all persons who seek unsurpassed bodhi.
Therefore, they do not belong to the lineage of the two vehicles,
nor are they designated by the names of the two vehicles;
this is because they have already resolved their minds upon the Mahāyāna.
Although they are called "śrāvakas," this is not the name used for those of the Hīnayāna.
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
that Ānanda turned his mind toward the Mahāyāna.
The Buddha bestowed upon him the prediction of enlightenment, naming him Tathāgata Śikhin Sāgarabuddhi-vaiśāradya-abhijñā-rāja.
When it came time for the compilation of the teachings, he attained arhatship;
how could this be considered a retreat from the Mahāyāna mind?
They seek after minor fruits.
Furthermore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra states: Kāśyapa said:
Since that time, I have no longer exhorted others toward the practices of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
For what reason, then, did you exhort Ānanda to attain the fruit of arhatship on the day of the council?
Thus, one knows that the fruit of arhatship is not the fruit of the Lesser Vehicle.
All the practices undertaken by Ānanda after receiving his prediction from the Buddha were entirely directed toward Buddhahood.
Thus, one should know that this is precisely the practice of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva.
However, for those who proceed directly, they first sever the afflictions of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha-kleśa*).
For those who cultivate the Way, they sever the afflictions of attachment to the person (*pudgalagrāha-kleśa*) until reaching the Diamond-like Mind (*vajropama-citta*).
By suddenly eliminating [these obstacles], one immediately attains Buddhahood.
From the very beginning, the bodhisattvas who proceed directly have intended solely to sever and eliminate attachment to dharmas.
Therefore, one intentionally retains afflictions until they are exhausted, at which point one possesses the Buddha’s omniscience;
for the subtle afflictions of dharma-attachment are difficult to eliminate and obstruct the great fruit of perfect enlightenment (sambodhi).
In relation to the śrāvaka, this is pure and neutral;
in relation to the bodhisattva, it is obscured and neutral.
The bodhisattva specifically detests it.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The extreme blindness and darkness of the cognitive obstruction refers to the separate apprehension of the ultimate and the conventional."
For this reason, they are biased toward and prioritize severance.
Ordinary people cling to afflictions, which obstruct them from nirvana;
śrāvakas, for their part, feel profound revulsion toward birth and death.
Seeking only their own benefit,
they are unable to cultivate and study the Buddha’s omniscience;
therefore, they lack the intention to sever the afflictions of clinging to phenomena.
Because the afflictions of clinging to phenomena do not obstruct *nirvāṇa*,
all śrāvakas attain *parinirvāṇa* once they have completely severed clinging to a personal self (*pudgala-grāha*).
These śrāvakas are currently at the stage of the seven preparatory practices (*saptavidha-prayoga*) or in the stages prior to them.
Those of the middle three grades first seek the state of a śrāvaka;
they deeply loathe the afflictions of grasping at a self and apply mental attention to sever these delusions.
Although they have now been reborn in the Western Land and have turned their minds toward seeking the fruit of Buddhahood,
they do so primarily because they have grown weary of the afflictions of human grasping.
Returning to their original habitual tendencies, he teaches them the Four Noble Truths,
causing them to fully sever the afflictions of both the delusions of view and the delusions of cultivation that constitute those persons' attachments.
At the time of severing those delusions:
One must perceive the principle of the Four Noble Truths and employ the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*) to sever these afflictions.
Severing the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) is called "stream-entry" (*srotāpanna*);
it is not by abiding in that path itself that one is named a stream-enterer.
Having severed the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, one is called an Arhat.
Just as an Arhat is free from all afflictions,
this name [of "Arhat"] is applied here merely as a designation for the practice of a Bodhisattva.
Both the gradual and the sudden practitioners perform the bodhisattva practices and together seek the fruit of Buddhahood;
although both are equally named "bodhisattvas," [they differ in their approach].
Nevertheless, those who follow a circuitous path may also be called "śrāvakas," for they awaken to the Way by means of sound; furthermore, because they are originally of small capacity,
they may also be called "bodhisattvas."
Because they seek after great enlightenment,
and because bodhisattvas proceed directly toward it,
they are simply called "bodhisattvas."
They are not called śrāvakas because they did not originally awaken to the Way by means of sound.
The Buddha uses these two names to distinguish between those disciples who follow the gradual and those who follow the sudden path.
Therefore, it is said that his immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples are all arhats,
beyond what can be known through calculation; the same is true for the bodhisattvas as well.
Question: The World of Universal Fragrance and the Land of Ultimate Bliss are both Mahāyāna pure buddha-fields.
For what reason is there not even the name of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas in the World of Universal Fragrance (Sahagandhā),
where there is only a pure assembly of great bodhisattvas,
whereas in the World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) there are immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples?
"Is this assembly of śrāvakas not of the Hīnayāna?
The commentary states:
"Although these two buddha-fields are both realms of that Mahāyāna,"
However, among the noble assembly, there are both those with universal capacity and those with limited capacity.
In the World of Fragrant Incense, there are only those who aspire to the Mahāyāna;
here in this Sahā world, one practices the eight dharmas.
Free from all blemishes,
they are born in that Pure Land,
where they hear only the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, the Sūtra states:
"Therein there are only a pure assembly of great Bodhisattvas;
even the names of the two vehicles do not exist."
In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, those śrāvakas who have turned their minds from the Lesser Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle are all reborn in that Pure Land; there,
they universally hear the teachings of both the gradual and sudden Mahāyāna, which harmonize the three vehicles and return them to the One.
They resolve upon the Great Mind,
practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, and,
by virtue of their prior habitual cultivation, sever the delusions of grasping at a person.
Although they practice the bodhisattva path,
because they have first severed the seeds of their afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), they are named śrāvaka arhats.
Although they are called śrāvakas,
it is by means of the sound of the Buddha-way that they cause all to hear.
Although they are called arhats, [it is for this same reason].
They are worthy of receiving offerings from all the worlds.
Therefore, both are equally within the realm of the Mahāyāna; the distinction lies only between the two groups: those who proceed directly and those who take a circuitous route. Question:
As it is among the roots of goodness of the four stages of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) in the Hīnayāna:
at the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), one does not accept false teachings;
at the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), one does not sever the roots of goodness.
Through patience, one is not reborn in the evil realms;
through the Supreme Mundane Dharma, one necessarily enters the Noble Path.
This refers to reaching the stage of the inferior grade of patience.
Only then does one attain the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the evil destinies.
Although Bodhisattvas do not undergo the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) for the sake of benefiting sentient beings,
they have not yet personally attained the non-analytical cessation of the three evil destinies.
How is it that an extremely evil ordinary person,
by reciting the Buddha’s name even once or ten times throughout their life,
immediately attains the permanent severance of the three evil realms and is no longer reborn there?
The commentary states:
Those in the stage of the Small Vehicle who possess the roots of goodness of the *nirvedhabhāgīya* reside in a defiled land, a place of regression.
Because the two roots of goodness of the "Heated" stage (*ūṣmagata*) are still subject to regression,
it is only upon reaching the root of goodness of "Patience" (*kṣānti*) that one attains the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the evil destinies.
However, the Sarvāstivāda school also permits another interpretation.
Prior to the stage of patience (kṣānti), one attains the non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) of the miserable destinies;
however, this is not certain.
Thus, even if born in the Western Land [of Sukhāvatī], one may still remain in a superior state.
May they constantly behold the assembly of sages and perpetually hear the sublime Dharma;
may their extraordinary practices and vows increase and advance in every thought-moment.
Successive evil karmas are gradually extinguished,
while successive wholesome qualities are cultivated and increased moment by moment.
Because those adverse conditions for evil are absent, one attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Having attained non-retrogression,
they go to the various evil realms by the power of their vows to rescue and deliver those who are submerged and sinking.
Taking birth through the power of vows,
one does not go there by means of karma and does not fall into the evil destinies;
thus, the meaning is not contradictory.
*An Explanation of the Multitude of Doubts Concerning the Pure Land*, Fascicle Five.
*An Explanation of the Multitude of Doubts Concerning the Pure Land*, Fascicle Six.
Composed by the Great Virtue Huai’gan of Qianfu Monastery in the Western Capital.
Question: Do all sentient beings who seek rebirth in a Pure Land necessarily attain it, or are there some who do not?
If all were to attain rebirth, the realm of sentient beings would be inexhaustible.
For what reason would the Land of Ultimate Bliss have a day of exhaustion,
or Amitābha Buddha have a time of parinirvāṇa?
Furthermore, why would Flower-Cluster Bodhisattva and Mountain-Ocean Wisdom Bodhisattva not have made vows [to that effect]?
If there should be even a single sentient being who has not yet reached birth in the land of Amitābha Buddha,
and I were to attain birth first, I would never take supreme enlightenment;
