nor can it be said that all sentient beings have been born and I am the very last to be born.
If there are those who do not cause [the aspiration] to arise,
for what reason can those who have committed the five heinous crimes, the ten evil deeds, or the extremely grave offense of slandering the True Dharma attain rebirth?
Why would there be any sinner more extreme than these who could not be born [there]?
Furthermore, a sutra states: "It shall also cause all sentient beings to attain birth in the Pure Land.
Those who cannot be born there would, [by that logic], not be sentient beings."
Furthermore, since the Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One’s mind of loving-kindness is all-pervasive,
for what reason is this one person alone excluded from that number and not allowed to be born [in the Pure Land]?
There would be the fault of inequality regarding infinite great compassion.
The commentary states:
There are two interpretations of this.
First interpretation:
All sentient beings are caused to attain birth [in the Pure Land],
because the Buddha’s great compassionate mind is immeasurable.
Arousing a mind of loving-kindness, they bestow benefit upon all;
their great vows of universal resolve do not discriminate between enemies and kin.
Therefore, there is no sentient being who does not receive [this benefit].
If that is so, how can the objection previously raised be resolved?
The answer is:
although [the Buddha] causes all to be born [in his presence], the aspirations and intentions of sentient beings are diverse and differentiated.
Some do not believe in the True Dharma;
some take pleasure in and are attached to the Hīnayāna;
some love to dwell in defiled regions.
Some, out of great compassion, dwell in this defiled land to uproot suffering and rescue all sentient beings;
others prefer to be reborn in other Buddha-fields to practice and make offerings.
Such various and diverse practices and mentalities cannot all be made to arise simultaneously in the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
although they may all attain birth there, those who are born are inexhaustible.
For example, although all sentient beings possess buddha-nature,
even though they are destined to become buddhas, it is not necessarily the case that they will all do so;
for if they were all to become buddhas, the realm of sentient beings would come to an end.
This case is likewise.
The previous argument remains unimpeded;
for now, observe that the karmic conditions of one class of beings who delight in being born in the Western Paradise have, for the most part, come to an end.
The Bodhisattva makes a vow that even after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, there shall be those who are not led to be born in the Western Land.
This is the second explanation.
Furthermore, there are also those who do not cause others to be born in the Western Land.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"All those who were to be delivered have already been delivered.
It further says:
When his work of transformation was completed, he transferred his spirit into nirvana.
From this we may infer that [the previous statements] were spoken in reference to those with whom he had a karmic connection.
This is not discussed by taking all sentient beings as a whole.
Although the Buddha’s vast mind encompasses the entire realm of sentient beings,
those who receive his transformation and are delivered are only those with whom he has a karmic affinity.
Therefore, there is the possibility of an end to rebirth;
the Tathāgata has a day of parinirvāṇa;
and the Bodhisattva reaches his final departure.
Avalokiteśvara has attained the rank of a successor to Buddhahood;
therefore, those who attain rebirth there are not universal in number.
Question: Since it has already been stated that there are no women in the Pure Land,
how is this so in the *Dhāraṇī-sūtra of King Drum-Sound*?
It is said that the land of Amitābha Buddha is named Qingtai (Pure Peace).
The city where the Holy King resides is ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
and it is filled with those of the Kṣatriya caste.
His father was named Candra-vimala-cakravartin,
his mother was named Viśeṣavatī-suvaktrā,
and his son was named Candraprabha.
The disciple who serves him is named Vimalakīrti;
the disciple of wisdom is named Prabhāsa;
and the one diligent in spiritual power is named Mahāvikurvaṇa.
The Māra was named Ajita; Devadatta was named Śāntamati.
If there were no women, how could there be a mother?
The commentary states:
Now, there are three explanations.
The first explanation says:
The Buddha has both the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) and the Transformation Body (nirmāṇakāya).
According to the *Amitābha Sūtra*,
that which is described there is the Enjoyment Body.
The one who expounds the *Drum-Sound-King Sūtra* is the Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body). Furthermore,
within the Saṃbhogakāya (Enjoyment Body), he emanates for the sake of Bodhisattvas at various stages who have undergone the transformation of birth-and-death.
In the state of manifesting a womb-born body, there are parents and so forth;
in the state of transformation through emanation, one manifests an emanation-born body and thus has no parents.
Two interpretations state this.
These—parents, cities, and so forth—are all dharmas of merit.
As it is said in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra:
"Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of Bodhisattvas."
"Skillful means as the father," and so forth;
likewise, by means of various merits, he assumes various names and teaches various dharmas.
Just as Mañjuśrī encountered the youth Sudhana to the east of the city of Vairambhya—
where "east of the city of Vairambhya" is itself a name for a meritorious quality—
it is the same here as well.
All merits are designated as "parents" and so forth.
As for the phrase "the kingdom is pure and tranquil," this reveals the Tathāgata’s most perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*.
Its nature is pure, hence it is called "clear" (qing). Its substance is expansive, hence it is termed "serene" (tai).
Because all virtues rely upon it, it is called a "land" (guo).
That city, ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth,
manifests the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) of the Tathāgata;
this wisdom fully encompasses the ten knowledges (daśa-jñāna).
It possesses the ten powers;
because it is accomplished through the ten perfections, it is called ten thousand yojanas.
Within it, the Kṣatriya caste is fully present.
The Kṣatriya caste refers to the royal lineage.
Within the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) reside the seeds of all dharmas and the merits of a Dharma-king as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
therefore, it is said to be "filled with the Kṣatriya lineage."
The father named Candrottara is this Vajrasamādhi. Now,
the moon has the capacity to dispel darkness.
The function of samādhi is to eliminate delusions.
As for the Wheel-Turning Sage King:
generally, a Golden Wheel-Turning King is honored above all minor regional kings.
The diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) excels all other samādhis.
As for "the face of supreme and wondrous beauty":
among all parts of the body, the face is foremost.
Among the six perfections, Prajñāpāramitā is honored as supreme.
This Prajñā, being preeminent, is the mother of the Great Teacher;
her son is named Candraprabha.
The Buddha is likened to the sun;
the supreme radiance of the Bodhisattva’s merit is called his "son," and next is termed the "lunar light."
The disciple who serves him is named Vimalakīrti;
this reveals the Tathāgata’s wisdom of equality,
which constantly contemplates the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) and is thus termed "serving."
Not coexisting with afflictions, he is named Vimalakīrti;
his wise disciple is named Prabhāsaṃgṛhītṛ.
This reveals the Tathāgata’s *pratyavekṣaṇājñāna* (the wisdom of profound observation).
All dharmas are clearly understood without exception;
therefore, it is called "Gathering Light.
The disciple of divine power named Mahāvikurvaṇa is as follows.
This reveals the Tathāgata’s wisdom of accomplished action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*),
which manifests various transformations of body, speech, and mind; therefore,
it is called the "basis of supernormal power" (*ṛddhipāda*).
These three wisdoms follow the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) and are thus called its younger brothers;
because they arise from the mirror-like wisdom, they are called its sons.
The Māra king is named Ajita (The Unconquerable).
This reveals the merit of the Tathāgata’s great compassion.
Out of great compassion, the Buddha takes pity on sentient beings;
he constantly dwells within the cycle of birth and death to uproot suffering for those who possess it.
Māra delights in birth and death;
therefore, he is called the Māra King.
This great compassion surpasses the compassion of the two vehicles.
Therefore, he is named "Unsurpassed" (Ajita).
As for Devadatta being named "Quiescent Mind" (Śāntamati), it is because the afflictions are turbulent and agitate the practitioner; thus, Devadatta serves as a metaphor for them.
The Tathāgata contemplates all afflictions as being precisely nirvāṇa;
therefore, Devadatta is named "Quiescence.
This is explained in terms of his various merits.
The names "father" and "mother" are established for this purpose;
it does not mean that within the Pure Land, Amitābha Buddha has a separate set of parents born from a womb.
The third explanation states:
As stated in the Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra and other texts,
the Buddhas attain enlightenment in both pure and impure lands;
the manifestations of their attainment of enlightenment vary in various ways.
There may be bodhisattvas who,
having been born in that land, cultivate the bodhisattva practices and there attain perfect enlightenment.
The world remains unchanged;
the names and the eons likewise do not differ.
There may be some bodhisattvas.
Born in that land, one attains perfect enlightenment in that very land;
the world remains unchanged.
The names and the eons are established with distinct titles.
There may be bodhisattvas who are born in that land and cultivate the bodhisattva practices.
He immediately attained equal and perfect enlightenment in that land.
At the time of his becoming a Buddha, the world was transformed so as to surpass the previous world;
both his name and the name of the eon were completely changed.
As explained in detail in the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*,
there may be bodhisattvas who,
having been born in this world, [practice as follows].
They shall go to other worlds and attain perfect enlightenment,
as described in detail in the Karuṇāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra.
These are all the differing vows made by bodhisattvas during their causal stage.
Therefore, there are such distinctions.
Furthermore, as in various sūtras,
there may be some bodhisattvas.
A youth leaves the household life and attains equal and perfect enlightenment;
or there may be a bodhisattva who takes a wife and fathers children.
Having renounced the five desires, he attained equal and perfect enlightenment.
Some were born in this world and attained the Way therein;
others were born in another world and attained the Way in that other world.
As stated in the Lotus Sūtra:
for example, the dragon girl was born here in this Sahā world within the realm of animals.
Thereafter, she went to the stainless world in the southern quarter; there,
she cast off her female body and was immediately transformed into a male,
attaining equal and perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata Puṣpaprabha was born from a womb;
he attained perfect enlightenment within a pure land.
Thus, the sūtra says:
When the Buddha was a prince, he abandoned his kingdom and renounced worldly glory;
in his very last existence, he left the household life and attained the Way of Buddhahood.
By this one may know [the truth].
The Buddha Huaguang underwent womb-birth in another world and attained perfect enlightenment within a pure land; had he not been born from a womb, [he would not have done so].
It would be better to be a prince who abandons his kingdom and renounces worldly glory;
now, Amitābha Buddha is also like this.
He received that womb-birth in the Land of Purity and attained equal and perfect enlightenment in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
It was asked:
If those such as Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana could not transcend the trichiliocosm with the five supernormal powers they had attained,
how could an ordinary person be born there?
One is immediately able to descend as far as to see and hear the supernatural powers [of others] and so forth,
surpassing hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddha-worlds;
by this one may infer accordingly.
Those who attain rebirth in the Pure Land are all Bodhisattvas of great capacity and great practice;
it is not something that ordinary beings are able to achieve.
The commentary states:
This meaning is not fixed.
One cannot claim that the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) attained by sages in an impure land are superior to those of ordinary beings in a pure land.
Just as it is certain that those in Uttarakuru have a fixed lifespan of a thousand years,
what prevents those in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception from having a lifespan of eighty thousand kalpas while still undergoing premature death?
How could it be that because the karmic retribution of the heavens is long,
one does not permit the existence of a lifespan cut short by premature death?
It is the same with the Pure Land.
Although they are ordinary beings,
because their karma for rebirth is superior,
or because the retribution of the pure land is powerful, they ride upon the fundamental vows of the Buddha.
Either by relying on the majestic spiritual power of the sages,
or by being endowed with favorable conditions for sustaining life,
or by attaining the wondrous samādhis of the Mahāyāna.
It is by relying on this that one attains supernormal powers; since those who excel in this are truly sages,
what is there to marvel at?
Furthermore, when those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the five destinies are about to seek rebirth,
the supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) they obtain through their karma surpasses that attained by the two vehicles through cultivation.
What hindrance is there to the beings in the Pure Land attaining a supernormal power superior even to these sages?
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The untainted roots of goodness of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are not equal to the tainted roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva who has first resolved upon the path and begun their practice."
Question: It is not yet known whether the sentient beings who are reborn in the Western Paradise undergo the cycle of birth and death characterized by fragmentation (*vibhaṅga-jarāmaraṇa*).
"This refers to the death and rebirth of transformation.
The commentary states:
"In that land, from the eighth stage upward, the bodhisattvas exclusively undergo the death and rebirth of transformation."
From the seventh stage downward and from the first fruit upward,
there is either the death-and-rebirth of the segmented realm (prādeśika-maraṇa) or the death-and-rebirth of the transformation realm (pariṇāma-maraṇa).
Those who proceed directly— the three grades of sages and those of the ten stages of faith and so forth—
all still undergo only the transformation of birth and death (fen-duan). Nevertheless, their lifespans are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas.
He possesses the thirty-two marks;
his body is of a true golden color—an empty body and an infinite essence.
He is sovereign in the five supernatural powers, subtle and inconceivable.
Question: Since it is said that there is no suffering within the Pure Land,
I do not yet know [how this relates] among the three sufferings and the eight sufferings.
"There is no suffering whatsoever.
The commentary states:
"If one relies on the explanations in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and other texts of the Hīnayāna,"
The Buddha’s body still possesses the three types of suffering;
among the eight sufferings, five still remain:
namely, the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging.
Only three types of suffering are absent:
namely, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of encountering the hated, and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;
for the fifteen elements (dhātus) of the Tathāgata’s body are with outflows (sāsrava).
These refer to the five sense faculties, the five objects, and the five consciousnesses.

The three realms— namely, the mind element (manodhātu), the mental-object element (dharmadhātu), and the mind-consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu)— comprise both the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava).
Because this is a body subject to outflows (*sāsrava*),
there are the five types of suffering, such as birth; yet,
one cuts off the fetters of all afflictions (*kleśa*), such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
There are no three types of suffering.
This is because the suffering of separation from what is loved is the fetter of craving,
and the suffering of encountering what is hated is the fetter of aversion.
The suffering of not obtaining what one seeks is the fetter of craving (*rāga*).
Although the Buddha took pity on the Śākyas who were slaughtered by King Virūḍhaka,
this was not the suffering of being separated from what is loved (*priyaviprayoga*).
Devadatta caused blood to flow;
Cañcā tied a bowl [to his neck];
a pit of fire and poisoned rice were prepared, and a multitude of enemies gathered.
It is not the suffering of association with the disliked; rather,
it is returning from village-to-village almsrounds with an empty bowl,
or encountering a time of famine where one cannot obtain anything through begging.
Although this belongs to this category,
it is not the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
Within the Mahāyāna, however...
Because the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, are all untainted (*anāsrava*).
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"That which the Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma."
Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal.
Furthermore, it is said:
"One abandons impermanent form and attains eternal form."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states:
"The Buddha-body is without outflows."
"All outflows have been exhausted.
In such Mahāyāna sūtras as these, it is stated that the Buddha's body is exclusively without outflows (*anāsrava*).
The three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering are exclusively *sāsrava* (tainted).
Therefore, the bodies of the Buddhas are free from all such sufferings.
Regarding the period from the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) down to the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there are two interpretations.
One interpretation states:
among the three types of suffering, there are the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*);
among the eight types of suffering, there is one type of suffering.

This refers to the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*). From the first stage (*bhūmi*) downward, because one experiences the various retributive bodies— both subject to transformation and subject to fragmentation— that are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), there is also the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).
The flux of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
All contaminated pleasures are pleasant when they arise,
pleasant while they endure, and painful when they perish.
Therefore, there is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
In that state, there is no oppression of body or mind, nor the suffering of grief;
there is only the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*) in its absence.
At the initial reception of that body,
although it is termed "birth," it is not the locus of manifold sufferings.
Furthermore, there is no oppression from the womb,
nor is there the suffering of birth;
their lifespan is exceedingly long, extending for immeasurable and boundless incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Even if ordinary beings were to re-enter the cycle of death and rebirth through transformation,
they would ultimately attain Buddhahood and be free from the suffering of death;
therefore, one should relinquish that life-force and vow to be born in a defiled land.
To save suffering sentient beings,
even death is not suffering;
for with a joyful heart, one vows to relinquish karmic retribution to cultivate loving-kindness and compassion.
These five aggregates of retribution, arising from afflictions, are by nature outflowing (sāsrava);
they are precisely the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging (pañcopādānaskandha).
In contrast, the four great elements of a purified buddha-field are stable and free from the suffering of illness.
Their physical forms suffer no decay;
they are free from the suffering of old age;
and as superior friends always gather around them, they are free from the suffering of being separated from those one loves.
Evil people will not arise;
there will be no suffering from association with those one hates; and one’s necessary provisions and conditions will never lack.
There is no suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
A second explanation states:
in the world of Ultimate Bliss, the eight sufferings are the same as those previously mentioned.
Among the three types of suffering, there is only the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
This is because they experience the retribution of both fragmented and transformative rebirths;
thus, although there may be pleasant sensations (*sukha-vedanā*), they are exclusively pure.
Constantly and perpetually continuous without interruption,
one ultimately and eternally realizes the bliss of nirvāṇa;
even when there is a slight respite, suffering does not arise.
It is not the suffering of change.
Therefore, that Pure Land is said to be without suffering;
it is without the suffering of suffering and the suffering of change.
Question: Although that Pure Land lacks the suffering of suffering and so forth,
it still possesses the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) and the like.
How is it that it is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī)?
The commentary states:
Among the three types of suffering, there is only one form of suffering present.
Within the eight sufferings, there is likewise only one suffering;
since two are absent among the three,
seven are missing from the eight.
Although there remains a single [remaining] thing, it is not called "possessing suffering.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Just as a river with little water is also called 'waterless.'"
For example, eating even a small amount of salt may still be called "saltless.
Furthermore, as the Abhidharma says:
"A single drop from the great ocean; a single mote of dust from Mount Sumeru."
One cannot say that there are mountains and seas;
this case is likewise. Even if there is a slight amount of suffering, it is the same.
It is therefore fitting to name it "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī).
Furthermore, that which is oppressive and unstable,
whether residing in the body or the mind, is termed sorrow and suffering (duḥkha).
That land is devoid of both [suffering and joy], and is thus named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī).
Question: The *Amitābha-sūtra* (Contemplation Sūtra) says:
He emanates transformation bodies as Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
gathering them in the Land of Ultimate Bliss to deliver sentient beings from suffering.
Since that land is called "Ultimate Bliss," [it is so named].
In that case, there would be no sentient beings who suffer.
For what reason, then, do you say that the Land of Ultimate Bliss gathers in and delivers suffering sentient beings?
The commentary states:
Now, when it is said that one "delivers sentient beings from suffering," does this mean delivering those who suffer within one's own land, or those who suffer in other lands?
Answer: It universally delivers sentient beings suffering in both one's own land and the lands of others.
Question: Why is this so?
Since there are no suffering sentient beings in one's own land,
how could one deliver the suffering sentient beings of one's own land? Although there are suffering sentient beings in other lands, [how could one deliver them from afar?]
One ought to go there to deliver beings from suffering;
for what reason, then, would one gather [beings] in Sukhāvatī to deliver them from suffering in distant other lands?
Answer: Although the sentient beings of their own land do not experience suffering [from external calamities],

they nonetheless possess two kinds of suffering— the suffering of the conditioned (saṃskāra-duḥkha) within the outflowing, conditioned states of both the fragmented birth-and-death (paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa) and the transformative birth-and-death (pariṇāma-jāti-maraṇa).
The Tathāgata gathers them together and expounds the sublime Dharma for them,
causing them to swiftly transcend the two kinds of birth-and-death and achieve the Dharma-body; therefore,
it is called "crossing over suffering."
For sentient beings in other lands who may require his personal presence to be directly rescued and delivered,
the emanation bodies of the Buddha pervade the ten directions.
Thus, when the karma for a pure land has been perfected by sentient beings here, an emanation Buddha comes to welcome them to that realm at the moment of their death.
Alternatively, it may be appropriate to return and bring benefit from afar;
thus, one gathers [disciples] in one's own land to rescue those submerged in suffering from a distance.
Or, it is said that this is for the purpose of delivering sentient beings from their suffering.
The emanated buddhas gather the emanated bodhisattvas from within their own lands and cause them to give rise to great compassion,
relinquishing the bliss of their own lands.

They dispatch [bodhisattvas] to other directions to practice the conduct of great compassion and to teach and transform sentient beings with whom they have a karmic connection throughout the ten directions. Therefore,
it is said that they gather [beings] into the Land of Ultimate Bliss to deliver suffering sentient beings,
as stated in the sūtras and śāstras.
Because Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage have extensively realized the principle of suchness through profound tranquility,
they are reluctant to emerge from meditative absorption to teach and transform sentient beings; thereupon,
the Buddhas stroke their heads with their hands.
This is precisely the meaning of exhorting [the bodhisattvas] to emerge from meditative concentration in order to teach and transform sentient beings.
Thus, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
The bodhisattvas of this land possess firm and steadfast great compassion for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, it is said that these individuals are even able to relinquish a pure land.
And yet you have come to delight in this place of many enmities and harms.
It is asked:
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* says:
The sentient beings in that land are free from all suffering and experience only various forms of bliss.
It is not yet known how many seeds of consciousness exist among the eight consciousnesses.
"And is it associated with pleasant sensation?
The commentary states:
"Among the eight consciousnesses..."
The seventh and eighth consciousnesses continue as a homogeneous stream;
their objective conditions are so subtle that they are difficult to discern,
even when situated in the place of extreme suffering within the Avīci Hell.
Even if one is born in the place of ultimate bliss of the third dhyāna,
these two consciousnesses are associated exclusively with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*);
this remains true even up to the pure consciousnesses associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom and the Wisdom of Equality at the stage of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, it is always associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). By analogy with this,
one should know that in the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), these seventh and eighth consciousnesses are also constantly associated with the feeling of equanimity.
The remaining six evolving consciousnesses are associated with three types of sensation—
namely, joy (*prīti*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
In the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is associated with the sensations of joy and pleasure.
In the five consciousnesses, it is associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*);
neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is associated with all [five].
This is because the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states that there is no physical or mental sorrow or suffering whatsoever.
There is only immeasurable, pure, and joyful bliss;
therefore, it is named the World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī).
By this one may infer accordingly.
Among the six consciousnesses of the Pure Land, while there is no sorrow or suffering, it is not precluded that there may be equanimity (*upekṣā*).
This is because, following states of various joys and pleasures,
when one reaches a stage of subsiding and diminishing, they for the most part correspond with that feeling of equanimity.
Furthermore, that neutral feeling (upekṣā-vedanā) is not oppressive in its nature;
as it is induced by wholesome karma,
it can therefore be associated with that neutral feeling.
Furthermore, since those sentient beings give rise to the *anāgamya* concentration, the intermediate dhyāna, and all concentrations from the fourth dhyāna upward,
why is it not admitted that these are associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*)?
By this analogy, one should understand that although it is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī), it can also be associated with the feeling of equanimity (upekṣā-vedanā).
If one were to claim otherwise, [it would contradict the following].
That [feeling] also cannot be associated with joy (*saumanasya*),
because that land is named the "Land of Ultimate Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*).
Although the land is named "Ultimate Bliss," it can indeed be associated with joy.
What prevents us from naming it "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī) while also associating it with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*)?
A question is asked:
Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts, [they state that] birth-and-death through limited segments (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*)...
It is said that there are worm-bodies and flesh-bodies.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Within the body of an avaivartika bodhisattva, there are no eighty thousand families of worms."
Since he possesses birth-and-death in discrete segments,
he must necessarily possess a body with worms.
If such a body exists, [then...]
The *Amitābha Sūtra* states that in that Buddha-land there are no three evil realms;
yet how can there be eighty thousand families of worms?
These two accounts are mutually contradictory.
How is this to be explained?
The commentary states:
Although the sentient beings in the Pure Land undergo the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) birth-and-death, [they do so differently from those in the defiled lands].
Yet those eighty thousand families of worms do not exist [there].
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* state that these worms' bodies are described according to the defiled lands (*saṃkliṣṭa-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, regarding this defiled land:
although the gods of the Form Realm are still ordinary beings,
there are not even eighty thousand families of worms within their bodies.
Furthermore, when the three calamities arise at the end of the kalpa of destruction, the three evil destinies are destroyed first.
At that time, even those among humans who experience [birth] do not yet have the eighty thousand families of worms within their bodies.
Since the three evil realms have already been destroyed and exhausted,
how much more so the pure, wondrous form-body of the Pure Land,
even though it is of the nature of *pariccheda* (segmented existence).
Yet there are no such bodies of these insects.
Question: For what reason is it praised that the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* says this?
To the west, passing from this world beyond hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayuta buddha-fields—
this refers to the four types of distance— and among these,
it is the distance of location.
The *Contemplation Sūtra* states that Amitābha Buddha is not far from here;
these two passages appear to be contradictory.
Please clarify their meaning.
The commentary states:
According to the records, the land of Ultimate Bliss is situated at a distance from this world of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of buddha-fields;
it is indeed a place far removed.
Now, when it is said that [the Buddha] is not distant, there is a distinct meaning; I shall briefly present ten explanations to harmonize this text.
First, the power of the Buddha is not distant.
Second, skillful means are not distant;
third, responsive manifestations are not distant;
fourth, one's own mind is not distant.
Fifth, not being distant from the five protections;
sixth, not being distant from those with whom one has a karmic connection;
seventh, not being distant from one’s original vow.
Eighth, the coming to welcome is not far off.
Ninth, rebirth [in the Pure Land] is not far off.
Tenth, non-negligence is not far off.
Regarding "the power of a single Buddha," the Sūtra says:
"By the power of the Buddha, one shall be able to see him."
Regarding the second, the skillful means:
the Sūtra says,
"There is another skillful means by which you may come to see."
Third, regarding the manifestation of the response:
the sutra states that Amitābha Buddha stands in mid-air.
Regarding the fourth, one's own mind:
the Sūtra says, "This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha."
Regarding the five guardians,
the Sūtra states:
"They constantly come to the place where that practitioner dwells."
Regarding the sixth point, "possessing objects," the Sūtra states:
"All sentient beings who possess objects [of perception] are able to see."
Regarding the seven original vows,
the sutra states:
"By the power of his past vows."
Those who possess recollective visualization will certainly attain accomplishment.
Regarding the eight who come to welcome [the practitioner],
the Sūtra says:
They come together with the various emanation Buddhas to welcome the practitioner.
Regarding the ninth type of rebirth,
the Sūtra says:
One will be reborn in that land as quickly as a finger-snap.
Regarding the ten forms of non-negligence,
the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle thirty, states:
Now, as for those who are heedless,
even though they may be near the Buddha and his disciples,
they are still said to be far away.
Now, if one can simply concentrate the mind and refrain from negligence,
this is called being near to the Buddha;
it is not called being far from him.
Because these ten meanings are complete, it is called "not distant.
Question: The *Amitābha Sūtra* says:
This mind makes the Buddha;
this mind is the Buddha.
The ocean of the Tathāgatas' perfect and universal knowledge arises from the perceptions of the mind.
"How is it that this very mind can become a Buddha?
The commentary states:
According to the principle of *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only).
There is no dharma apart from the mind;
the myriad dharmas and myriad characteristics are all one's own mind.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"When the mind arises, all phenomena arise;
when the mind ceases, all phenomena cease.
As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"According as the mind is pure, so is the Buddha-field pure.
It further says:
"Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled."
Because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure.
Thus, one knows that all phenomena are manifestations of the mind.
When one uses this mind to contemplate that Buddha, [one realizes this truth].
Amitābha Buddha is the mark of one's own fundamental nature.
When sentient beings contemplate the mind and take that Tathāgata as their object,
they cannot perceive the true form of the Buddha outside of the mind.
One should contemplate that the mind transforms into the appearance of an image;
this appearance of an image is called the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect),
and the observing mind is the *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect).
Both the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) and the image-part (nimitta-bhāga) are inseparable from the self-verifying-part (svasaṃvitti-bhāga).
Because the power of the seeing-part is able to manifest the image-part,
it is said that this mind creates the Buddha.
This objective aspect (nimittabhāga) is none other than the self-verifying aspect (svasaṃvittibhāga) of the mind;
it has no separate substantiality.
Therefore, it is said that this mind is the Buddha.
If one wishes to contemplate all the merits of the Tathāgata,
they are entirely images manifested by one's own mind; therefore,
it is said that the ocean of the Buddhas' perfect and universal knowledge arises from the mind.
Alternatively, by means of mental contemplation, one cultivates various practices;
because these serve as the cause for the myriad virtues, they are called the "Ocean of Perfectly Complete Knowledge" (Samyaksaṃbuddha), which arises from mental contemplation.
Thus, the second chapter at the beginning of the *Bhadrapāla-sūtra* states:
The Bodhisattva is likewise:
with a single-minded and skillful contemplation, he beholds all the Tathāgatas;
having beheld them, he immediately abides [in that state].
Having settled there, he inquired about the meaning;
upon its explanation, he rejoiced and was able to reflect:
"From where has this Buddha come?"
"Furthermore, from where does this body of mine emerge?
When I observe that Tathāgata, I find he has no place of coming or going;
my own body is likewise."
Since there is fundamentally no point of departure, how could there be any returning?
Furthermore, one should reflect in this way:
Now, these three realms are mind-only.
Within this mind there is the Buddha. Why is this?
Following the movement of that thought, one again perceives the mind itself.
Now, from the mind I see the Buddha;
my own mind creates the Buddha.
My mind is the Buddha;
my mind is the Tathāgata; my mind is my own body.
My mind perceives the Buddha;
yet the mind does not know the mind,
nor does the mind see the mind.
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra also says:
"The mind is like a skilled painter;
it paints the various five aggregates."
There is nothing in all the worlds that it does not create.
As is the mind, so too is the Buddha;
as is the Buddha, so too are sentient beings.
The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.
When the mind is in a state of defilement, it is called a sentient being;
when the mind is purely pure, it is called a Buddha.
This is precisely its meaning.
Question: The *Amitābha Sūtra* states:
If one sees the white tuft of hair between the eyebrows,
the eighty-four thousand marks will naturally be seen.
How then could one fail to see the mark of the invisible crown of the head?
The commentary states:
Some commentators say that since this mark of the invisible crown is called "invisible crown," it is so named because it cannot be seen.
In truth, it cannot be seen.
However, when it is said that one sees eighty-four thousand marks,
this actually excludes the mark of the invisible crown of the head.
One merely sees the remaining eighty-three thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine marks;
because the few are subsumed under the many,
it is collectively termed "seeing."
In reality, not even this single characteristic is perceived.
Were it otherwise, name and meaning would immediately contradict one another;
it would be like Mount Sumeru being consumed by fire until only a single atom remains.
When the great ocean is about to dry up and only a single drop remains,
one cannot say that there is still a mountain and an ocean present.
This case is also like this when one contemplates all characteristics as a whole.
All are completely pervaded;
yet this single characteristic alone cannot be perceived.
One must not say that it is because one does not perceive any characteristics.
Some commentators explain:
"Although this characteristic differs from the other characteristics,
it is for the most part not perceived."
It is called the mark of the invisible crown of the head.
Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, sentient beings are empowered so that they may once again behold it within their meditative practice.
However, the bodies of enjoyment for others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*),
from head to foot, manifest for the sake of sentient beings,
enabling them to behold and thereby benefit them.
Since he is not perceived,
there is no benefit; how, then,
can he be called the Body of Enjoyment for Others?
This very single characteristic is not for the sake of others' enjoyment; rather,
it is to manifest this characteristic as preeminent and supreme so that beings may revere it,
for it is rarely seen.
This is called the mark of the invisible crown of the head.
Furthermore, he manifests these various marks for the sake of sentient beings,
so that others may experience them and cultivate respect for the practitioner.
What prevents you from seeing it?
Just as Śākyamuni Buddha allowed [Ānanda] to see the crown of his head by having his hair shaved off,
so too did that Buddha.
One must not grasp the meaning by clinging to the literal text.
This causes all sentient beings to behold this sign. He asked:
As stated in the ninth visualization of the *Amitābha-sūtra*,
one originally intends to contemplate the physical marks and radiant light of Amitābha Buddha; once the calculation is complete,
the visualization is accomplished.
One should simply focus on beholding Amitābha Buddha.
For what reason would one behold Amitābha Buddha and yet further come to behold the Buddhas of the ten directions?
The commentary states:
This has three meanings. First, one attains the vision of all Buddhas of the ten directions.
First, because the merits of all Buddhas are entirely equal,
and because their self-benefit, benefit for others, and transformative benefits are all impartial,
one who contemplates a single Buddha sees all Buddhas of the ten directions.
Therefore, the *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* speaks of the Samādhi of One Practice, saying:
"If one can maintain the continuous succession of mindfulness toward a single Buddha from moment to moment,
within that very mindfulness one will be able to see all Buddhas of the past, future, and present."
Why is this? Because the merit of recollecting the virtues of a single Buddha is immeasurable and boundless;
it is also non-dual with the merit of immeasurable Buddhas.
The inconceivable Buddha-dharma is equal and without discrimination;
all ride upon the single suchness to achieve supreme perfect enlightenment,
fully endowed with immeasurable merit and eloquence.
Second explanation:
Because one attains the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) and eliminates obstacles and extinguishes transgressions by seeing even a single Buddha,
one is able to see the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Third explanation:
Amitābha Buddha’s radiance shines universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions;
by means of this light, one is able to see the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* states that the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla addressed Śākyamuni Buddha, saying:
"How may sentient beings of the future come to see the Buddhas of the ten directions?"
Buddhism instructs one to recollect Amitābha Buddha,
whereby one immediately beholds all Buddhas of the ten directions;
this is because this Buddha has a special affinity with the sentient beings of the Sahā world.
If one first single-mindedly recites the name of this Buddha,
samādhi will be easily attained,
obstacles removed, and transgressions extinguished.
The light shines everywhere, and one sees the Buddhas of the ten directions.
It is asked:
The *Amitābha Sūtra* says:
One who practices this visualization will be born before all Buddhas.
For what reason do you say that by visualizing Amitābha Buddha one vows to be born in the Western Land?
One should simply say that one is born before Amitābha Buddha.
Yet it is said that one is born before all Buddhas.
The commentary states:
There are four explanations for this.
One commentator says:
when performing this ninth visualization of the true body,
one does not merely see Amitābha Buddha.
They also behold all Buddhas of the ten directions; therefore,
they do not merely take birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss,
but may also be born in the various Buddha-lands according to their vows.
Therefore, it is said that one is born before all Buddhas.
A second interpretation states:
although one sees the Buddhas of the ten directions, [one is nevertheless born before them].
However, since this contemplation was originally intended for rebirth in the Western Land,
how can it also lead to rebirth in the lands of all Buddhas?
Regarding the phrase "before the presence of all Buddhas," it means that by virtue of this superior contemplation,
when the practitioner is born in the Western Land, [they will be there].
It is not merely that one sees Amitābha Buddha;
one sees all Buddhas of the ten directions.
Therefore, it is said that one is born before all Buddhas.
Third, the explanation states:
Although this Amitābha Buddha is a single body,
the number of transformation buddhas within his land is immeasurable.
At the time of the practitioner's initial birth, transformation Buddhas gather like clouds;
they all come to rub the crown of his head and preach the Dharma for him.
The manifested Buddhas are not one;
therefore, it is said that they are born before all Buddhas.
Fourth, the commentary says:
Although Amitābha Buddha manifests as a single body,
this single body is a transformation shared by many Buddhas; thus,
while the appearance is one, it is so.
Their substance is indeed manifold,
for many Buddhas all have a karmic affinity with a single sentient being,
and they transform it together in concert.
Amitābha Buddha resides in the same place [as the practitioner].
It is like many lamps whose lights are distinct from one another yet do not obstruct each other, appearing as if they were a single light;
the Buddha’s body is likewise.
Each of the Buddhas individually transforms themselves into one body;
although it appears to be a single body, in reality there are many bodies.
Although one is born before a single Buddha, this is immediately called being born before all Buddhas.
Question: The Lotus Sūtra says:
"Suppose the entire world were filled with people like Śāriputra."
Even if they exhaust their thoughts and deliberate together,
they cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
This means that ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles are unable to fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.

Furthermore, the treatise states that the knowledge of others' minds belonging to different stages (*bhūmi*), different vehicles (*yāna*), or different faculties (*indriya*) cannot take one another as objects. How, then,
is this consistent with what the *Sūtra on Contemplation* says?
If one sees the Buddha’s body, one sees the Buddha’s mind.
The Buddha’s mind is the mind of compassion.
As a sutra says:
The monkey offering honey also knew the Buddha’s mind.
Furthermore, a sutra states that Mahāmaudgalyāyana observed the Buddha’s mind with his knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Consider Ānanda as the attendant;
it is like the sun rising in the east and illuminating the western wall.
As the preceding sutra stated, one cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
The latter sūtra speaks of being able to contemplate the Buddha’s mind.
Since these two sūtras differ,
how should they be harmonized?
The commentary states:
The Sarvāstivādins explain this meaning by saying that the Buddha possesses two kinds of mind.
First, the mind that has already been attained;
second, the mind never before attained.
If the Buddha were to give rise to a mind never before attained, [it would be impossible].
Śāriputra and the others exhausted their powers of thought and deliberation, yet they were unable to know it.
If one were to give rise to a mind that has previously attained [such knowledge], even monkeys and the like would know the Buddha’s mind.
In the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, the Buddha himself explains that the mind as the perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) cannot be known by bodhisattvas of the ten stages and others,
whereas the mind as the perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is known by all ordinary beings.
The statement that one "also sees the Buddha-mind" refers to seeing the mind as its objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*).
The sutra states that the Buddha-mind is none other than great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-karuṇā*).
However, the Buddha possesses a mind of internally realized wisdom that takes principles as its object,
and a mind that externally observes sentient beings that takes phenomena as its object.
Just as with the mind of internally realized wisdom that takes principles as its object...
This is the mind of self-attestation;
Buddhas know one another through it,
while those on the ten stages cannot fathom it.
When observing the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) of sentient beings externally through both phenomena and principle,
even Buddhas know one another at the tenth stage, yet it remains unfathomable.
When observing the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of sentient beings externally through both principle and phenomena, [it is likewise unfathomable].
Through the Tathāgata’s empowerment,
even a monkey came to know the Buddha’s mind.
[The interlocutor] asked:
By what stage or level are the nine grades of beings distinguished?
The commentary states:
Regarding the coarse nine grades, there are two schools of opinion;
as for the fine nine grades, there are many explanations.
As for what are called the "two schools":
One interpretation:
these nine grades are all bodhisattvas of the ten stages of faith;
they are categorized according to whether they abide or regress.
By performing good or evil deeds,
one ascends or descends differently, resulting in nine grades.
The first three grades consist of those who have attained non-retrogression within the ten stages of faith and abide in their fundamental positions.
Their practice varies in depth,
resulting in the three superior grades.
Those of the three middle grades regress from the Mahāyāna mind and give rise to the intent of the Hīnayāna.
They retreat from the practice of the Mahāyāna and cultivate the karma of the Hīnayāna.
Depending on whether their practice is shallow or deep, they are categorized into three middle grades.
Those of the three lower grades abandon the Mahāyāna mind and give rise to the mind of saṃsāra.
To retreat from Mahāyāna practice is to commit the offenses that lead to birth and death;
these offenses vary in gravity, resulting in the three lower grades.
A second interpretation states:
They give rise to the great bodhicitta and practice the conduct of a bodhisattva;
according to the varying depths of their practice, they achieve the three superior grades.
They give rise to the small bodhicitta and practice the conduct of a śrāvaka.
The practices vary in depth, resulting in the three grades of the middling level.
One neither generates the mind of either the Great or Small Vehicles,
nor cultivates the practices of either the Great or Small Vehicles.
One gives rise only to the mind of birth and death,
and one commits only the offenses of birth and death.
Among these committed offenses, there are degrees of gravity and lightness.
These constitute the three lower grades;
this is the coarse classification into nine grades.
As for the fine classification into nine grades:
Furthermore, regarding the three types of superior practitioners, various masters hold differing views on what is included or excluded.
One master states that those who attain the highest birth of the superior grade are Bodhisattvas of the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages.
Those of the highest grade of middle birth are Bodhisattvas of the first through third stages;
those of the highest grade of lower birth are Bodhisattvas of the thirty minds prior to the stages.
One master says:
The highest grade of highest birth corresponds to the ten stages of Dedication;
the highest grade of middle birth corresponds to the ten practices;
and the highest grade of lowest birth corresponds to the ten abidings.
One master says:
"The highest grade of the highest birth refers to the thirty minds prior to the ground;
the highest grade of the middle birth refers to the final mind of the ten abidings."
Regarding the initial stage of the ten faiths for those of the lower birth in the highest grade,
one master says that the upper birth in the highest grade corresponds to the stages of the ten practices and the ten dedications.
Those of the highest grade who are born in the middle rank attain the ten abodes;
those of the highest grade who are born in the lower rank attain the ten faiths.
One master says:
The highest grade of the highest birth corresponds to those at the initial stage of the ten abodes;
the middle grade of the highest birth corresponds to the stage following the ten faiths;
and the lowest grade of the highest birth corresponds to the initial stage of the ten faiths.
One master says:

"Regarding the highest grade of the highest birth, those who have attained the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), as well as those prior to the ten stages of faith who are able to give rise to the three minds and cultivate the three practices,
are all termed those of the highest grade of the highest birth."
Those of the highest grade of middle birth and those of the highest grade of lower birth consist exclusively of ordinary persons who,
prior to the stage of the ten faiths, have resolved their minds on bodhi and cultivated wholesome roots.
The two categories are distinguished according to the depth of their practice and realization.
As for why various masters differ in their assessment of the relative status of these three categories,
it is because the treatises on the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena) assign these stages either to a lower or a higher level.
The *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is attained in the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages;
this is also taught among the various treatises.
The patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) exists either in the first stage (bhūmi) or in the stage of patience (kṣānti-avasthā);
this is stated in the *Bodhisattva-mūla-karman-avaivarta-sūtra* (Pusa benye yingluo jing).
The *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena) is situated at the stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*).

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* is situated at the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). The *Sūtra on the Examination of the Grounds for the Propagation of the Dharma* states:
The patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) exists within the stage of ordinary beings prior to the ten stages of faith;
therefore, various masters each maintain that one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas at a specific stage,
resulting in different levels of superiority and inferiority among the three grades of the higher [stages].
Regarding the three grades within the middle [level], one master says:
those born in the upper grade of the middle level are persons who have attained the three fruits;
those born in the middle grade of the middle level are persons who have practiced the seven stages of expedient means.
Those who attain rebirth in the lower grade of the middle class are persons who have cultivated the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
One master says that those who attain rebirth in the upper grade of the middle class are persons at the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).
Those in the stage of the Peak (*mūrdhan*) are reborn in the middle of the middle grade;
those in the stage of the Patience (*kṣānti*) are reborn in the lower of the middle grade.
One master says:
Those of the middle grade, superior birth are persons at the stage of *kṣānti* (receptivity) on the summit of the peak;
those of the middle grade, middle birth are persons who possess the three roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*);
and those of the middle grade, inferior birth are persons who have previously planted the roots of goodness conducive to liberation.
One master said:
"The three middle grades of persons are all those who have planted the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
This is due to the varying degrees of depth in their observance of the precepts, as well as those who do not observe the precepts but merely practice worldly virtues."
They are divided into three grades;
this classification is not based on the higher or lower levels of the stages (bhūmi).
As for those in the lower three grades, they differ solely due to the varying amount and gravity of the offenses they commit upon encountering specific conditions.
These are divided into the lower three grades;
there are no distinct stages or levels.
There are six stages of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
First is the wisdom of hearing,
which exists prior to the ten stages of faith;
second is the arising of resolute understanding.
The three types of wisdom through reflection occur after the ten stages of faith;
the wisdom through cultivation occurs after the ten abodes.
Fourth is the cultivation of wisdom,
which occurs after the stage of heating;
fifth is realization.
In the first stage,
there are six continuities;
in the eighth stage, [there are none].
This refers to the perfection of the Buddha-fruit while still within the causal stage.
A question is asked:
It is not yet known whether all those who attain rebirth there will achieve non-retrogression.
Why is it said that those of the highest grade of middle birth shall,
after seven days, immediately attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?
The commentary explains:
This refers to a person of superior birth among the middle grade,
who is prior to the fifth mind of the ten faiths.
The sixth mind of the ten faiths is called the "non-retrogressive mind."
Having been born for seven days, they attain that sixth stage of non-retrogression;
therefore, they are said to have attained non-retrogression regarding bodhi.
Those who, at the very moment of their initial birth, are called non-retrogressive—
This is explained in terms of non-retrogression regarding the stage.
These two scriptural passages each rely on a single meaning;
they are not contradictory.
Question: For what reason do those of the nine grades of rebirth all have Amitābha Buddha come to welcome them,
in accordance with his original vow, as they travel to the Buddha-land?
Regarding the fact that only the description of the middle-grade lower birth does not mention the arrival of the noble assembly to welcome [the practitioner],
what is the intended meaning?
The explanation states:
In accordance with the forty-eight great vows:
"If I do not come to welcome [you], may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, even those of the lowest grade who undergo three more births shall still have a saint come to receive them.
Following the pattern above and below,
there must certainly have been a formal reception by the sages;
however, that it is not recorded here may be due to an omission by the translator.
Alternatively, it may be omitted without being described.
One interpretation states that for these three types of persons of middling capacity, the Buddha employs great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Because they come to welcome one at the time of death,
this is not their original vow; thus,
there is the birth in the lower grade of the middle level.
It is not that the Buddha does not come to welcome [the practitioner]; it is simply that this was omitted from the text of the sutra,
for it is spoken within the forty-eight great vows.
If, when I attain Buddhahood,
sentient beings of the ten directions should give rise to the bodhicitta and cultivate various merits.
One should make a sincere vow,
desiring to be born in my land;
even if, at the time of death, I do not appear before that person together with the great assembly.
"I shall not attain perfect enlightenment.
Within this vow, it is stated that one should resolve upon bodhicitta and cultivate all manner of meritorious virtues.
If I do not manifest before the great assembly and appear before those individuals,
may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
This is the utterance of the resolve for bodhicitta.
These have generated the unsurpassed mind of great enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*).
Among these, the three types of persons, such as those of middling capacity and so forth, have not yet generated the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment;
they merely cultivate various merits with the aspiration to be born [in that realm].
Although one attains rebirth there, the Buddha does not come to welcome them;
this does not contradict his original vow,
as such a person has not resolved to attain bodhicitta.
This is not merely a matter of fulfilling great vows;
in the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra*,
it is taught that eight bodhisattvas show the way so that one may be reborn in the Western Land.
This means that the Buddha does not come to welcome [the practitioner].
If the Buddha were to come and welcome them, he would personally lead them away so that they might reach the Western Land;
why, then, would it be necessary for the Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light Buddha to dispatch eight bodhisattvas to show them the way?
Therefore, one should know that the reason no Buddha comes to welcome them is not because it violates their original vow;
for although those individuals previously cultivated the path, [they failed to do so with sincerity].
Because their resolve was not single-minded and determined,
and because they did not make a sincere vow with all their heart to be reborn in that land,
the *Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra* states that they were "undetermined."
If one makes this vow with a sincere heart,
then one is no longer a person of indeterminate nature.
Furthermore, this is the practice elucidated in that sutra.
These three types of people of intermediate capacity do not fulfill their original vows. Furthermore,
the *Bodhisattva-tsaotai jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb) states:
Sentient beings who perform deeds for the Western [Pure Land] mostly do not attain rebirth in the West; instead,
they are born in the land of *Kṣāntimāna* (the Land of Indolence).
This is not the case for those who have single-mindedly cultivated the practice of the Western Pure Land and made their vows with a sincere heart;
because their practice was not exclusive and their vows were not fully realized,
they do not accord with their original aspiration.
Therefore, he did not come to welcome [the Buddha].
If the Buddha were to come and welcome him, it would mean that his karma for the Pure Land of the West had already been perfected;
how could it be possible for the Buddha to welcome one who has been reborn in the Land of Indolence?
As stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*,
those of the three grades all resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of bodhi and are all welcomed by the Buddha.
Even if they do not see him in person, they shall surely see him in a dream and attain rebirth in that land.
Question: Why does the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* state that for those of the highest grade of the lowest level of rebirth,
one must invoke the Buddha with a sincere mind?
One extinguishes the sins of birth and death accumulated over fifty billion kalpas.
Those of the middle grade of the lower level hear of the Buddha’s merits;
those of the lower grade of the lower level invoke the name of that Buddha.
One simultaneously extinguishes the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
Why is it that by recollecting a single Buddha,
one's merit is no different?
The extinction of those transgressions differs slightly [from the previous case].
The commentary states:
There are two meanings here.
One interpretation states:
Since the merit of recollecting the Buddha is uniform, it should logically extinguish transgressions without distinction;
however, this is because the evil karma of persons belonging to the three grades varies in its degree.
Those of the lower grade who are born in the superior way have few offenses;
they have only the offenses of fifty billion kalpas that obstruct birth in the Western Land.
For those of the two lower grades, their offenses gradually increase;
thus, they incur offenses lasting for eighty billion kalpas and so forth.
This is because there are gradations in their offenses.
The explanations regarding the extent of what is extinguished differ;
it is not that the merits of the Buddha’s mindfulness are unequal such that they cause differences in the extinction of offenses.
It is, for example, like a strong man with great strength who is able to carry eight pecks of rice.
There was a man who possessed only five *dǒu* [of grain].
He sent a strong man to carry it;
for one who is not strong cannot lift much.
It is simply that five *dou* of rice [is the measure];
this principle is likewise.
For those of the lower grade who are born above, there are only fifty billion *kalpas* of transgressions remaining.
The Buddha, according to the gravity of those offenses,
declares that [the retribution] is extinguished after fifty billion kalpas; however,
for those born in the middle grade of the lower level, the offenses are more serious than those of the preceding category.
For thirty billion kalpas, one follows along with their karmic obstacles;
it is said that eighty billion kalpas are extinguished.
Those born in the lowest grade of the lowest level have the most severe offenses.
Therefore, by causing one to fully complete ten recitations while invoking the name of Amitābha Buddha,
the sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas are extinguished in every single thought-moment.
For this reason, these three grades differ in their specific explanations regarding the extinction of sin.
It is not that there is any difference in the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name.
The second commentator says:
although the names of the Buddhas one recites are no different, [the merit varies].
Due to the differences in the sincerity of the mind that recollects the Buddha,
the extent to which transgressions are extinguished varies.
Those who attain birth in the lower grade have light and thin karmic offenses.
At death, there will be no signs of evil,
and the mind will not be overcome by extreme fear;
although one merely recites the Buddha’s name with utmost sincerity, it is sufficient to extinguish the sins of fifty billion kalpas of birth and death.
In the middle grade of the lower level of rebirth, the fierce fires of hell arrive all at once.
The sinner, in a state of frantic terror, recites the Buddha’s name with utmost sincerity;
through this, the mind penetrates deeply, extinguishing the grave offenses of eight billion kalpas.
Question:
If that is so, then for those of the lowest grade who are reborn in the lowest level, their agitation and fear are most intense;
one should say that they must recite the Buddha’s name even more—many hundreds of millions of times—to extinguish it.
Why is it the same as before, eighty billion kalpas?
Answer: At the time of the practitioner’s death, their vital strength becomes depleted.
I have exerted my utmost strength with the utmost sincerity; yet, as this power has its limits,
how could it be much?
Because their transgressions are so numerous, they are obstructed from being born in the Pure Land;
therefore, one must cause them to possess ten recitations so that their sins may be extinguished, and only then can they attain rebirth in the pure Buddha-land.
For example, just as a divine sword can cut through great timber:
if one exerts much force, the entry into the wood will be deep;
if one does not exert much force, the cutting of the wood will be shallow.
It is not that swords have sharpness or dullness;
rather, it is simply that human strength varies.
This case is also like this.
Although the merits of the Buddha are indeed without distinction,
those who recollect him differ in their sincerity; therefore,
the extent to which their transgressions are extinguished varies accordingly.
Question: For what reason does merely hearing the titles of the twelve divisions of the scriptures extinguish the heavy sins of a thousand kalpas?
A single recitation of the Buddha's name extinguishes the grave offenses of fifty billion kalpas.
The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra states:
"Upon hearing this sutra, one does not oppose it."
This is a superior offering to eight hundred and forty trillion nayutas of Buddhas.
The commentary states:
In that sutra, making offerings to the Buddhas is the "proper time."
However, making offerings to the Buddha is a mind characterized by signs (*sanimitta-citta*),
and thus its merit is small. To uphold this sutra during such an evil age [is of far greater merit].
One should cultivate a mind free of marks;
the merit of upholding this sutra is great.
Now, both hearing this sutra and recollecting the Buddha occur during this same period of decline.
All these are merely signs;
yet, their past karmic conditions with Amitābha Buddha have long since matured.
In this degenerate age, it is extremely difficult for people to give rise to faith upon hearing the name of the Buddha.
The Buddha can propagate the sutras;
therefore, it is said that the Buddha's eradication of sins is greater than that achieved by hearing the sutras. Question:
Regarding those born in the lowest grade of the middle level, although their offenses are many, why is it that those in the lowest grade of the middle level—
who have committed the five heinous crimes and slandered the Dharma—
attain birth merely by hearing of the Buddha’s merits?
One attains rebirth immediately.
For the lowest of the low grades of birth, however, it is necessary to possess ten recitations;
only by invoking the name of Amitābha Buddha can one be born in the Pure Land?
The commentary states:
There are two interpretations.
First, it says:
Regarding the transgressions such as the five heinous crimes,
one ought to receive punishment for only six kalpas;
yet there are those who have offenses spanning eight or ten billion kalpas.
Because this person has committed such a grave offense,
it causes all other past karmas to grow and become fully potent.
It can bring about the retribution of birth and death for nine hundred and eighty billion kalpas.
Just as a single thought of anger manifests before one,
it can incinerate all wholesome dharmas.
It is capable of obstructing hundreds of thousands of Dharma-gates;
this case is likewise. One who commits such a grave offense [is similarly obstructed].
They can increase past evil karma;
all possess power and influence capable of inducing retribution for evil deeds.
This obstructs birth in the Pure Land.
There are two explanations:
these five heinous crimes result only in suffering for five kalpas.
However, regarding the sin of slandering the Dharma, the sūtras state that the duration of suffering is vast and long-lasting,
as explained in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra and the Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra.
Those who slander the Dharma fall into this Avīci Hell.
When this world-system undergoes destruction and is reborn, one is instead born in the hells of other directions.
Thus one wanders through countless kalpas.
Therefore, it is necessary to recite the Buddha’s name ten times to extinguish the heavy sins of eighty billion kalpas and attain birth in the Pure Land.
Question: For what reason,
among the various dharma-gates for rebirth [in the Pure Land],
is the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha specifically enjoined on the day of one's impending death?
"What is the meaning of not teaching other virtues?
The commentary states:
For those whose lives have come to an end, one should specifically instruct them to recite the Buddha’s name;
because these seven meanings are superior,
one does not instruct them in other dharmas.
What are the seven meanings?
First, superiority;
second, scarcity.
Third, change;
fourth, cessation;
fifth, conditions.
Sixth, welcoming;
seventh, birth.
Regarding the phrase "one word is superior":
Among all ordinary beings and sages, all persons and dharmas,
none surpasses the Buddha;
he is the most honored and supreme.
The two obstacles are completely severed;
the myriad virtues are perfectly fulfilled;
self-awakening and awakening others reach ultimate perfection in both realization and practice.
Out of compassion for sentient beings,
which exceeds that felt for an only son,
he is the great refuge for all these living beings.
He is the island and the peninsula;
he is the rescue and the refuge.
Therefore, one must invoke the name of the Buddha with utmost sincerity.
Second, regarding "fewness":
among all practices for cultivating goodness, this recitation of the Buddha's name alone involves the fewest words;
all other dharma-gates involve many more.
On the day of one's death, when life hangs by a thread, how could one possibly cultivate many other dharmas?
Regarding the "three changes," among all the dharma-gates of practice:
This mindfulness of the Buddha alone is the most easy to practice.
At the moment of death, one is entangled by a hundred sufferings and one's physical strength has declined.
Having renounced all worldly affairs,
even if one is exhorted to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, there is still fear that it may not be accomplished; therefore,
other gates [of practice] are further explained.
It is truly difficult to practice and study;
therefore, this simple and easy method is set forth to instruct others so that they may cultivate it.
Regarding the four types of cessation:
this refers specifically to the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, which is easy to cultivate.
A single thought of utmost sincerity can immediately extinguish the grave transgressions of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
It is to forever sever the retributive suffering of the three miserable realms within this Sahā world.
Regarding the five conditions:
since the time of immeasurable kalpas past, Amitābha Buddha...
The karmic connection formed with sentient beings is extremely profound.
Through conditions such as making offerings, seeing, hearing, rejoicing, or practicing together,
one relies on these past causes to single-mindedly recite the name.
Seeking their voices, one shall rescue them so that they forever sever the five fires of torment.
Sixth, regarding "welcoming":
by reciting the Buddha's name, the defilements of sin are extinguished.
Amitābha Buddha, by virtue of his fundamental vow,
personally comes to welcome [the practitioner] accompanied by the assembly of holy ones;
this is not the case with other dharmas.
Therefore, one must practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
Regarding the "seven births," it is as stated in that vow: "If, even with ten recitations, I do not attain birth [in the Pure Land], may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
Because these seven meanings surpass all other dharma-gates,
I thus exhort sentient beings to practice mindfulness of the Buddha at the time of death.
Question: One may attain rebirth in the Western Land by reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times in a single thought-moment.
Is it that one attains rebirth there solely through this practice of mindfulness of the Buddha?
"Must one rely on other dharma-gates in order to give rise to it?
If one grasps only this mindfulness,
one has not yet understood this mindfulness."
Although the Sūtra states that this is the complete possession of unsurpassed merit,
how can one become possessed of unsurpassed merit in a single thought-moment?
The commentary says:
Merit is immeasurable.
Why must it necessarily depend upon cultivation over a long period of time to become immeasurable?
There are cases where one has cultivated for a long time and extensively, yet the merit is small.
There are times when one has practiced for only a short duration yet possesses great merit.
What is the meaning of this?
As it says in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*:
During the first, middle, and last watches of the day,
he would each time give away his body and life as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River;
in this manner, he would give his body as an offering for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas.
If, moreover, there should be someone who hears this sutra and believes it with a mind free from opposition,
their merit shall surpass that of the former [beings] by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas— a period of vast duration.
He sacrificed bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
and in each instance, his life was taken, resulting in immense suffering.
Although he thus possessed these three "many" qualities, [he did not attain enlightenment].
Yet their merit is small. Furthermore,
if there is another person whose body is small and who hears this sutra for only a short time, [their merit is likewise small].
Those with faith who do not act contrary [to the Dharma] are few;
yet the merit they obtain exceeds the previous blessings.
This is the evaluation of the supreme sages.
This is not something that ordinary, inferior beings can fathom;
how could one not believe it?
This single thought-moment of reciting the Buddha's name is itself endowed with unsurpassed merit.
This is also the Master’s true word;
how can you harbor doubt?
Furthermore, because reciting the Buddha's name for even a single thought-moment transcends the cultivation of the path for hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas.
The merit and virtue attained are vast.
As stated in the Lotus Sūtra:
"If there should be another person..."
They uphold the names of bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty-two billion Ganges Rivers, and further provide them with food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine for as long as they live.
What do you think, Ajita? Is the merit of these good men and good women great or not? Ajita replied: "It is great."
"Very many, World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"If there are people who receive and uphold the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva..."
Even if one were to worship and make offerings to them at a single time,
the merit of these two persons would be exactly equal and without distinction.
This is even more so if one were to uphold the names of bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty-two billion Ganges Rivers.
Furthermore, they provided the four requisites of worship for a duration that,
when calculated, already constitutes hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas,
yet it was merely for the brief moment of reciting the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
There is one kind of offering wherein the merit over a long period is equal to the blessing of a short period.
This is stated in the *Daśacakra Sūtra*.
