If a person were to single-mindedly recite the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva for a hundred great kalpas,
it would not equal reciting the name of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva for the duration of a single meal.
If one contemplates Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva for even a hundred great kalpas,
how much more so than the previous calculation;
it shall equal making offerings to the names of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of unspeakably many Ganges-sands of bodhisattvas.
If one were to contemplate Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva for many kalpas,
it would not equal a single utterance of the name of Amitābha Buddha with a sincere heart;
the merit [of the latter] is immeasurable and boundless.
In this way, the Buddha is compared to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva;
Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva is compared to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva;
and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is compared to the other bodhisattvas, numbering as many as sixty-two billion Ganges sands, for the purpose of evaluation.

A single recitation of the Buddha's name possesses merit superior to that of making offerings of the four requisites to as many bodhisattvas as there are grains of sand in immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges Rivers.
This means that a single thought-moment of reciting the Buddha's name surpasses the recollection of all other bodhisattvas.
Having practiced the path for one *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa and two *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas,
how could the merit of recollecting the Buddha be small?
One should know that its merit is vast by means of such a comparison.
Question: If,
by this calculation, it is truly established that immeasurable merit is accomplished,
it is entirely appropriate to have deep faith.
If one joyfully recites [the name], one will certainly attain rebirth there.
Yet, the Lotus Sūtra states:
"If a person, with a distracted mind, enters a stupa or temple..."
"By reciting 'Namo Buddha' even once, all have already attained the path to Buddhahood.
If one utters the name of the Buddha even a single time,
one shall immediately attain rebirth in the Western Land."
Furthermore, by reciting the Buddha's name even once, one immediately attains the path of Buddhahood. If this were indeed the case,
there would be not a single ordinary person remaining in the worlds of the ten directions.
All who are able to invoke the name of the Buddha shall attain Buddhahood.
If one invokes the name of the Buddha even once but has not yet attained Buddhahood,
this nevertheless serves as a remote cause for attaining Buddhahood.
Furthermore, one must gradually accumulate merit and perfect the mind of great compassion;
only when the myriad practices are complete and the three great kalpas have been fulfilled does one attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
If this is so, why would one necessarily attain rebirth through a single thought or ten thoughts at the moment of death?
Furthermore, one must also gradually cultivate and perfect all the *pāramitās* before attaining rebirth in the Pure Land.
The commentary states:
This does not constitute a valid precedent.
The Buddha possesses no ninefold gradations of difference;
he must be fully endowed with all ten thousand virtues,
and it is only by relying upon a long duration of many kalpas that the Way is finally perfected and one attains Right Enlightenment.
The Lotus Sūtra makes such a statement for the sake of those who are śrāvakas,
saying that they need only be able to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
Even distracted mindfulness of the Buddha is ultimately a cause for the fruit of Buddhahood; later,
one will be able to extensively cultivate the various perfections.
One immediately attains perfect enlightenment;
whereas śrāvakas, even if they cultivate the path extensively,
do not proceed toward unsurpassed bodhi.
For this reason, one cannot achieve the unsurpassed fruit.
That sutra makes such a statement because it addresses the assembly of śrāvakas to bring the two vehicles together into one.
This does not conform to the doctrine of rebirth in the Pure Land found in texts such as the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*.
Although one may attain rebirth in the Pure Land through the merit of reciting the Buddha’s name once or ten times, [the specific conditions for that rebirth differ].
They remain ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Sentient beings who attain rebirth differ according to nine grades,
as it is acknowledged that their practices vary in degree.
Or rather, they are still comprised among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
What prevents them from being born in the Buddha-land in a single thought-moment?
If there were no distinction of the nine grades, [what would be the point?]
As causes, all require the same kind;
one must necessarily cultivate the ten thousand practices to become a World Hero of the ten directions.
Therefore, it cannot be taken as a precedent.
*An Explanation of the Various Doubts Concerning the Pure Land*,
Scroll Six *An Explanation of the Various Doubts Concerning the Pure Land*,
Scroll Seven Compiled by the Great Virtuous Huai’gan of Qiānfú Monastery in the Western Capital.

Question: It has been established above, through the full citation of scriptural passages and comparative analysis, that the merit obtained from mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha is immeasurable and boundless.
As you have excellently explained, I accept and shall practice accordingly.
However, I do not yet know whether the merit of reciting the names of other Buddhas is likewise immeasurable.
The commentary states: This has two meanings.
One interpretation says:
One should reflect that all Buddhas have attained immeasurable merit without distinction,
for all Tathāgatas are fully endowed with boundless merit.
Having completely severed all obstacles of persons and phenomena,
their merits are fully perfected.
For this reason, there is no thought of superiority or inferiority, nor any difference in their merits.
If this is so, why does the Tathāgata, throughout the various sūtras,
specifically praise the immeasurable merit of mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha? Answer:
In truth, all merits are of one and the same kind;
it is only because beings of shallow understanding and ordinary capacity are unable to contemplate them universally that the Tathāgata specifically praises the merits of a single Buddha.
He causes them to collect their thoughts with a sincere mind;
the merit of such sincerity is indeed great.
This is the Tathāgata’s skillful means of intentional secrecy.
It is just as when one receives the full ordination within the Sangha:
all are pure and capable of serving as preceptors,
with no distinction of superiority or inferiority.
Just as a recipient of the precepts designates a single teacher as their upādhyāya,
and the very arising of that causal condition for the precepts is superior to others,
so it is in this case as well.
The merit of focusing one’s mind on a single Buddha is already vast,
for it arises from the intensity of that single-mindedness.
Furthermore, another commentary states:
Although the merits of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are entirely equal and without distinction of superiority or inferiority,
yet because sentient beings have established different conditions for connection with those Buddhas over the course of long ages in the past.
As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and other texts:
sentient beings, by the power of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*),
belong to different teachers.
Either many belong to one,
or one belongs to many;
if they belong to a particular Buddha, that Buddha alone is able to deliver them.
Those who do not belong to other Buddhas and are not delivered by other Buddhas,
but belong to this Buddha,
will have great merit simply by invoking his name with a sincere heart.
They will immediately come to rescue and deliver them;
as for those who do not belong [to the teaching],
their remembrance of its merit will not be great.
Nor do they come to rescue them.
It is asked:
As it says in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*:
Even those bodhisattvas of minor practice and those who have cultivated little merit shall all be born in the World of Ultimate Bliss.
As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"One cannot be born in that land through small roots of goodness or causes and conditions of merit.
How should these two sutras, which appear contradictory, be reconciled?
The commentary states:
Each has its own intent;
though their bases differ,
they do not contradict one another.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Wúliàngshòu jīng) speaks of "few," meaning a small number;
the *Amitābha-sūtra* (Āmítuó jīng) speaks of "many," meaning a large number.
That person merely recollects Amitābha Buddha and does not further cultivate the other six pāramitās or any of the dharmas of the bodhipakṣa;
they do not perform difficult practices or asceticism for long periods or throughout many kalpas.
There is only the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha and no other blessings from practicing the path;
therefore, it is called "small."
This mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha—
once the single recitation has been made— is itself immeasurable, boundless, and supremely meritorious;
therefore, it is called "many."
Therefore, the lower fascicle of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
all together praise the inconceivable majestic power and meritorious virtues of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life."
All sentient beings who hear his name shall rejoice with faith and joy.
Even with a single thought-moment, one attains rebirth there and dwells in the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, it says:
Whoever hears the name of that Buddha and experiences joy and exultation for even a single thought-moment,
you should know that such a person has attained a great benefit.
This is to be fully endowed with unsurpassed merit.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"To hear the name of the Buddha Amitāyus, with its immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable merits..."
Based on these scriptural passages,
it is known that this constitutes many merits; therefore,
it is so designated in terms of both number and function.
To call it "few" or to call it "many" is not contradictory;
it is like a single mani jewel, which may be called both few and many.
As for its being small in size:
this jewel is but one,
and its dimensions are not large.
Fools do not distinguish it and consider it small;
therefore, they treat it with contempt and do not take it up.
It is also called "great."
The value of this single jewel exceeds that of the trichiliocosm;
it is highly esteemed by those who possess discernment,
and for this reason, it is said to be "much."
The same applies to the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*):
whether it is called by many names or few depends on the difference in their underlying meanings.
Question: As explained above, one should practice mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha.
By means of various arguments and comparisons,
the vastness of his superior merits is revealed,
thereby giving rise to profound faith and reverence.
I do not dare to slander it.
Nevertheless, the merit obtained from this is exceedingly great,
because one acts without signs by means of a mind that apprehends nothing.
When contemplating the true Dharma-body of Amitābha Buddha,
are his merits many?
Or is it merely by means of a mind that grasps at existence that one creates the appearance of them?
Question: Are the merits of the nirmāṇakāya, saṃbhogakāya, and other bodies also many?
Explanation:
All are indeed so. The Dharma-body is free from marks and is the true essence of myriad virtues;
it can, by means of a mind of non-attainment, [manifest all things].
The principle of nianfo (recollection of the Buddha) is the realization of reality; yet its merit is inconceivable,
as is the case for those of shallow learning.
They were unable to cultivate the thought of signlessness; rather,
with a mind that grasps at objective existence,
they contemplated the Tathāgata’s pure form-body, its sublime marks and signs, and its myriad virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Reciting with utmost sincerity also yields boundless and supreme merit,
as in the case of the three types of people in the lower grade who,
having committed evil throughout their lives, recite the name of that Buddha at the point of death.
How could one possibly produce that thought of signlessness?
One can thus know with certainty that even thoughts of a mind with signs obtain boundless, supreme merit.
Furthermore, one desires to sever the two obstacles.
One must necessarily cultivate the mindfulness of formlessness;
yet, in planting those causes now, one also cultivates the mindfulness of the Buddha with form.
Furthermore, the true Buddha and the provisional Buddha differ in their principles and phenomena.
The causes cultivated through the signless and the signful are also distinct;
there is no contradiction in principle.
A question is asked:
If one practices the contemplation of the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*),
one can extinguish subtle karmic obstacles;
this is superior to the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha for extinguishing coarse karma.
"Why, at the moment of death, do you not instruct them to contemplate the true nature of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*),
but instead urge them to recite the name of the Buddha?
The commentary says:
It is indeed as you have criticized.
However, for four reasons, it is impossible to instruct them in the realization of the true nature (dharmatā).
First, because of their wickedness.
Second, the dharmas are profound;
third, one is oppressed by suffering;
fourth, time is short.
Regarding those who dislike [the practice]: these people have never cultivated goodness since birth;
they might even fear that they are not yet proficient in merely reciting the Buddha's name.
How much less could they understand the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena?
As for the profundity of phenomena:
it is the equality of the *dharmatā* of the two kinds of emptiness and true suchness (*tathatā*).
The principles are profound and far-reaching;
they are ultimately difficult to accomplish and cannot be taught [in their entirety].
Regarding those oppressed by suffering:
even those who have studied throughout their lives and constantly practiced this contemplation fail to achieve it when beset by painful afflictions.
How much more so for this person, who from birth has never practiced;
it is unreasonable to first instruct them to practice while they are already entangled in manifold sufferings.
Regarding those for whom time is short:
throughout their entire lives, he extensively expounded the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) to them,
and they reflected upon it for many years.
If one cannot yet understand even this,
how much less so when one has only just begun to practice for such a brief moment?
To seek [certainty] will certainly not succeed;
it is merely to establish teachings in vain.
One who thoroughly understands the circumstances of the times is called a Great Dharma Master.
The Great Sage should know that learning [in this manner] is necessarily impossible;
therefore, he does not instruct them to contemplate the true nature (dharmatā).
This profoundly reveals the Buddha’s wisdom as being skillfully adapted to the capacities of sentient beings.
For these four reasons, one does not teach the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). Question:
If a person, throughout their entire life, has practiced the three types of merit and the sixteen contemplations, [why is this so?]
Or, at the time of death, one may encounter a virtuous friend who causes them to recite the Buddha’s name ten times; thus,
the roots of their transgressions will be extinguished.
They shall attain rebirth there.
This person’s life may not yet have ended at that time;
it is only after many more days have passed that their lifespan finally comes to an end.
"Is it necessary to further practice mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) in order to be born in the Pure Land,
or can one attain rebirth there even without practicing mindfulness of the Buddha?
The commentary states:
They shall attain rebirth. However,
because that person’s karma has already been completed and their defilements have been extinguished,
they will attain rebirth even if many days are extended.
However, there are two types.
The first is one who, after performing meritorious deeds,
does not die for many days and does not commit further grave offenses.
At that time, various neutral states of mind may arise;
these minds cannot bring about the retribution of good or evil.
Therefore, by relying on the preceding mindfulness of the Buddha, one immediately attains rebirth in the Pure Land.
Second, after that person has practiced mindfulness of the Buddha,
they may not die for a long time,
during which they further give rise to evil thoughts and commit unwholesome deeds.
Such a person will likely not be reborn in the Pure Land due to their many fears.
As the sutra says:
"A single thought of anger obstructs hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates."
It is further said:
"The harm of anger destroys all wholesome dharmas;
as a thief that plunders merit, nothing surpasses anger."
Although such a person may possess prior wholesome practices such as contemplative visualization and mindfulness of the Buddha,
these are all impaired by anger,
and they will not attain rebirth there.
How much more so for other virtuous deeds that are obstructed by karmic hindrances;
as it is said in the sūtras:
"At the time of death, the karma one has created is the very first to receive its retribution."
If, at the time of death, the mind is heavy, one experiences [the retribution] first;
if the weight is equal, the one that was first [committed] is experienced first.
Such a person will have many offenses for their future existence.
"I fear that I shall not be reborn there. He asked:
"As stated in the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisāgara-sūtra*:"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If there are sentient beings who kill their father or harm their mother..."
Those who revile their six kin and commit such sins will,
at the time of their death, find copper dogs with gaping mouths before them.
He transformed eighteen chariots so that they resembled golden chariots,
with jeweled canopies above them;
all the flames were transformed into jade maidens.
When the sinner sees them from afar, joy arises in his heart, and he thinks,
"I wish to go among them. Yet,
when the wind-swords dismember him, the cold becomes so intense that he loses his voice.
"It would be better for me to sit upon a chariot with a fine fire,
which then spontaneously bursts into flames.
Having formed this thought, he immediately passed away.
In the space of a single flick of the hand, he was already seated upon a golden chariot;
looking back, he beheld the jade maidens,
all of whom were grasping iron axes.
They cut his body to pieces.
Furthermore, it says:
"There are also sentient beings."
They violate the four grave prohibitions,
consume the offerings of the faithful in vain,
slander with false views, and fail to recognize cause and effect.
They abandon the study of Prajñāpāramitā,
disparage the Buddhas of the ten directions,
and steal the property of the Saṃgha.
Lustful and unprincipled,
he coerced and abducted pure bhikṣuṇīs, sisters, and female relatives,
showing no sense of shame or remorse.
Having brought disgrace upon their kin and committed numerous evil deeds,
when this person’s retribution for their sins arrives at the moment of death,
The wind-knives dismember the body;
one sits prostrate and restless,
as if being struck by whips and canes.
His mind became deranged and gave rise to delusory thoughts of madness;
he saw his own house, its men and women,
both great and small, as being entirely impure things.
Feces and urine, smelling of rot, overflowed outside.
At that time, the offender spoke these words:
"Why is there no fine city wall or beautiful mountain forest here for me to enjoy?"
Thus they dwell amidst such impure things.
Having spoken these words,
the rakshasa wardens take up great iron forks.
He took up the Avīci Hell and the various mountains of blades,
transforming them into jeweled trees and refreshing ponds;
he transformed the flames into golden-leafed lotuses.
The iron-beaked insects transform into wild ducks and geese;
the cries of agony from the hells sound like the melody of chanting songs.
Upon hearing this, the offenders think: "Such a pleasant place as this—this is where I shall go to roam."
Having formed this thought, he immediately sat upon a fire-lotus.
How could he have known that the lotus arriving today to welcome him was not merely a spark of fire?
The commentary states:
For four reasons, one knows that these are not the "chariot-fires" (hellish chariots):
first, by their movement;
second, by their appearance.
Third, by means of speech;
fourth, by means of the Buddha.
These four meanings differ from the sparks of fire.
First, regarding the practitioner:
the *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states that when a person commits a transgression, [they should practice as follows].
They commit the four grave prohibitions,
even to the point of insulting and dishonoring their own kin,
yet they feel no remorse for their transgressions.
Because they did not encounter virtuous friends who instructed them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha,
the flowers they saw were manifestations of the hells.
These three types of people— the lower grade and so forth— [now...]
Although one may have committed sins throughout one's life,
at the time of death, if one encounters a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and recollects the Buddha with a sincere heart,
by virtue of that mindfulness of the Buddha, the offenses of many kalpas will be extinguished.
Having accomplished supreme merit,
he causes flowers from within a jeweled pond to come and welcome him;
how could these be the same as the flowers mentioned before?
Regarding the two signs,
that sutra states:
"The wind-knives dismember the body."
Lying prostrate and restless,
as if being whipped and beaten,
his mind becomes wild and distracted, giving rise to thoughts of madness and delusion.
He sees his own house, with its men, women, children,
and adults— all of whom are impure things—
while foul-smelling excrement and urine overflow outside.
Now, through this mindfulness of the Buddha, my body and mind are peaceful and stable;
all evil thoughts have been extinguished,
and I see only the assembly of sages.
Because a strange fragrance was perceived,
it was unlike [ordinary things].
As for the three utterances:
In that sutra it is said:
"The sounds of suffering in hell are like the melody of a song.
Having heard them, the offenders [experience joy]."
I shall travel within such excellent benefits.
As it is praised in the sutra:
"Good son, you who invoke the name of the Buddha..."
"Therefore, all your sins are extinguished;
I have come to welcome you"—
these were the sounds of their singing.
This is the statement regarding the extinction of sins through confession.
Since the two sounds are distinct, they are not the same.
Regarding the four Buddhas:
in that sutra, all the flames are transformed into jade maidens;
when the sinners see them from afar, joy arises in their hearts.
I wished to go into the center;
having mounted the golden chariot, I looked back at the jade maidens,
who all seized iron axes and severed their own bodies.
The *Contemplation Sūtra* states:
"At that time, that Buddha immediately dispatched an emanated Buddha, an emanated Avalokiteśvara, and an emanated Mahāsthāmaprāpta to appear before the practitioner."
Based on these four points,
one should understand that the lotus flower coming to welcome [the practitioner] differs from what is described in the *Buddhānusmṛtisamādhisāgara-sūtra*. Question:
The births of those in the nine grades differ in their excellence or inferiority;
the welcoming by the sages varies in frequency, and the blossoming of the flowers differs in timing.
The precious terraces and jeweled flowers all possess degrees of distinction.

For what reason is it that those of the highest grade who are born in the lower [level] and those of the lowest grade who are born in the lower [level] are alike in having golden flowers, such that there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority between them?
The explanation says:
This has three meanings.
One interpretation states:
this is not the flower that goes to the person.
This may be the flower upon which the Buddha rides when coming to welcome [the practitioner].
Because that person’s karmic obstructions are heavy, they do not feel moved to see the Buddha;
they merely see the Buddha’s seat, yet even this is not clearly discerned.
It is like the orb of the sun appearing hazy, as if one were looking at it;
there are two explanations for this:
such a person’s obstructions are so heavy that they do not receive the Buddha’s welcome.
One merely attains the golden lotus that leads to rebirth in the Pure Land;
therefore, the *Amitābha Sūtra* states that [the Buddha] stands before such a person. If one were instead to sit upon the flower, [it would imply a different stage].
Why does the Sūtra not state that he sits upon a precious flower?
There are three explanations for this:
this refers to sitting upon a flower.
Although they are equally made of golden petals,
there are distinctions between the large and small,
the superior and inferior, and the coarse and exquisite; thus, the two grades of lotuses differ from one another.
What prevents there also being distinctions?
A question is asked:
"In the middle birth of the lower grade, the flower blooms after six kalpas."
Regarding the statement that for those born in the lowest grade of the lowest level, the lotus flowers open after twelve kalpas:
is this kalpa calculated by accumulating the days, months, and years of the sun and moon in this world-system,
or is it calculated by the days, months, and years of the sun and moon in the Pure Land?
The commentary states:
The masters of the Pure Land school also offer this explanation:
one takes the number of days, months, and years of this world-system.
It is accumulated over kalpas.
How is this known? It is because Śākyamuni Tathāgata attained enlightenment here in this very place.
This sutra was spoken for the sake of the sentient beings of this Sahā world; when those flowers bloom,
may these beings attain understanding.
Thus we know that it is simply by means of this kalpa that the blooming of those flowers is clarified.
Now, [I shall] explain.
Not so; a kalpa is established by using the number of days, months, and years according to that particular region.
This reveals the temporal limits of that flower’s blooming. How is this known?
There are three points of meaning.
One may come to know this through three aspects: first, the examples; second, the teachings; and third, the principles.
For example, regarding the length of life of the various heavens of the six classes of desire, such as the Heaven of the Four Great Kings,
it is all explained in terms of the days and months of those respective heavens.
For instance, the lifespan of the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings is five hundred years;
a day and night in that heaven is equivalent to fifty years among humans.
This constitutes one day and night for the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Thirty such days and nights constitute one month,
and twelve months constitute one year.
Thus, the lifespan of those devas is five hundred years.
If calculated by the days, months, and years of Jambudvīpa,
this corresponds to eighteen thousand years for a single month.
Two hundred and one million six thousand years constitute one year [of that heaven].
Thus, the lifespan of those devas is five hundred years,
calculated by the standards of the Jambudvīpa year.
Their number is extremely great.
From these five heavens upward, lifespans gradually increase,
days gradually lengthen, and years all increase by double compared to the heaven below.
Thus, one should know that those gods take up their lifespan using the days and nights of that very heaven,
calculating months by means of days.
Using months to calculate years,
and using years to calculate a lifetime;
thus one knows that in the Pure Land, months are calculated by means of days.
Years are calculated by months,
and kalpas are calculated by years;
this does not employ the system of days, months, and kalpas used in this region.
Regarding the second teaching:
as stated in the "Middle Birth" chapter of the preceding section,
this purple-golden platform is like a great precious flower.
It blooms after one night has passed.
Thus we know that when it is said to bloom after one night,
this refers to the day-and-night reckoning of that region.
At night the flowers close,
and during the day they bloom;
thus, half an eon constitutes one day.
When the flowers bloom, half an eon constitutes their night;
when the flowers close, it constitutes their day.
This reveals the timing for the blossoming of the flowers for those of the highest grade of middle birth;
it refers to the time when the great precious flowers that have remained overnight open.
Since the flowers of one who is of the highest grade of middle birth bloom after one night, [the same applies to the others].
For those of the highest grade who are born in the lower level, the lotus flower opens after one day and one night;
thus we know that this still employs the days and nights of that [Saha] world.
Otherwise, [it would not be so].
How could it be permissible for the great jewel lotuses of the Pure Land to bloom during these very days?
If those great jewel lotuses bloom, they take their own local day and night as the measure.
Those of the highest grade who are born in the middle rank have their lotuses bloom at the same time as those aforementioned;
for those of the highest grade who are born in the lower rank, the lotus blooms after one day and one night,
which corresponds to a single day and night in this world.

The blooming of the flower for those of the highest grade who are born in the middle level contradicts the meaning of the delayed or rapid blooming of the flower for those of the lowest grade who are born in the upper level. Thus, the principles are inconsistent.
This is logically impossible.
Therefore, we know that it refers to the sun and moon. Since this is the case for the sun and moon, [the same applies to other phenomena].
The kalpas may also be known.
Regarding the third point, "by means of reasoning":
if it concerns the blooming of flowers by the sun and moon, one should employ the sun and moon of that particular region.
If one were to calculate the kalpas of this region by the number of kalpas required for the lotuses to bloom,
then the blooming of the lotuses after seven days in the middle grade of rebirth would correspond to seven kalpas according to the reckoning of this region.
The middle grade of the lower class [of lotuses] opens only after six kalpas;
yet, when compared to that region, this would correspond to merely six days.
How could it be possible for the day on which a middle-grade flower blooms to be later than the blooming of a lower-grade flower after six kalpas?
Furthermore, according to the *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Highest Grade*, it takes seven weeks for the lotus flower to open;
this is also slower than the forty-two kalpas required for rebirth in the middle grade of the lowest class.
By applying this principle through comparative analysis, one may infer the relative durations of the other grades.
Therefore, we know that those kalpas do not employ this method of kalpa.
A question is asked:
"Since it is said that the lotus flower only opens after a kalpa has passed," [how is this so?].
Is it because of the presence of karmic obstructions that the flowers bloom so late,
or is it due to superior merit?
Therefore, one remains within those flowers for many kalpas.
The commentary states:
This is based on the description of the lowest birth in the lowest grade.
Only after twelve great kalpas had passed did the lotus flower finally open.
Then Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, with voices of great compassion,
extensively expounded for them the true nature of all phenomena and the methods for extinguishing sinful karma.
By this one may infer that he also possesses karmic obstructions;
due to these karmic obstructions, it takes aeons for his flower to bloom.
Otherwise, for what reason would the nine grades of karmic actions differ,
such that the blooming of the flowers occurs at varying times with their respective degrees of difference?
Question: If those with karmic obstructions have their flowers bloom late due to such hindrances,
why do they not experience the retribution of suffering as a result of these same karmic obstacles?
The commentary states:
Although there are seeds of transgression,
because they have previously generated the bodhicitta in former lives, [they are purified].
By sincerely reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha, all transgressions are extinguished;
even if there remain subtle seeds of karma,
they cannot act as the ripening cause to draw forth the fruit of suffering.
It is solely because the seeds of their karma are extremely weak that one knows the merit of recollecting the Buddha diminishes their power; furthermore,
it is by the power of the merit of recollecting the Buddha [that this occurs].
One attains a sublime body in the Pure Land,
upon which the fruits of suffering have no means of arising.
Furthermore, by the power of the Buddha’s original vow,
[the lotus] cannot open; there remains only a residual obstruction hindering the lotus so that it cannot quickly unfold.
Thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"It is because of doubting that Buddha’s inconceivable wisdom that one is born into that womb-palace."
There is no manifold suffering;
it is simply that for five hundred years one remains confined within the womb.
This case is also like this.
The obstructing flower has bloomed.
Although there is no suffering within the flower once it has bloomed,
these seeds of transgression possess only the power to obstruct the flowering of that flower.
There is no merit that invites a painful retribution;
it is just as the ripening fruit (niṣyanda-phala) of the karma of killing can obstruct the reward of long life among humans and devas.
Question: The *Amitābha Sūtra* states that those of the lowest of the low grade attain rebirth by reciting the Buddha’s name ten times.
In every thought-moment, one extinguishes the sins of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death.
Since the sins have already been extinguished,
for what reason does Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva preach the Dharma for eliminating sins— the Dharma of True Reality— after the flowers have opened?
If there are transgressions that can be eliminated,
for what reason would they not obstruct birth in the Pure Land,
such that one is able to attain rebirth there?
The commentary states:
Because there remains a subtle obstacle that has not yet been exhausted,
the Sūtra speaks of its removal.
However, although their karmic obstacles are slight and inferior, their goodness in recollecting the Buddha is powerful;
by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they are not prevented from being born in the Pure Land,
even though those sinners have committed many grave offenses.
The power of karma can cause one to be reborn in the evil realms and suffer without end; yet,
by virtue of the roots of goodness derived from the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha, [one may be liberated].
The power of those heavy misfortunes that would have resulted in karmic fruition is extinguished,
such that they can no longer draw one toward rebirth in the evil realms;
however, the coarse and subtle obstacles remain within the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Therefore, after the flower has blossomed, upon encountering those two Honored Ones who explain the profound reality-mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena,
that person is finally able to contemplate the Buddha of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Only then can the subtle objects and wisdom begin to eliminate the functional power of the seeds of subtle karmic obstructions and transgressions.
Therefore, it is said that explaining the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena serves to eliminate and extinguish transgressions. Question:
For what reason are there forty-eight great vows in the first fascicle of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*?
It is said that even those with as few as ten recitations shall attain rebirth, with the sole exception of those who have committed the five heinous crimes.
Yet, the lower fascicle of the *Śūramgama-sūtra* states that even those with a single recitation shall attain rebirth.
What is the reason for this, given that both belong to the same teaching?
The preceding and succeeding passages state "one" and "ten," respectively,
thus creating a distinction.
The commentary explains:
There is no difference here.
Although the phrasing differs, the meaning is fundamentally the same.
Within the vows, this extends even to ten recitations.
This refers to proceeding from the few to the many;
the subsequent mention of "even down to a single thought-moment" refers to proceeding from the many to the few.
These points are presented alternately and do not inherently contradict one another;
the Bhikṣu Dharmākara proceeded from the few to the many.
And they made this vow:
"For those who are at the point of death,
we shall only suddenly encounter superior conditions to urge them to recite the Buddha's name for rebirth in the Pure Land."
Some may utter the name of the Buddha once and then pass away;
others may utter the name of the Buddha twice and immediately reach the end of their lives.
Or they may further attain [the name] three, four, five, six, or even seven, eight, ninety, or more times;
whether few or many, all shall be born in the Pure Land.
However, these people, from birth, did not commit the five heinous crimes nor did they slander the True Dharma.
No matter how many times one recollects [the Buddha], all shall attain rebirth there,
even those who have committed the five heinous crimes or slandered the true Dharma.
Suddenly encountering a superior condition, they were taught to recite the Buddha's name;
however, it was required that ten recitations be completed before rebirth could be attained.
If there were only one or nine recitations, they would consequently fail to go.
Therefore, it is said "up to ten recitations.
This excludes those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander the Dharma; this is an exclusion stated in terms of number.
This is not a case of ultimate eradication.
Those who have studied and recited this for a long time understand the meaning of these vows;
however, beginners who encounter them for the first time are often confused by their intent.
This constitutes a divergent interpretation that fails to accord with the essential path.
The Great Sage Śākyamuni foresaw that future generations would be deluded by this sacred scripture and would frivolously give rise to speculative investigations.
Therefore, it is said "even down to a single thought-moment.
This vow holds that if this teaching can be contemplated for many moments, those with grave offenses will all be reborn;
even if it is for but a single thought-moment, they shall likewise be reborn.
This immediately eliminates perverse slanders;
by explaining the teachings clearly through the mutual discourse of higher and lower levels,
it is intended to bring about awakening to the teaching in the future.
Question: It is not yet known that by recollecting the Buddha one can extinguish the heavy sins of eighty billion kalpas and attain rebirth in the Western Land.
Is it for the sake of extinguishing the seeds?
Or is it for the sake of extinguishing the manifest mind?
If it is for the sake of extinguishing the seeds...
The eradication of seeds requires the Noble Path;
only by realizing the emptiness of persons and phenomena can one extinguish these seeds.
Although the merits of the Buddha’s mindfulness are indeed boundless, [they cannot alone achieve this].
These are wholesome states of mind consisting of hearing, reflection,
and so forth; how can they be equivalent to the Noble Path in their ability to extinguish the seeds of sinful karma?
If the superior mind is extinguished,
the two karmas of sin and merit cannot arise simultaneously;
when the karma of sin arises, one cannot recite the Buddha's name.
When practicing mindfulness of the Buddha, one must not commit transgressions.
Good and evil do not coexist;
there can be no two superior states of mind at once.
How can the recitation of the Buddha's name extinguish offenses committed with a superior mind?
The explanation states:
it does not extinguish the seeds.
It does not mean that the superior mind is extinguished; rather, the transgression of the superior mind is extinguished of its own accord in a single instant,
without the necessity of recollecting the Buddha for it to be eliminated.
Furthermore, good and evil do not coexist;
at the time one recollects the Buddha, one's offenses have already been extinguished,
or they have not yet arisen.
When one is actually committing a transgression, the recollection of the Buddha has already ceased;
thus, the recollection of the Buddha cannot extinguish the transgression of that active mental state.
It can only extinguish the seeds—the functional capacity for the continuous succession of moments to evoke the evil retribution of the three miserable realms.
If one does not recollect the Buddha,
these seeds of transgression possess the power to bring about the retribution of rebirth in the evil realms as their future fruit.
By the power of mindfulness of the Buddha,
the capacity of those seeds to produce their respective fruits is weakened and rendered incapable of summoning retribution; therefore,
it is called the "extinction of sin."
Although seeds exist within the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and arise in succession,
they lack the power to produce retribution,
just like a person who is emaciated and ill.
Although the body remains upon the bed,
it lacks the capacity for movement or purposeful action;
sin is likewise.
Because there is no power capable of inducing the retribution of the evil destinies in the future,
it is called "cessation.
This refers to the cessation of the power of the seeds.
It is not the essence of the extinction of seeds; therefore,
among the six types of transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti),
it is called the transformation that weakens [the defilements] and strengthens [the capacity for goodness].
Question: This power of mindfulness of the Buddha can extinguish the capacity of the seeds to bring about their results;
however, it is not yet known whether the power of these seeds has already been extinguished.
If later one encounters adverse conditions,
can these seeds again gain the power to bring about retribution in the evil destinies?
The commentary states:
Existence is not abandoned either;
it is like the various bodhisattvas who cultivate wholesome dharmas to suppress and counteract the seeds of affliction.
Although its power has declined and it cannot manifest,
it later regains the strength to bring about actualization;
this is due to the power of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the manifest afflictions.
It causes the seeds of affliction to become more potent.
It is also like the two mindless attainments (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti* and *nirodha-samāpatti*), which cause the six consciousnesses to be averse [to arising] so that they do not manifest;
yet once one has emerged from those attainments, the mind is able to arise again.
It is the same with evil karma:
through the power of mindfulness of the Buddha and so forth,
it causes the seeds that would produce retribution to lose their functional capacity.
Subsequently retreating and failing to cultivate wholesome deeds,
one further creates unwholesome karma;
this also causes the capacity of past karma to produce its fruit to arise once more and continue in succession.
If, moreover, one subsequently encounters superior conditions for a long period,
unwholesome dharmas will gradually diminish and wholesome dharmas will gradually flourish.
One is able to enter the Noble Path, whereby the substance [of suffering] is ultimately extinguished.
A question is asked:
Since the seeds of evil karma are already [transformed] by means of mindfulness of the Buddha, [how can they be further extinguished?]
It eliminates the capacity within the seeds to induce rebirth in the evil destinies,
rendering them unable to bring about the fruits of the three lower realms;
yet it remains unknown how this compares to other virtues such as the recollection of the Buddha.
It possesses the functional capacity to summon rebirth in the pure lands of the happy realms;
even for one who has committed grave offenses,
it causes the seeds of wholesome karma from mindfulness of the Buddha to bring about the fruit of rebirth in a pure land.
Is its functional capacity extinguished?
The commentary states:
By virtue of the principle that the good is the opposite of the evil, this meaning should also apply here.
Just as a single thought of anger can obstruct hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates,
as the *Śāriputra-prokta-śāsana-sūtra* states:
"The harm of anger destroys all wholesome dharmas."
Furthermore, it is said:
"No thief of merit is greater than anger.
Thus we know that evil can also destroy the good.
It is not that the seeds of wholesome karma or their capacity to produce results are extinguished;
rather, one should know that wholesome and unwholesome states are mutually contradictory and thus cancel each other out.
For example, if one cultivates wholesome deeds in a single lifetime, this can lead to rebirth in a fortunate realm.
As death approaches, one loses mindfulness and gives rise to various evil karmas,
which ultimately extinguish all the wholesome qualities cultivated throughout one's life;
falling into these subsequent evils, one immediately descends into the three miserable realms.
Suppose there is one who, from birth, has been possessed of all manner of unwholesome deeds— the five heinous crimes and the ten evil acts—
leaving no sin uncommitted;
yet, at the moment of death, they recite the Buddha’s name ten times with full devotion.
By this one may extinguish all grave offenses and attain birth in a pure land; by this standard,
one should observe practitioners until the day of their death.
You must apply your mind with diligence; do not give rise to evil thoughts that would cause you to lose all wholesome qualities.
Concentrate your mind on the Buddha and seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
The sutras contain this sincere teaching.
Is this not something one should believe?
A question is asked:
"Regarding those who now study the practice of the Pure Land,"
Having already practiced the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection,
we do not yet know what specific teachings this dharma contains;
currently, many among the clergy and laity in various regions have given rise to doubts and confusion.
I fear that there may be those who falsely practice the Buddha-dharma under the guise of the holy teachings,
thereby inducing the foolish and ignorant to greatly increase their slander.
I pray that you will set forth the ultimate teaching to eliminate this web of doubt.
The commentary states:
The Mahāyāna sūtras contain an immense number of passages concerning this samādhi;
for instance, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* mentions the buddhānusmṛti-samādhi in numerous locations.
The texts on this subject are extremely extensive;

they are explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara Sūtra*, the *Bhadrapāla Sūtra*, the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*, the *Avalokana Sūtra*, the *Dundubhisvara-rāja Sūtra*, the *Candragarbha-parivarta* of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, the *Daśacakra-kṣitigarbha Sūtra*, the *Vicāraṇa Sūtra*, the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā Sūtra*, the *Puṣpottara Sūtra*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, among others.
As the *Huashou jing* (Flower-Pinnacle Sūtra) is named the Samādhi of One Mark;
the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā* is named the Samādhi of One Practice;
and the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra* is named the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha.
The *Bhadrapāla-sūtra* refers to this as the "Samādhi of Contemplating All Buddhas Manifesting Before One.
The *Kusumaśekhara-sūtra* states:
"In this way, the bodhisattva [contemplates] the marks of the Tathāgata and the marks of the dharmadhātu."
One should constantly contemplate in this way and practice in this way,
never departing from these conditions.
At that time, the image of the Buddha appeared before him and preached the Dharma for him.
Mañjuśrī-prajñā said:
Facing the direction where the Buddha resides,
sit upright and turn toward him without grasping at his physical appearance;
fix the mind on a single Buddha and single-mindedly recite his name.
Moment after moment, there is no rest.
Within this very mindfulness, one is able to see the Buddhas of the three periods of time—past, present, and future. Why is this?
To contemplate the merit of a single Buddha as immeasurable and boundless is to find it no different from the merit of immeasurable Buddhas;
this is called the Samādhi of One Practice.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"If a person can, with a sincere heart, constantly practice the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*),
the Buddhas of the ten directions will always behold this person."
As if appearing before one's very eyes,
the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra* and the *Bhadrapāla-sūtra* most extensively clarify this buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*).
It cannot be fully described here.
I exhort all practitioners:
by searching through the sacred teachings, you shall come to know this for yourselves.
It is asked:
For those who practice and study the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance,
is this the sequential order of the path within the bodhisattva practices,
or is it practiced without such a sequence?
The commentary states:
This is precisely the sequence of the bodhisattva’s path of cultivation.
How is this known to be so?
As stated in the forty-fifth chapter of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra:
At that time, Mañjuśrī turned his gaze toward Sudhana like an elephant king.
He spoke these words:
"Excellent, excellent, noble son!"
One is thus able to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and seek out virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Such are the various praises [of this practice].
He briefly expounded the Dharma for him and immediately sent him to seek the bhikṣu Guṇamegha to request instruction in the bodhisattva practices.
As for that bhikṣu Guṇamegha:
He immediately instructed Sudhana in the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).
Thus we know that the primary spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is Mañjuśrī,
who observes the arousal of the bodhicitta.
The second spiritual friend, the bhikṣu Guṇamegha,
immediately taught him the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).
In this manner, they traveled successively through one hundred and ten cities.
Seeking spiritual friends,
each spiritual friend teaches one dharma-gate;
one mounts one dharma-gate.
Later, I obtained a Dharma-gate that entirely sets forth the sequence for the bodhisattva’s cultivation and study.
Thus, one knows that the arousal of the bodhicitta is the foremost of all practices.
This study of the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) follows the sequence of the myriad practices.

By this standard, one should know that the *nien-fo samādhi* is precisely the sequential order of cultivation for a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind on enlightenment (*prathamacittotpādika*).
Question: Regarding this *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, it is not yet known for whom it is attained—
whether by noble ones or ordinary persons, those who maintain the precepts or those who violate them.
The commentary states:
This samādhi is accessible to both the noble ones and ordinary beings, whether they maintain the precepts or violate them.
All of these can be studied.
As the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states:
"The bhikṣu Guṇamegha is none other than a holy person, a great bodhisattva."
One attains the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).
As stated in the *Bhadrapāla-sūtra*:
"If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās..."
One who maintains pure precepts and is fully endowed with all practices—
by this one may infer that such a person who upholds the precepts is precisely the one suited to cultivate the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha.
This refers to the manifestation of the Samādhi of the Purity of the Roots of Precepts;
for those who violate the precepts, it is difficult to achieve samādhi.
This is according to the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra*.
This Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha is the medicine for all sentient beings who have committed offenses and the protection for those who have violated the precepts.
If a person who has violated the precepts does not obtain this samādhi, [they cannot be saved].
What is meant by "protection"?
Furthermore, the subsequent sutra states:
"The Tathāgata now..."

For the sake of sentient beings in future ages who suffer from the five kinds of suffering— such as bhikṣus who violate the precepts, unwholesome and evil persons, and those who commit the five heinous crimes or slander—
I shall preach the method for eliminating their offenses for the sake of such individuals.
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, these foolish people will be without a protector and without a place of refuge.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, among the various sentient beings in the age of turbid evil, those who wish to eliminate their transgressions and faults [should do so by this means]."
One should even diligently practice the Buddha-contemplation samādhi.
Therefore, it is known that even those who have broken the precepts or committed the five heinous crimes can all learn and attain this samādhi.
Question: Among the three bodies (trikāya), which body is it that one perceives when seeing the Buddha through the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha?
The commentary states: Generally speaking, mindfulness of the Buddha involves recollecting all three bodies (trikāya),
thereby attaining the samādhi of signless mindfulness of the Buddha.
By recollecting the Dharma-body Buddha,
one attains the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha with signs; by recollecting the Reward-body and Transformation-body Buddhas, [one likewise attains it].

However, according to the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the *Bhadrapāla-sūtra*, the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sāgara-sūtra*, the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*, the *Dundubhisvararāja-sūtra*, the *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and others:
It extensively clarifies the contemplation of the Buddha’s form-body (rūpakāya),
which is termed the buddhānusmṛti-samādhi.
Furthermore, according to the first fascicle of the Bhadrapāla-sūtra:
Upon recollecting Amitābha Buddha,
once they have seen him,
Amitābha Buddha will extensively expound for them the true nature of all phenomena (dharmas).
This means that all phenomena are fundamentally indestructible,
and there is no destroyer.
This is because form is indestructible, and so on, up to consciousness, which is also indestructible.
In this way, up to not even thinking of that Tathāgata,
nor apprehending that Tathāgata;
having thus thought of the Tathāgata, he—
In this sequence, one attains the samādhi of emptiness.
Good son, this is called the samādhi of the right mindfulness of all Buddhas appearing before one’s eyes.

By this one may infer that the prior visualization of Amitābha Buddha’s form-body (*rūpakāya*) is precisely the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) of contemplating his reward and transformation bodies.
The subsequently attained emptiness samādhi is precisely the mindfulness of the Buddha through contemplation of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Furthermore, it is by means of this very principle that...
Those who practice contemplation proceed from the coarse to the subtle;
first, they perform the contemplation of the physical body.
Next is the contemplation of the Dharma-body;
this is the sequence for cultivation and study. Question:
Regarding the causes by which one attains the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*),
the realized spheres of experience differ for each individual.
Some may perceive the pure land (*śuddhakṣetra*) but fail to see the Buddha.
Some may see the Buddha but not the pure land;
some may see the pure land and see the Buddha;
and some may see both the Buddha and the land.
Furthermore, one sees the various karmic signs of sentient beings— the good and evil deeds performed throughout their entire lives—
all of which are clearly perceived within the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi).
As for these perceived signs, are they authentic or spurious?
Furthermore, how is this seen?
Please set forth its teaching.
The commentary states:
Among all those who practice the Path, there is no distinction between the monastic and the lay;
if one's cultivated practices are not performed in accordance with the Holy Teachings, one is not a disciple of the Buddha.

The commentary states:
As explained in the third fascicle of the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisāgara-sūtra*.
The Buddha rose from his seat and had the fourfold assembly behold the physical body of the Buddha.
Among the assembly of Śākyas, there was one who...
The five hundred Śākyas saw the Buddha’s physical body as being like a person covered in ashes.
Among the assembly of bhikṣus, one thousand people saw the Buddha’s physical body as being like a person smeared with red earth.
Among the assembly of upāsakas, there were sixteen who saw the Buddha’s physical body as being like the leg of a black elephant.
Among the assembly of upāsikās, twenty-four people perceived the Buddha’s physical body as being like a mass of ink.
Within the community of bhikṣuṇīs,
there was a bhikṣuṇī who beheld the physical body of the Buddha.
They were the color of white silver.
Among the assembly of upāsikās,
there was a certain upāsikā.
The fourfold assembly saw the Buddha’s form-body as being like the color of indigo dye.
Thus it was with the fourfold assembly.
When contemplating the Buddha’s form-body (rūpakāya), what is seen differs;
one cannot perceive the Buddha’s body of true golden color.
They confessed their transgressions and repented of all their sins,
prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground.
Like a great mountain collapsing,
he tore out his hair and threw his entire body to the ground.
She rolled over and struck herself;
blood flowed from her nose,
and her transgressions were extinguished.
The mind’s eye was opened,
and he beheld the Buddha’s physical body,
majestic and exquisitely subtle.
